descriptors.title: Repeating patterns
descriptors.description: recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns represented in different ways
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal experience noticing and creating patterns in play (e.g. arranging blocks in a sequence, singing songs with repetition). They have not yet formally identified or described the repeating unit in a pattern, or continued a pattern beyond what they can see.

nodes.label: Noticing repetition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that a pattern repeats and point to where the repetition occurs.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate 'pattern' with any arrangement cannot identify the repeating unit — the concept nodes 2 and 3 require. Without unit identification, copying becomes visual mimicry and continuing becomes guessing, not algebraic reasoning.
criteria: Student points to the part of a pattern that repeats and states that it repeats
Student identifies at least one pattern represented in two different ways (e.g. colours and shapes)

width.minimum: Identify one example of a repeating pattern using materials or shapes, and say 'it repeats'.
width.typical: Identify repeating patterns across materials, shapes, sounds and movements; point to the part that repeats and say what comes next.
wider: Identify repeating patterns in images generated by dynamic geometric software or a generative AI tool
Identify repeating patterns observed on Country/Place and in First Nations Australians' artwork and material cultures (e.g. shell and seed necklaces)

modes.reason: Students at Foundation often confuse a 'pattern' with any arrangement. Encountering repeating patterns across multiple sensory modalities (visual, auditory, movement) helps them isolate the defining feature — repetition of a unit — rather than pattern meaning 'colourful' or 'organised'. Breadth across representation types is what resolves this confusion.

nodes.label: Copying a pattern
nodes.checkpoint: Students can copy a repeating pattern using the same or different materials.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot accurately reproduce a repeating unit cannot continue one — node 3 depends on students holding the unit in mind precisely enough to project it forward. Inaccurate copying produces patterns with a defective unit, making continuation unreliable.
criteria: Student produces an accurate copy of a repeating pattern with at least two full repetitions of the unit
Student matches the order and type of elements in the original pattern

width.minimum: Copy one repeating pattern (e.g. red-blue-red-blue) using the same materials as the original.
width.typical: Copy repeating patterns using a range of materials, shapes, sounds and movements; copy patterns made with materials using a different medium (e.g. copy a bead pattern with stamps).
wider: Copy repeating patterns from First Nations Australians' artworks or cultural objects using art materials
Copy a movement or sound pattern (e.g. drumbeats or dance moves) and transfer it to a different medium (e.g. draw the sound pattern)

modes.reason: Accurate copying requires careful one-to-one attention to the repeating unit. Students commonly copy an incomplete unit or lose track mid-copy. Repeated practice with the same and different materials builds the precision needed before continuing patterns.

nodes.label: Continuing a pattern
nodes.checkpoint: Students can continue a repeating pattern by identifying what comes next.
criteria: Student correctly extends a pattern by at least two elements and explains what element comes next
Student can identify the repeating unit in the pattern they have continued

width.minimum: Continue a given repeating pattern by adding at least two more elements, explaining what comes next.
width.typical: Continue repeating patterns of two or more elements represented in different ways; describe what comes next and why; connect pattern continuation to familiar routines (e.g. setting a table, a repeated song).
wider: Continue and describe repeating patterns from First Nations Australians' cultural contexts (e.g. continuing a pattern from a dance, song or artwork)
Create an original repeating pattern and invite a partner to continue it — explaining the rule to check their partner's response
Continue patterns involving more than two alternating elements, describing the repeating unit

modes.reason: Continuing a pattern requires students to have identified the repeating unit, not just the surface feature. Patterns that look familiar (only two alternating colours) can be continued by guessing without understanding the unit. Broader contexts — sounds, movements, mixed-attribute patterns — require students to isolate and apply the repeating rule rather than pattern-match by surface similarity.

This node integrates recognising (node 1) and copying (node 2) into productive use — students must hold the repeating unit in mind and project it forward. The coordination of noticing and reproducing is the key learning here.

descriptors.title: Measurement attributes
descriptors.description: identify and compare attributes of objects and events, including length, capacity, mass and duration, using direct comparisons and communicating reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal experience with size and weight in play and daily life (e.g. 'this is big', 'that's heavy'). They have not yet systematically distinguished between different measurement attributes or used direct comparison with explicit reasoning.

nodes.label: Naming measurement attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and distinguish between the four measurement attributes — length, capacity, mass and duration — and connect each to the correct measurement language.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate measurement attributes will compare the wrong attribute in node 2 — measuring length when asked about mass, or using mass language for capacity comparisons. Attribute confusion produces confidently incorrect comparisons and undermines the reasoning communication demanded in node 3.
criteria: Student correctly names at least three of the four measurement attributes when shown an example of each
Student uses at least one appropriate comparative word for each attribute named (e.g. longer, heavier, holds more, takes longer)

width.minimum: Name two of the four measurement attributes and use at least one correct word for each (e.g. 'long/short' for length, 'heavy/light' for mass).
width.typical: Name all four measurement attributes and use appropriate language for each (tall/short/long/wide for length; holds more/less for capacity; heavier/lighter for mass; takes longer/shorter for duration); connect measurement words to familiar everyday objects and events.
wider: Investigate objects that have interesting or surprising combinations of attributes (e.g. something tall that is also light) — discussing which attribute you are describing
Connect measurement language to familiar contexts on Country/Place (e.g. comparing lengths of natural objects, duration of familiar activities)

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate measurement attributes — particularly confusing length with size in general, or mass with size. Encountering each attribute named correctly across many different familiar objects (not just one canonical example) helps students build distinct categories for each attribute rather than using size as a catch-all term.

nodes.label: Direct comparison of a single attribute
nodes.checkpoint: Students can directly compare two objects or events on a single measurement attribute and state which has more or less of that attribute.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 demands that students communicate reasoning about comparisons — but that reasoning can only be articulated if the comparison itself was performed correctly and on the right attribute. Students who habitually compare the wrong attribute, or who lack physical comparison technique, cannot produce valid reasoning at node 3.
criteria: Student performs a direct comparison using an appropriate strategy for the attribute (e.g. lines up objects for length, hefts for mass)
Student states which object has more or less of the attribute and demonstrates or explains how they know

width.minimum: Directly compare two objects on one attribute (length or mass), state which has more of that attribute, and demonstrate or explain how they know.
width.typical: Directly compare pairs of objects on each of the four measurement attributes; use direct comparison strategies (lining up bases for length, hefting for mass, filling for capacity, starting at the same time for duration); justify comparisons using attribute language.
wider: Compare the same pair of objects on two different attributes (e.g. which is longer AND which is heavier) and discuss how different attributes give different information about the same object
Compare objects from the kitchen pantry, classroom or natural environment — including objects found on Country/Place — on a chosen attribute, communicating reasoning

modes.reason: A common error is comparing the wrong attribute — e.g. comparing the colour or general size of an object rather than the specified attribute. Comparing across many pairs of objects, with the attribute named explicitly, helps students focus on the attribute rather than a general sense of 'bigger'. Different attribute types (length vs mass vs capacity) all require this focus shift.

Direct comparison requires physical manipulation and careful alignment or measurement technique (e.g. lining up bases). Students need repeated practice with the physical comparison process before they can reliably demonstrate reasoning.

nodes.label: Communicating reasoning about comparisons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare objects or events on a chosen measurement attribute and communicate their reasoning using attribute-specific language.
criteria: Student compares two objects or events on a specified attribute and correctly states which has more of that attribute
Student communicates at least one reason for their comparison using attribute-specific language

width.minimum: Compare two objects on a measurement attribute, state the result, and give at least one reason for the comparison (e.g. 'I put them next to each other and this one sticks out further').
width.typical: Compare objects and events across all four measurement attributes; explain or demonstrate how they know which has more or less of the attribute; use appropriate measurement language to communicate reasoning in familiar contexts.
wider: Compare objects found in everyday home or community contexts (including objects on Country/Place) on a self-chosen attribute, communicating reasoning to a partner
Investigate and discuss situations where direct comparison is tricky (e.g. comparing the mass of a large light object with a small heavy object) and reason about what the comparison shows
Compare the duration of two familiar events by starting them at the same time, describe which took longer and explain why duration comparison requires a shared start point

modes.reason: Communicating reasoning about measurement comparisons requires students to articulate not just the result but the method — how did they know? The reasoning scaffold (what did you do? what did you find out? how do you know?) is the specific thinking move Foundation students need to develop. Simply naming the result without method is a very common truncation.

This node integrates attribute naming (node 1) and direct comparison technique (node 2) into coherent communication — students must coordinate knowing the attribute, applying the comparison method, and explaining the result. The coordination of these three moves is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Days and times of day
descriptors.description: sequence days of the week and times of the day including morning, lunchtime, afternoon and night time, and connect them to familiar events and actions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal awareness of daily routines and some days of the week from home and pre-school contexts. They have not yet formally sequenced the days of the week in order or connected times of day consistently to named categories.

nodes.label: Times of day
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the four times of day (morning, lunchtime, afternoon, night time) and connect each to at least one familiar event.
criteria: Student correctly names at least three times of day
Student connects at least one familiar event to each time of day named

width.minimum: Name at least three of the four times of day and match each to one familiar event (e.g. morning → getting dressed, night time → going to bed).
width.typical: Name all four times of day; connect multiple familiar school and home events to the correct time of day; order images of daily events on a timeline, justifying placement by time of day.
wider: Order events from a story in the sequence they occurred, using times-of-day language to justify placement
Investigate and compare how different families or communities might spend the same time of day — connecting times of day to diverse lived experiences

nodes.label: Sequencing days of the week
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and sequence the days of the week in order, and recognise that the sequence repeats.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to locate specific events on specific days — which depends on automatic recall of the day sequence. Students who cannot reliably sequence the days cannot connect events to days or use temporal language (yesterday, tomorrow) accurately.
criteria: Student sequences all seven days of the week in correct order
Student correctly identifies today, yesterday and tomorrow on at least three occasions

width.minimum: Recite or sequence the days of the week in order from Monday to Sunday.
width.typical: Name and sequence all seven days of the week in order; identify today, yesterday and tomorrow; distinguish school days from weekend days; recognise that the days repeat in a cycle.
wider: Use a classroom roster or weekly schedule to identify which day specific events occur — connecting the sequence to real school-week planning
Create a pictorial weekly diary showing events on each day, reading it back to describe what happened on which day

modes.reason: Sequencing seven items in a fixed order requires rote fluency. Students need repeated practice reciting and ordering the days before they can reliably use the sequence to reason about yesterday, today and tomorrow. Practice and repetition (songs, daily routines, calendar activities) build the automaticity the descriptor assumes.

nodes.label: Connecting events to days and times
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect familiar events and actions to specific days of the week and times of day, using temporal language to describe and justify sequences.
criteria: Student connects at least three familiar events to the correct day or time of day and justifies at least one placement using temporal language
Student correctly uses at least two temporal words (before, after, yesterday, today, tomorrow, next) in context

width.minimum: Connect at least three familiar events to the correct day and time of day, and use at least one temporal word (before, after, yesterday, tomorrow) to describe the sequence.
width.typical: Connect familiar school and home events to specific days and times of day; use temporal language (before, after, next, yesterday, today, tomorrow) to describe and justify sequences; create or interpret a pictorial weekly diary or roster.
wider: Create and interpret a classroom roster connecting tasks to specific days, and answer questions like 'Who watered the garden yesterday?' or 'Whose turn is it today?'
Explore how different families and communities organise their week — including cultural or community events on specific days — and connect these to the days-and-times framework
Investigate events that happen at the same time each day (routines) and events that happen on the same day each week, distinguishing daily from weekly patterns

modes.reason: Connecting events to days and times requires students to use temporal language as a reasoning tool — not just label an event, but justify why it goes where it does ('It happens in the morning because we do it when we arrive at school'). The reasoning scaffold distinguishes this node from simple recall.

This node integrates times of day (node 1) and day sequence (node 2) into a unified temporal framework. Students must coordinate knowledge of the daily cycle and the weekly cycle to place events correctly — this coordination is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Numbers to 20
descriptors.description: name, represent and order numbers including zero to at least 20, using physical and virtual materials and numerals
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal number experience from pre-school and home contexts — counting objects in play, hearing number words in songs and stories. They have not yet formally connected number names, numerals and quantities in a consistent ordered sequence to 20.

nodes.label: Number names and numerals to 10
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name numbers to 10 and match number names to numerals and to quantities.
nodes.hinge_reason: Name–numeral–quantity correspondence to 10 is the foundation for extending to 20 (node 2) and ordering (node 3). Students with incomplete correspondence at 0–10 cannot reliably read teen numerals or place numbers on a number track — gaps here produce systematic errors across all subsequent number work.
criteria: Student reads and names numerals 0 to 10 in and out of order
Student matches each numeral 0 to 10 to a collection of the correct number of objects

width.minimum: Match spoken number names to the correct numeral and to a collection of objects for numbers 1 to 10.
width.typical: Name, read and write numerals 0 to 10; match each numeral to a quantity; recognise numerals in familiar contexts (books, labels, number tracks); connect number names to quantities in counting songs and stories.
wider: Explore numbers 0 to 10 across multiple representations (numeral, dot pattern, fingers, ten-frame) and connect between representations
Connect quantities to number names and numerals through First Nations Australians' counting contexts — e.g. Segur etug from Mer Island in the Torres Strait region

modes.reason: Number–numeral correspondence requires repeated exposure and practice. Students commonly know some number names from songs without connecting them reliably to numerals or quantities. Repeated practice connecting the three forms (name, numeral, quantity) is the primary support need here — breadth alone does not resolve incomplete correspondence.

nodes.label: Extending numbers to 20
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name, read and represent numbers from 11 to 20, recognising the pattern in the sequence.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to order all numbers 0–20 and use ordinal language — both depend on reliable numeral recognition across the full range. Students who confuse teen numerals (e.g. 14 vs 40, or 13 vs 30) cannot place numbers in correct sequence, making ordering unreliable.
criteria: Student reads numerals 11 to 20 correctly
Student correctly identifies one more and one less for numbers to 20 on at least three occasions

width.minimum: Name and match numerals to quantities for numbers 11 to 20.
width.typical: Name, read and write numerals 0 to 20; recognise the order in the number sequence to 20; connect teen number names to their quantities; identify one more and one less for numbers to 20.
wider: Investigate the pattern in teen number names (thirteen, fourteen... nineteen) and discuss how the number sequence is structured
Use instructive card games involving reading and ordering number cards to 20 — including numbers placed out of order to practise ordering
Explore how counting beyond 20 continues the pattern, making predictions about numbers in the twenties

modes.reason: Teen numbers are a common site of confusion — number names like 'fourteen' do not transparently communicate '4 more than 10' in English. Encountering teen numbers across many representations (number lines, tens frames, spoken sequences, written numerals) helps students build reliable connections rather than relying on rote recitation alone.

nodes.label: Ordering numbers and using ordinal language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can order numbers 0 to 20 from smallest to largest and use ordinal language to describe positions in a sequence.
criteria: Student places numbers 0 to 20 in correct order with no more than one error
Student correctly uses ordinal terms (first, second, third, last) to describe positions in a familiar sequence

width.minimum: Place at least five numbers (0 to 20) in correct order on a number track or line; use 'first' and 'last' to describe positions.
width.typical: Order all numbers 0 to 20; describe positions using ordinal terms (first, second, third... fifth... last); connect ordinal language to positions in familiar sequences (e.g. line-ups, races, card games); read and write numerals as labels for ordinal positions.
wider: Use a number track with cards 0 to 20 to explore 'before', 'after' and 'between' relationships — asking and answering positional questions
Connect ordinal language to First Nations Australians' counting and ordering contexts
Extend ordering beyond 20 — predicting where numbers like 25 or 30 would sit on a number line and justifying the placement

modes.reason: Ordering numbers integrates name–numeral knowledge (nodes 1 and 2) with understanding of the number sequence. Students must coordinate numeral recognition and sequence knowledge to place numbers correctly. Ordinal language adds a second layer — position in the sequence — that must be connected to the same framework.

descriptors.title: Subitising to 5
descriptors.description: recognise and name the number of objects within a collection up to 5 using subitising
descriptors.knowledge: Students can count small collections of objects using one-to-one correspondence. They have not yet recognised quantities instantly without counting — subitising as a deliberate strategy is new.

nodes.label: Instant recognition to 3
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and name collections of 1, 2 and 3 objects instantly, without counting.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable instant recognition of 1–3 is the perceptual base for extending subitising to 4 and 5 in node 2. Students who count rather than subitise for 1–3 do not develop the perceptual number sense needed to see 4 as '3 and 1 more' or 5 as '3 and 2' — structured subitising at node 2 depends on fluency at this node.
criteria: Student names a collection of 1, 2 or 3 objects immediately (without counting) on at least three consecutive occasions
Student can distinguish a subitised response from a counted response ('I just knew' vs 'I counted')

width.minimum: Recognise collections of 1, 2 and 3 objects instantly in standard arrangements (e.g. dot cards, dice) and name the quantity without counting.
width.typical: Recognise and name collections of 1, 2 and 3 in a range of arrangements (different dot card layouts, small groups of objects); use subitising to identify quantities in quick-look games.
wider: Recognise collections of 1, 2 and 3 in non-standard arrangements and in familiar objects (e.g. 3 buttons on a shirt, 2 eyes)
Compare two collections of 1–3 objects using subitising — stating which has more without counting

modes.reason: Instant recognition requires fluency built through repeated exposure to quick-look activities. Students need practice with many examples across arrangements to build reliable perceptual number sense for 1–3 before extending to 4 and 5.

nodes.label: Extending subitising to 5
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and name collections of 4 and 5 objects using subitising.
criteria: Student correctly names collections of 4 and 5 objects without counting, across at least two different arrangements
Student uses subitising in a quick-look game context, naming quantities up to 5 immediately

width.minimum: Recognise collections of 4 and 5 objects instantly in standard arrangements (e.g. dice patterns, dot cards) and name the quantity without counting.
width.typical: Recognise and name collections up to 5 using subitising across a range of arrangements; use subitising to play card games requiring quick recognition of quantities; compare and order collections up to 5 using subitising.
wider: Use subitising to play instructive card games (e.g. memory games with dot cards in different arrangements) — connecting subitising to game contexts
Investigate structured subitising for 4 and 5 as part-part combinations (e.g. 5 as 4+1, 3+2) — beginning to connect subitising to part-part-whole thinking
Explore subitising in everyday contexts — dice, dominoes, tally marks — describing the strategy used

modes.reason: Students commonly subitise familiar standard arrangements (dice patterns) but revert to counting for unfamiliar arrangements of 4 and 5. Encountering 4 and 5 in varied spatial arrangements — not just canonical dice patterns — builds flexible perceptual recognition rather than pattern memorisation.

descriptors.title: Quantifying and comparing collections
descriptors.description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal counting experience and can name numbers. They are developing reliable one-to-one correspondence. They have not yet systematically applied counting principles (each object counted once, arrangement does not affect quantity, last number = total) or used counting to compare and justify.

nodes.label: Counting principles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can count a collection of objects accurately, demonstrating that each object is counted once, arrangement does not affect quantity, and the last number counted tells how many.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 depend on accurate counting. Students who misapply counting principles — skipping objects, double-counting, or believing arrangement changes quantity — produce wrong counts, making purposeful counting and comparison unreliable. Both the conservation misconception and procedural tracking errors cascade through all downstream counting tasks.
criteria: Student accurately counts a collection of 10–20 objects in a scattered arrangement with no double-counting or skipping
Student states the total correctly when asked 'How many?' after counting
Student demonstrates (without recounting) that rearranging a counted set does not change the total

width.minimum: Count a collection of up to 10 objects in a fixed arrangement accurately, demonstrating one-to-one correspondence; state the total when asked 'How many?'
width.typical: Count collections of objects to at least 20 in varying arrangements; demonstrate that rearranging objects does not change how many there are; apply counting principles across different types of objects and counting contexts (physical, virtual, moving objects).
wider: Use body-tallying systems from First Nations Peoples of Australia that use body parts and one-to-one correspondence to count to 20
Compare how different cultural tools (e.g. an abacus, Chinese hand gestures) represent the counting process — connecting to the universal counting principles

modes.reason: Students commonly misapply counting principles in specific situations — they may count correctly in a line but miscount scattered objects, or not understand that rearranging a counted set doesn't change the total. Encountering collections in varied arrangements resolves the conservation misconception more effectively than repeated practice with a single arrangement type.

One-to-one correspondence with physical objects requires procedural care — students commonly double-count or skip objects. Repeated counting practice across many collections builds the tracking precision needed before comparison tasks.

nodes.label: Counting for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use counting to determine a quantity needed for a practical purpose, applying one-to-one correspondence.
criteria: Student uses counting to determine the correct number of items needed for a group and collects that quantity
Student explains why their count gives the right answer (connecting count to purpose)

width.minimum: Count the members of a group and use that count to collect the right number of items for the group.
width.typical: Use counting and one-to-one correspondence to quantify items required for a practical purpose (e.g. collecting one item per person, setting a table, distributing materials); explain reasoning about why the count gives the right number.
wider: Investigate quantifying situations that involve multiple sets (e.g. collecting two items for each person) and use counting to determine the total needed
Explore First Nations Australians' counting contexts where quantity serves a practical purpose — e.g. gathering enough for a group

nodes.label: Comparing collections using counting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the size of two or more collections using counting and justify which has more or fewer.
criteria: Student counts two collections of up to 20 objects accurately and correctly states which has more
Student explains reasoning — naming the counts of both collections and using them to justify the comparison

width.minimum: Count two collections and compare them, stating which has more and how they know.
width.typical: Count and compare collections of up to 20 objects; justify which collection has more or fewer using the count; apply comparison to practical situations (e.g. 'Do we have enough scissors for everyone?').
wider: Compare three or more collections, ordering them from fewest to most and justifying the order with counts
Investigate comparison situations where counting is needed because subitising is not reliable (collections greater than 5) — connecting comparison strategy to quantity size
Explore how different cultures represent and compare quantities — connecting to the universality of counting as a comparison tool

modes.reason: Students commonly compare collections by visual impression (which pile looks bigger) rather than counting. The reasoning scaffold here is: count each collection, then compare the counts. Getting students to explicitly articulate this two-step process — count first, then compare — is the key teaching move at this node.

Comparison integrates counting principles (node 1) and purposeful counting (node 2) into a reasoning task. Students must count accurately AND use the counts to draw a justified conclusion about relative size. This coordination is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Part-Part-Whole to 10
descriptors.description: partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships and subitising to recognise and name the parts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can count collections to at least 20 (AC9MFN03) and subitise collections to 5 (AC9MFN02). They have not yet systematically split a collection into two named parts and used part-part-whole language to describe the relationship.

nodes.label: Recognising parts within a whole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can look at a structured representation of a number up to 10 and identify and name two parts that make the whole.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (partitioning in different ways) requires students to hold the whole in mind while varying the parts — which depends on first being able to see and name a part-part structure at all. Students who attend only to 'how many' cannot partition flexibly or combine in node 3.
criteria: Student identifies two parts within a structured representation (e.g. ten-frame, domino) for at least three different numbers up to 10
Student describes the part-part-whole relationship using appropriate language

width.minimum: Identify and name two parts in a ten-frame or domino arrangement of a number up to 10 (e.g. '7 — I can see 5 and 2 more').
width.typical: Recognise numbers represented in physical or virtual ten-frames, dominoes and dot cards; identify two parts within the arrangement; describe the part-part-whole relationship using language ('___ is ___ and ___ more').
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' number groupings and different ways of representing these groupings to form and partition numbers — connecting cultural representations to part-part-whole thinking
Use subitising to identify parts within standard number configurations (dice, dominoes) without counting individual dots

modes.reason: Students commonly describe 'how many' without attending to the internal structure of the number. Structured representations (ten-frames, dominoes) across several numbers make the part-part structure visible, but students need to encounter the same number in multiple structured arrangements to see that the parts can differ while the whole stays the same.

nodes.label: Partitioning a collection in different ways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a collection of up to 10 objects into two parts in more than one way, naming both parts and the whole each time.
criteria: Student partitions a collection of up to 10 objects into at least two different pairs of parts
Student names both parts and the whole for each partition using part-part-whole language

width.minimum: Partition a collection of 6 objects into two parts in at least two different ways, naming both parts and the whole each time.
width.typical: Partition collections of up to 10 objects in multiple ways using physical or virtual materials; name each part-part-whole relationship; demonstrate that the same whole can be partitioned into different pairs of parts.
wider: Investigate all the ways to partition a number to 10 systematically, recording part-part pairs and looking for patterns
Explore partitioning in First Nations Australians' counting and grouping systems — applying this to quantities of objects in the environment on Country/Place

modes.reason: A key misconception is that a number has only one partition (often the canonical split students see first, e.g. 5 as 4+1). Seeing a collection partitioned multiple ways — into different part pairs — is what builds the flexible part-part-whole thinking the descriptor requires. Breadth of examples is the resolution.

nodes.label: Combining parts to make a whole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine two given parts to name the whole, using subitising or counting to verify.
criteria: Student correctly names the whole when given two parts (total up to 10), using subitising or counting to verify
Student moves flexibly between partitioning and combining for the same number (e.g. can both split 8 into parts and combine given parts to name 8)

width.minimum: Given two groups of objects (total up to 10), name the whole by combining the parts — using subitising or counting to verify.
width.typical: Combine two parts to name the whole across a range of part-part combinations to 10; represent part-part-whole relationships using physical or virtual materials, dominoes and standard number configurations; use both partitioning (whole to parts) and combining (parts to whole) flexibly.
wider: Represent the same part-part-whole relationship in multiple ways (objects, drawings, numerals) and connect between representations
Connect part-part-whole thinking to familiar real-world situations — e.g. sharing items into two groups and recombining them
Explore part-part-whole relationships using structured tools (rekenreks, ten-frames) to compare which representations make which combinations easiest to see

modes.reason: Combining integrates part recognition (node 1) and flexible partitioning (node 2) into bidirectional thinking — students move fluently between 'what are the parts?' and 'what is the whole?'. The coordination of both directions is the endpoint demand and the foundation for additive reasoning in Year 1.

descriptors.title: Addition and subtraction situations
descriptors.description: represent practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can quantify and compare collections using counting (AC9MFN03) and use part-part-whole reasoning to partition and combine collections to 10 (AC9MFN04). They have not yet represented joining and separating situations as mathematical relationships using materials or drawings.

nodes.label: Representing additive situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical addition or subtraction situation using materials or drawings, showing what is happening in the story.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to use counting or subitising on a representation to find a result — but if the representation shows only the final state (not the action), there is nothing for the strategy to operate on. Students who represent endpoint-only cannot use their representation to solve the problem or communicate the mathematical situation in node 3.
criteria: Student represents an addition or subtraction situation with materials or drawings that show both the starting state and the action (joining or separating)
Student can describe what their representation shows in relation to the story

width.minimum: Use materials or a drawing to represent one addition or subtraction story situation (e.g. objects joining a group, or objects leaving a group).
width.typical: Represent a range of practical addition and subtraction situations using materials or drawings; connect representations to oral story contexts; show the action (joining, separating) in the representation as well as the result.
wider: Represent additive situations from First Nations Australians' stories (e.g. 'Tiddalick the Greedy Frog') and leaf games from the Warlpiri Peoples of Yuendumu — describing the mathematical relationship
Compare addition and subtraction situations side-by-side, identifying what is the same (a change in quantity) and what is different (joining vs separating)

modes.reason: Students commonly represent only the final state (the answer), not the additive action. Encountering addition and subtraction situations through varied stories and contexts — particularly those requiring active role-play — makes the joining and separating actions visible in the representation. Varied contexts resolve the tendency to show just the endpoint.

nodes.label: Finding results using counting or subitising
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use counting or subitising to find the result of a represented addition or subtraction situation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to represent and solve quantification situations across varied context types — which depends on reliably applying a counting or subitising strategy. Students who lose track mid-count cannot solve varied situation types or connect mathematical representations to real-world contexts.
criteria: Student finds the result of an addition or subtraction situation using counting or subitising and records it with a numeral
Student selects an appropriate strategy (counting all, counting on, subitising) for the quantities involved

width.minimum: Represent an addition or subtraction situation and use counting to find and state the result.
width.typical: Use counting or subitising strategies to find results of addition and subtraction situations; record the result with a numeral; apply strategies across a range of practical story contexts including simple quantity comparisons.
wider: Role-play simple money transactions using $1 coins — representing the situation, counting coins to find the result, and connecting the count to the transaction context
Compare counting-on as a strategy (starting from the larger group) with counting-all — discussing which is more efficient for different quantity sizes

modes.reason: Reliable use of counting strategies requires fluency in one-to-one counting under the pressure of a story context. Students commonly lose track when objects are added to or removed from a group mid-count. Repeated practice across varied situations builds the procedural reliability needed.

nodes.label: Representing quantification contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent and solve practical quantification situations (comparing, enough for a group, simple transactions) using materials and counting.
criteria: Student correctly represents and solves an addition, subtraction or quantification situation using materials and counting or subitising
Student connects their mathematical representation to the real-world context (can explain what the materials or drawing shows)

width.minimum: Represent and solve one quantification situation (e.g. 'do we have enough for everyone?') using materials and counting.
width.typical: Represent and solve practical situations involving addition, subtraction and quantification across a range of everyday contexts; connect mathematical representations to the real-world situation; use counting or subitising strategies to find results across all situation types.
wider: Represent and solve additive situations from First Nations Australians' instructive games (e.g. leaf games from Warlpiri Peoples) — connecting mathematical structure to cultural context
Create own story situations that involve addition or subtraction and represent them for a partner to solve
Investigate how the same additive structure (joining, separating, comparing) can appear in very different story contexts — connecting mathematical sameness across varied stories

modes.reason: Quantification situations (enough for a group, comparing, transactions) require students to identify the additive structure of a real-world problem, represent it, and solve it — integrating nodes 1 and 2 in a purposeful context. The integration of representation and strategy selection across varied situation types is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Equal sharing and grouping
descriptors.description: represent practical situations that involve equal sharing and grouping with physical and virtual materials and use counting or subitising strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can quantify collections using counting and have experience with part-part-whole relationships to 10 (AC9MFN04). They have not yet applied the idea of equal groups — sharing so that each person gets the same amount, or forming groups of the same size.

nodes.label: The idea of equal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when a sharing situation is equal and when it is not, and explain what needs to happen to make it equal.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both require students to verify equality of groups — which depends on understanding that equal means same-amount-each, not just distributed. Students who conflate shared with equal cannot confirm their distributions are valid or detect when grouping has produced unequal groups.
criteria: Student distributes a collection into equal groups and confirms each group has the same amount using counting or subitising
Student identifies an unequal distribution and adjusts it to make groups equal

width.minimum: Distribute a small collection of objects between two groups and state whether the groups are equal, adjusting if they are not.
width.typical: Identify and create equal and unequal distributions; explain what makes sharing equal ('everyone has the same amount'); compare two groups using counting or subitising to check for equality.
wider: Explore equal sharing in familiar everyday contexts (fruit at snack time, cards dealt in a game) and discuss what equality means in each context
Investigate situations where objects cannot be shared equally (leftovers) — discussing what happens to the remainder at Foundation level

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate 'shared' with 'equal' — just distributing objects satisfies sharing in their view. Encountering varied sharing situations where equality is verified by checking each group helps students develop the precision of equal as same-amount-each.

nodes.label: Representing equal sharing situations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical equal sharing situation using materials and find how many each person receives using counting or subitising.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (grouping contexts) requires students to form equal groups systematically — the same systematic allocation process as sharing. Students who cannot reliably execute the one-at-a-time distribution strategy cannot form equal groups of a specified size.
criteria: Student distributes a collection of up to 10 objects equally between 2–3 people using a systematic strategy
Student counts or subitises each group to confirm equal distribution and states how many each person received

width.minimum: Represent a sharing situation using materials (distribute a collection of up to 10 between 2 or 3 people) and count each group to find how many each person receives.
width.typical: Represent equal sharing situations across a range of practical contexts (fruit, cards, coins, beads); distribute collections of up to 10 objects between 2–4 people; use counting or subitising to determine the size of each equal group; confirm equality by comparing groups.
wider: Explore instructive games of First Nations Australians involving equal sharing — e.g. Yangamini of the Tiwi Peoples of Bathurst Island — investigating what makes sharing equal in a game context
Represent equal sharing using virtual materials or digital tools, comparing the process with physical sharing

modes.reason: The distribution process (one for you, one for me, one for you...) requires systematic allocation and tracking. Students commonly lose track or distribute unevenly. Repeated practice with the one-at-a-time distribution strategy builds the procedural fluency needed.

nodes.label: Grouping contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical grouping situation using materials, forming equal groups and counting or subitising to find the number in each group.
criteria: Student forms equal groups from a collection using materials and verifies equality by counting or subitising
Student can describe a grouping situation — naming the total, the group size, and the number of groups formed

width.minimum: Form equal groups from a collection (e.g. put 6 objects into groups of 2) and count to verify the groups are equal.
width.typical: Represent equal grouping situations using materials; connect grouping to sharing as two forms of the equal-groups idea; use counting or subitising to find the number of groups or the number in each group; apply across varied practical contexts.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' games that involve grouping or sharing, connecting the mathematical structure to cultural practice

Compare sharing (how many each) and grouping (how many groups) as different questions about the same situation — e.g. 'If I share 9 beads into groups of 3, how many groups do I get?' vs 'If I share 9 beads among 3 people, how many does each person get?'
Investigate what happens with collections that cannot be grouped evenly — identifying and counting the remainder

modes.reason: Students at Foundation see sharing and grouping as very different activities. Connecting them as two aspects of the equal-groups idea — through varied contexts where both questions arise — is the conceptual work that prepares students for multiplicative thinking in later years. Breadth across sharing and grouping contexts is what makes this connection visible.

Grouping integrates the equality concept (node 1) and sharing distribution process (node 2) into a new context. Students must apply the equal-groups idea in a direction that is less familiar (forming groups by size rather than distributing to people). The generalisation of equal groups is the integration point.

descriptors.title: Familiar shapes
descriptors.description: sort, name and create familiar shapes; recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal experience with shapes in play and everyday objects. They may be able to identify some shapes by name (circle, square) in canonical orientations. They have not yet systematically sorted shapes by attributes or described shapes within objects in the environment.

nodes.label: Naming and recognising familiar shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name familiar shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle, square) and recognise them in different sizes and orientations.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to identify shapes within environmental objects — which appear in arbitrary sizes and orientations, not canonical ones. Students whose recognition is prototype-based will fail to identify shapes embedded in objects or rotated in artworks, undermining the environmental description and reasoning the descriptor demands.
criteria: Student correctly names at least three familiar shapes in varied sizes and orientations
Student identifies a named shape within at least two everyday objects in the environment

width.minimum: Name at least three familiar shapes (circle, triangle, rectangle or square) and identify them in a collection that includes varied sizes and orientations.
width.typical: Name circles, triangles, rectangles and squares in a range of sizes and orientations; recognise these shapes in everyday objects; connect shape names to their defining features (number of sides, curved vs straight).
wider: Describe and name shapes observed on Country/Place — connecting shape recognition to the natural and built environment in First Nations contexts
Investigate shapes within familiar objects (bicycles, kitchen pantry items, toy vehicles) — identifying and naming the shapes they can see

modes.reason: Students commonly recognise shapes only in canonical orientations and sizes — a triangle must be upright and equilateral, a rectangle must be landscape. Encountering shapes in many sizes, orientations and colours (with colour, size and orientation explicitly varied) is what builds recognition based on defining features rather than prototype matching.

nodes.label: Sorting shapes by attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort a collection of shapes by a chosen attribute and describe how they sorted.
criteria: Student sorts a collection of shapes by a self-chosen attribute and correctly places each shape
Student names the sorting rule and explains at least one placement decision

width.minimum: Sort a collection of shapes into two groups using one attribute (e.g. number of sides, curved vs straight) and name the sorting rule.
width.typical: Sort shapes by different attributes (number of sides, colour, size, curved vs straight); re-sort the same collection using a different attribute; describe sorting decisions and give reasons.
wider: Sort shapes using two attributes simultaneously (e.g. shapes that are both triangles AND green) and describe the combined rule
Describe and sort shapes found on Country/Place or in First Nations artworks and cultural objects into groups based on shape

nodes.label: Creating shapes and describing shapes in the environment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create familiar shapes and recognise and describe familiar shapes within objects in the environment, giving reasons for their identification.
criteria: Student creates at least two familiar shapes using materials that are recognisable as the named shape
Student identifies a familiar shape within an object in the environment and gives at least one reason based on shape features

width.minimum: Create at least two different familiar shapes using materials (e.g. drawing, tracing, blocks); identify and name a shape within one object in the environment and give a reason.
width.typical: Create familiar shapes using a range of materials; recognise and name familiar shapes within objects in the environment; describe shape features that support the identification (e.g. 'it's a rectangle because it has four sides and they are all straight'); give reasons for shape identifications.
wider: Create a picture or pattern using combinations of familiar shapes, describing each shape used and explaining why it was chosen
Explore shapes found on Country/Place and in First Nations artworks — recreating shapes using art materials and sorting them into groups
Create shapes using groups of people (e.g. holding hands to form a circle or triangle) — connecting shape properties to physical experience

modes.reason: Describing shapes within objects in the environment with reasons requires students to name a shape and then justify the identification with reference to shape features — not just 'it looks like a square' but 'it has four equal sides'. This reasoning scaffold (name + feature evidence) is the specific thinking move the descriptor demands.

This node integrates shape naming (node 1) and attribute knowledge from sorting (node 2) into productive creation and environmental recognition. Students must apply feature knowledge actively — to create accurate shapes and to justify environmental identifications. The integration of creation and description is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Position and location
descriptors.description: describe the position and location of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects within a familiar space
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal spatial vocabulary from everyday experience. They may use words like 'in', 'on' and 'next to' informally. They have not yet consistently and precisely described their own position or the position of objects in relation to a reference point.

nodes.label: Positional language vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a range of positional words correctly to describe where an object is in relation to a reference point.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 require students to produce and interpret position descriptions — which are meaningless without precise positional vocabulary. Students who use vague terms ('there', 'over there') cannot give descriptions that allow a partner to locate an object, and cannot interpret descriptions given to them.
criteria: Student correctly uses at least four different positional words to describe object positions in relation to a reference point
Student uses positional words that specify the relationship clearly enough for another person to identify the described location

width.minimum: Use at least three positional words correctly (e.g. 'in', 'on', 'under', 'next to', 'behind') to describe the position of an object.
width.typical: Use a range of positional words (inside, outside, underneath, on top of, behind, in front of, next to, near, far, between) accurately to describe object positions in relation to reference points in a familiar space.
wider: Explore positional language in First Nations Australians' instructive games — e.g. Thapumpan from the Wik-Mungkan Peoples — using spatial language to describe position relative to other participants
Use positional language to describe the position of a robotic toy in relation to classroom objects as it moves, connecting spatial vocabulary to technology contexts

modes.reason: Positional vocabulary needs to become fluent and automatic so students can use it in real-time spatial description. Students commonly confuse similar terms (in front of / behind; under / on top of) or use general words ('there', 'over there') instead of precise positional terms. Repeated use in varied, concrete placement activities builds the vocabulary precision needed.

nodes.label: Describing position in a familiar space
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the position of themselves and objects in relation to other people and objects within a familiar space.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (describing movement) requires students to describe a changing position — which depends on being able to describe a static position first. Students who cannot produce the three-component description (what / in relation to what / which word) cannot meaningfully extend to describing where something moved to.
criteria: Student describes the position of an object or themselves in a familiar space using at least one positional word and a named reference object
Student locates an object by following a position description given by another person

width.minimum: Describe the position of one object in relation to another in a familiar space using positional language, and follow a position description given by someone else to find an object.
width.typical: Describe the position of objects and themselves in a familiar space using multiple positional references; interpret position descriptions given by others; describe positions from different reference points (e.g. from own position, from another person's position).
wider: Describe the position of objects in a familiar space well enough for a partner to find a hidden object — testing and refining the description
Explore First Nations Australians' instructive games involving position and movement descriptions within a space — e.g. Thapumpan from the Wik-Mungkan Peoples of Cape Bedford

modes.reason: Describing position requires students to identify a reference point, name the positional relationship, and specify what object is being located — three components that must be coordinated into a useful description. Students commonly omit the reference object or use vague references ('over there'). The reasoning scaffold here is: what is being located? in relation to what? using which positional word?

nodes.label: Describing movement and location
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe where they have moved themselves or objects in a familiar space in relation to other objects, using positional language.
criteria: Student describes the new position of an object or themselves after movement, using positional language and a reference point
Student's description is specific enough for another person to identify the new location

width.minimum: Describe where they moved an object (or themselves) in a familiar space using at least one positional word and a reference point.
width.typical: Describe movement of objects and themselves within a familiar space using positional language; give location descriptions that would allow someone else to retrace a path or find an object; connect movement descriptions to starting and ending positions.
wider: Describe and follow simple positional instructions to navigate a familiar space (e.g. classroom or playground) — testing whether descriptions are sufficient for the listener
Explore First Nations Australians' games involving movement and spatial description within a space — describing position and movement relative to other participants and objects
Use positional language to describe and predict where a robotic toy will be after a movement instruction — connecting spatial reasoning to technology

modes.reason: Describing movement integrates positional vocabulary (node 1) and static position description (node 2) into a dynamic context — students must track changing positions and describe the relationship after movement. The added complexity of movement (position is not fixed) is the integration challenge.

descriptors.title: Collecting and comparing data
descriptors.description: collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images in response to given investigative questions that relate to familiar situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal experience sorting objects and answering yes/no questions in everyday life. They have not yet participated in a structured data investigation — collecting data in response to a question, organising it, and using the organised data to answer the question.

nodes.label: Connecting a question to data collection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what data needs to be collected to answer a given investigative question and describe how they will collect it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 depend on students having collected data that is connected to the investigative question. Students who collect arbitrary data — not matched to the question — cannot sort it into meaningful categories or use it to answer the question. The question-to-data connection is what makes the whole inquiry cycle coherent.
criteria: Student identifies what information needs to be collected to answer a given investigative question
Student describes at least one way to collect the needed data

width.minimum: Given one investigative question, identify what information needs to be collected and describe one way to collect it.
width.typical: Connect a range of investigative questions to appropriate data collection strategies; distinguish between questions that can be answered by looking at existing objects and questions that require asking people; describe how collected data will answer the question.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians collect information from the environment to answer questions (e.g. predicting weather events) — connecting data collection to Country/Place knowledge
Investigate how an AI system needs to be 'trained' by collecting yes/no data to recognise objects — connecting data collection to digital contexts

modes.reason: Students at Foundation commonly try to answer investigative questions without systematic collection — they look at a collection and report an impression rather than identifying what data is needed. The reasoning scaffold (what is the question? what information would answer it? how would I collect that information?) is the thinking move that makes data collection purposeful.

nodes.label: Sorting and organising collected data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort collected objects or images into categories that correspond to the investigative question.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to compare organised categories to answer the investigative question — but disorganised data (items in multiple categories, incomplete allocation) cannot be meaningfully compared. Students who cannot sort systematically produce data that is uninterpretable at node 3.
criteria: Student sorts collected data into at least two named categories with each item in exactly one category
Student's organisation method makes it possible to compare the categories

width.minimum: Sort a collection of objects or images into two categories in response to an investigative question, naming each category.
width.typical: Sort collected data (objects or images) into relevant categories; choose or use a given organising method (e.g. physical grouping, sticker chart, line of objects); create simple classroom charts or rosters using objects or stickers.
wider: Sort data into more than two categories for investigative questions with multiple response options
Use one-to-one correspondence to line up or match objects from two categories — making the comparison visually clear
Explore how sorting and organising data from picture books (e.g. 'The Waterhole' by Graeme Base) can answer investigative questions

modes.reason: The physical process of sorting and organising data requires systematic allocation — each object goes in exactly one category. Students commonly create overlapping categories or re-sort mid-process. Repeated practice with the sorting process across varied investigative questions builds the systematic organisation habit.

nodes.label: Comparing organised data to answer a question
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare organised data to answer an investigative question and explain what the data shows.
criteria: Student compares two or more categories of organised data and states which is larger or smaller
Student connects the comparison to the original investigative question — stating what the data shows about the question

width.minimum: Compare two groups of sorted data and state which is larger or smaller, connecting the comparison to the original investigative question.
width.typical: Compare sorted and organised data to answer yes/no and comparison investigative questions; interpret classroom charts and simple representations; explain what the data shows in response to the question using comparative language.
wider: Investigate statistical contexts from picture books (e.g. 'The Waterhole' by Graeme Base) — asking investigative questions, collecting data from the book, and comparing results to draw conclusions
Role-play being an industrial robot or AI system that uses sorted data to make decisions — connecting data comparison to real-world automated sorting contexts
Explore what First Nations Australians' environmental observations tell us — discussing how collected information can be used to answer questions about Country/Place

modes.reason: Students commonly report what they see in the data (there are more shoes with laces) without connecting the observation back to the investigative question. The reasoning scaffold — 'the question was X; the data shows Y; so the answer is Z' — is the thinking move that makes data interpretation purposeful. This closure is the specific skill the descriptor demands.

Answering an investigative question integrates question-to-data connection (node 1) and sorting/organising (node 2) into a complete statistical inquiry. The data has been collected and organised for a purpose — using it to answer the question is where those moves pay off. The full inquiry cycle (question → collect → organise → compare → answer) is the endpoint demand.

descriptors.title: Skip counting patterns
descriptors.description: Recognise, continue and create pattern sequences, with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, formed by skip counting, initially by twos, fives and tens
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns (AC9MFA01). They can count to at least 20 (AC9MFN01). They have not yet connected skip counting to pattern sequences, or recognised the structural properties of skip-counting sequences (e.g. digit patterns, growing totals).

nodes.label: Recognise and continue skip counting sequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise the rule in a given skip counting sequence (by 2s, 5s or 10s) and continue it correctly.
nodes.hinge_reason: Skip counting fluency is a prerequisite for Node 2 (digit and structural pattern identification) and Node 3 (creating sequences) — students who cannot reliably continue a sequence cannot identify digit patterns or generate their own sequences.
criteria: Correctly identifies the skip-counting rule in a given sequence (2s, 5s or 10s).
Continues the sequence for at least five additional terms without error.

width.minimum: Identify the rule in a given sequence (count by 2s, 5s or 10s); continue the sequence for at least five more terms.
width.typical: Recognise and continue skip counting sequences by 2s, 5s and 10s using number charts, songs and rhymes; identify the rule; extend sequences starting from non-zero values; use patterns to check predictions about next terms.
wider: Explore skip counting sequences from other cultural contexts — including the Korean counting game Sam-yuk-gu — identifying how the pattern rule operates in a different representational form.
Investigate skip counting sequences on a hundreds chart, colouring the multiples and describing the visual pattern produced.

modes.reason: Skip counting fluency by 2s, 5s and 10s requires practice — the sequences must be automatic before students can use them reliably for quantification and pattern work. Songs and repeated oral practice are appropriate consolidation tools here.

nodes.label: Digit and structural patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify digit patterns in skip counting sequences and explain why they occur (e.g. fives always end in 0 or 5).
criteria: Identifies at least one digit pattern in a skip counting sequence and states it clearly.
Explains why the pattern occurs (e.g. because we are adding the same amount each time and the number system cycles in tens).

width.minimum: Identify and describe one digit pattern in a skip counting sequence (e.g. the last digit in the fives sequence alternates 0 and 5).
width.typical: Identify digit patterns in sequences formed by skip counting by 2s, 5s and 10s; explain why the pattern occurs using understanding of the number system; use patterns to predict distant terms without counting up term by term.
wider: Investigate digit patterns in skip counting by other numbers (3s, 4s), comparing with 2s, 5s and 10s and discussing which sequences have cleaner digit patterns and why.
Connect the digit pattern in the fives sequence to a real-world context — coin totals, clock faces — where the pattern is visible and meaningful.

modes.reason: Students who only work with skip counting sequences as recitation often miss the digit pattern insight. Representing sequences on hundreds charts, number lines, and in real contexts (coins, clock) helps the structural pattern become visible rather than just the oral sequence.

nodes.label: Create and represent skip counting patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create their own skip counting pattern sequence and represent it using numbers, objects or shapes.
criteria: Creates a skip counting sequence with a correctly applied rule.
Represents the sequence in at least two forms and explains the connection between them.

width.minimum: Create one skip counting sequence and represent it using at least two different formats (e.g. numbers and objects).
width.typical: Create skip counting sequences by 2s, 5s and 10s and represent them using numbers, symbols, shapes and objects; use materials to build growing patterns that match the sequences; connect the count of objects to the numerical sequence.
wider: Create a skip counting pattern using a design context — arranging shapes or tiles in a growing array — and connect the visual pattern to the numerical sequence.
Explore how skip counting sequences are used in practical assembly and packing contexts, creating scenarios where a chosen skip count is the most efficient counting strategy.

modes.reason: Creating a skip counting pattern requires students to select a rule, generate the sequence, and represent it in a chosen format — coordinating all three aspects of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Repeating patterns
descriptors.description: Recognise, continue and create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects, identifying the repeating unit
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, copy and continue repeating patterns (AC9MFA01). They have not yet identified the unit of repeat explicitly, represented patterns abstractly using letters or symbols, or recognised repeating structure in the natural number sequence.

nodes.label: Identify the unit of repeat
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the unit of repeat in a given repeating pattern and explain how they know where the repeat starts and ends.
nodes.hinge_reason: Correctly identifying the unit of repeat is a prerequisite for Node 2 — students who cannot isolate the unit cannot abstract it into letter notation. A prototype-based concept of pattern (expecting only AB) causes systematic failure when encountering longer units.
criteria: Correctly identifies the unit of repeat in a given pattern.
Explains how many elements are in the unit and where the unit begins and ends.

width.minimum: Identify the unit of repeat in a given repeating pattern; explain how many elements are in the unit.
width.typical: Identify the unit of repeat in a variety of repeating patterns (AB, ABC, AABBC types); explain why certain elements are part of the unit; describe the unit and how many times it repeats; distinguish the unit from the full pattern.
wider: Investigate repeating patterns in First Nations Australians' craft practices — such as the making of shell or seed necklaces — identifying the unit of repeat in the colour, size and shape sequence.
Explore repeating patterns in everyday environments (textiles, tiling, music) and identify units of repeat of different lengths and structures.

modes.reason: Students who only see AB patterns (two-element units) often fail to recognise longer or more complex units of repeat. Varied pattern structures — ABC, AAB, ABBC — help students focus on the structural property (the unit repeats) rather than pattern appearance.

nodes.label: Abstract representation of the unit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the unit of repeat using letters or symbols, and connect abstract representation to the physical pattern.
criteria: Represents the unit of repeat using letters or symbols correctly.
Explains the connection between the letter code and the physical elements of the pattern.

width.minimum: Represent the unit of repeat in a given pattern using letters (e.g. SSCSC); connect the letters to the physical elements.
width.typical: Represent units of repeat using letters, numbers or symbols across a variety of pattern types; explain the connection between the abstract representation and the physical pattern; use the representation to continue or predict the pattern; recognise that the same abstract pattern (e.g. ABCBA) can be realised in many physical forms.
wider: Explore the abstract pattern structure of counting games from different cultures — including the repeating structure in First Nations oral and gestural number sequences — and represent the unit using letters.
Investigate how the same abstract pattern structure appears in different modalities (movement, sound, shape, colour) and create a pattern in one modality based on a pattern seen in another.

modes.reason: Abstraction from a physical pattern to a letter-code requires students to see the pattern elements as instances of types rather than specific objects. This is an early algebraic move — scaffolding with the explicit labelling step (this is A, this is B, so the unit is AB) is the critical teaching act.

nodes.label: Create and extend repeating patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create their own repeating pattern, identify the unit, and extend the pattern or represent it in a different medium.
criteria: Creates a repeating pattern with a unit that repeats at least twice.
Identifies and states the unit of repeat in the created pattern.

width.minimum: Create one repeating pattern with a clearly identifiable unit of repeat; continue the pattern for at least two full repetitions.
width.typical: Create repeating patterns with numbers, symbols, shapes and objects; identify the unit of repeat in created patterns; represent patterns created by others in abstract form; use dynamic geometric software or generative tools to create geometric repeating patterns; connect the 0–9 digit repeat in the natural number sequence to the repeating pattern concept.
wider: Create a collaborative repeating pattern using dynamic software or a generative AI tool, articulating the instructions needed and testing whether the tool produces the expected result.
Investigate the digit repeat in the natural number sequence (0–9 cycling between decades) as an instance of a repeating pattern, and use this insight to predict two-digit numbers beyond 20.

modes.reason: Creating a pattern, identifying its unit, and representing it in another form requires students to synthesise identification, abstraction and generation — all three aspects of the descriptor working together.

descriptors.title: Order by length, mass, capacity, duration
descriptors.description: Compare directly and indirectly and order objects and events using attributes of length, mass, capacity and duration, communicating reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and compare length, capacity, mass and duration using direct comparisons (AC9MFM01). They can sequence days of the week and times of day (AC9MFM02). They have not yet compared indirectly using a mediating object, or ordered three or more objects using a single attribute and communicated the reasoning systematically.

nodes.label: Direct comparison and ordering
nodes.checkpoint: Students can directly compare and order three or more objects using a single attribute, using correct comparative language to communicate the order.
criteria: Orders three or more objects from shortest to longest (or lightest to heaviest, least to most) using direct comparison.
Uses correct comparative language to describe the order.

width.minimum: Order three objects by length (or mass or capacity) using direct comparison; describe the order using comparative language (e.g. shortest, shorter, longer, longest).
width.typical: Directly compare and order three or more objects using each of length, mass and capacity; use correct comparative language for each attribute; explain the comparison method used and the resulting order.
wider: Investigate comparative measurement in First Nations contexts — ordering tracks by animal length, comparing capacity of traditional water-carrying vessels — using the same language of ordering and reasoning.
Order objects by two attributes simultaneously (e.g. by both length and mass), discussing whether objects ranked the same on one attribute are necessarily ranked the same on another.

nodes.label: Indirect comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the length (or capacity) of two objects that cannot be placed directly side-by-side, using a mediating object or material.
criteria: Correctly uses a mediating object to compare two objects that cannot be placed side-by-side.
Explains the reasoning behind the indirect comparison and states the conclusion.

width.minimum: Use a piece of string or another mediating object to compare the length of two objects that cannot be placed directly side-by-side; state which is longer and explain the method.
width.typical: Compare lengths using string or rope as a mediating tool; compare capacities by pouring into a third container; use balance scales to compare mass indirectly; explain the reasoning behind each indirect comparison method.
wider: Explore historical and cultural indirect comparison methods — pacing, using body-length units, traditional balance tools — and compare their precision with string-based indirect comparison.
Design an indirect comparison challenge: identify two objects in the classroom that cannot be directly compared and determine a mediating strategy, explaining the choice.

modes.reason: Indirect comparison is conceptually distinct from direct comparison — students often fail to recognise that transitivity (A = C and B = C means A = B) is what makes indirect comparison valid. Working with different mediating objects and attributes helps students grasp the principle rather than just the procedure.

nodes.label: Comparing and ordering duration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the duration of events using informal timers and order events by duration, communicating reasoning using correct temporal comparative language.
criteria: Orders three or more events or activities by duration using an informal timer.
Uses correct comparative language to communicate the duration order and explains how the comparison was made.

width.minimum: Compare the duration of two events using an informal timer (sand timer, counting); state which takes longer.
width.typical: Compare and order the duration of three or more events using informal timers; create or select appropriate timers for comparison; use correct comparative language (faster, slower, shorter duration, longer duration); connect duration comparison to the time units studied in AC9M1M03.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars as representations of duration — discussing how the duration of seasons is described and compared across different language groups.
