Create and compare a set of sand timers using everyday materials, ordering them by duration and designing a timing challenge for peers.

descriptors.title: Measure length with informal units
descriptors.description: Measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare objects directly by length (AC9MFM01) and order objects by length using direct comparison (AC9M1M01). They have not yet iterated a unit along a length to produce a numerical measure, or reasoned about why units must be uniform and placed end-to-end.

nodes.label: Iterate units end-to-end
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure the length of an object by placing informal units end-to-end and counting them, producing a numerical measurement.
nodes.hinge_reason: Placement errors (gaps or overlaps) produce invalid measurements that undermine Node 2 — students who cannot iterate units accurately cannot meaningfully compare measurements or reason about why units must be uniform, because their measurements are not trustworthy to begin with.
criteria: Places informal units end-to-end without gaps or overlaps to measure a length.
Counts and records the number of units correctly.

width.minimum: Measure one object using a chosen informal unit placed end-to-end; count the units and record the measurement.
width.typical: Measure several objects using an informal unit (blocks, pop sticks) placed end-to-end; count and record each measurement; compare measurements to determine which object is longer; explain what end-to-end placement means.
wider: Measure the same object multiple times using the same unit, investigating whether the result is always the same and discussing what could cause variation.
Measure classroom features (door frame, table, corridor) using body-based units (footsteps, handspans) and record results, discussing how this connects to historical measurement practices.

modes.reason: Correctly placing units end-to-end without gaps or overlaps requires practice and physical care — it is a procedural skill that needs to become reliable before students can reason about unit consistency. Errors in placement directly undermine the validity of the measurement.

nodes.label: Units must be uniform
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why informal units need to be the same size (uniform) to produce a valid and comparable measurement.
criteria: Measures the same object with two different units and correctly states both measurements.
Explains why the two measurements are different, referring to the size of the unit.

width.minimum: Measure one object using two different-sized informal units; explain why the two measurements give different numbers.
width.typical: Measure the same object with two different informal units (e.g. pop sticks and pencils); compare the resulting numbers; explain why different units give different counts; articulate that larger units produce smaller numbers for the same length and vice versa.
wider: Explore historical body-based measurement units (handspan, cubit, pace) and investigate why non-uniform body units caused problems for trade and communication — connecting the historical reason for standard units to the Year 1 concept.
Compare measurements taken by different students using footsteps as the unit, explaining why results differ and what would make the measurements directly comparable.

modes.reason: Students frequently assume that different measurements must mean different lengths — they don't yet see that the unit is the variable. Using two different units on the same object, and comparing results across classmates using non-uniform personal units (footsteps), gives the contexts that make the uniformity principle vivid.

nodes.label: Compare using measurement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use informal-unit measurement to compare the length of two or more objects, stating how much longer one is than another.
criteria: Measures two objects with the same informal unit and states which is longer.
States the difference in length in units and explains why the same unit was necessary for a valid comparison.

width.minimum: Measure two objects with the same informal unit; state which is longer and by how many units.
width.typical: Measure and compare two or more objects using the same informal unit; state the length difference in units; explain why the same unit must be used for both to make a valid comparison; apply measurement comparison to practical contexts (does this object fit in this space?).
wider: Measure and compare lengths across a classroom investigation — designing a measurement challenge where the question requires comparing multiple objects using a chosen unit.
Investigate what happens to comparative measurements when a different unit is chosen — confirming that the ordering of lengths is preserved even when the unit changes.

modes.reason: Using measurement to compare requires students to apply unit iteration, count correctly, ensure uniformity, and interpret the result in context — all components of the descriptor operating together.

descriptors.title: Duration and sequence of events
descriptors.description: Describe the duration and sequence of events using years, months, weeks, days and hours
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sequence days of the week and times of day, connecting them to familiar events (AC9MFM02). They have not yet used the full hierarchy of time units (years, months, weeks, days, hours), compared the number of days across months, or represented event sequences using pictorial timelines.

nodes.label: Name and relate time units
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name years, months, weeks, days and hours as units of time and describe the relationship between them (e.g. a week is 7 days).
nodes.hinge_reason: Knowing the names and relationships between time units is required for Node 2 (duration estimation) and Node 3 (labelling timelines) — students who do not know the unit hierarchy cannot assign activities to appropriate units or label timeline events correctly.
criteria: Names years, months, weeks, days and hours correctly.
States the number of days in a week and hours in a day; identifies which months have 30 and 31 days.

width.minimum: Name at least four of the five time units; state the relationship between at least two adjacent units (e.g. 7 days in a week, 24 hours in a day).
width.typical: Name all five time units; describe the relationship between each pair of adjacent units; compare the number of days in different months; explain how months cycle from one year to the next; connect units to familiar experiences.
wider: Investigate how time units are named and structured across different cultures and languages, comparing unit names and observing that the structural relationships (7-day week, 24-hour day) are widely shared.
Explore First Nations Australians' seasonal calendars as alternative frameworks for dividing the year, comparing the number and duration of seasonal periods with the 12-month calendar.

modes.reason: The names and relationships between time units require rehearsal and connection to personal experience. The month/day count variation (28–31 days) is a specific factual knowledge point that needs practice.

nodes.label: Estimate duration using time units
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate whether a familiar activity takes closer to an hour, a day, a week, a month or a year, and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Correctly assigns at least three familiar activities to appropriate time units.
Gives a reason for the assignment that refers to the scale of the unit.

width.minimum: Assign at least three familiar activities to appropriate time units (e.g. sleeping — about 8 hours; a school term — about 10 weeks).
width.typical: Estimate and assign a range of familiar activities and events to appropriate time units; explain the reasoning (e.g. 'it takes less than an hour to walk to school because…'); discuss why some events are hard to assign (e.g. growing taller — weeks/months/years?).
wider: Investigate durations of natural phenomena — plant growth, animal gestation, migration cycles — assigning each to appropriate time units and explaining the estimates.
Explore and discuss time durations described in First Nations seasonal calendars — assigning each season's events to approximate time units and comparing with the calendar system.

modes.reason: Students develop robust time sense by encountering a wide range of durations — not just school-day events. Natural phenomena, seasonal events, and cultural calendars give varied contexts that help students develop calibrated intuitions for each unit.

nodes.label: Sequence events on a timeline
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence a set of familiar events in order and represent the sequence using a pictorial timeline, labelling each event with an appropriate time unit.
criteria: Places a set of events in correct chronological order on a timeline.
Labels each event with an appropriate time unit.

width.minimum: Place at least four events in correct chronological order; represent the sequence as a pictorial timeline.
width.typical: Create pictorial timelines for familiar event sequences (school day, week, year); label events with appropriate time units; describe the sequence using time unit language; distinguish events by whether they occur within days, weeks or months.
wider: Create a personal timeline spanning a year or longer, annotating key events with time units and discussing the relative spacing between events.
Compare a class-created timeline with a First Nations seasonal calendar representation, discussing similarities and differences in how time passage and event sequences are communicated.

modes.reason: Creating a timeline requires students to apply knowledge of time units, duration estimation, and sequential ordering simultaneously — integrating all three nodes of this standard into a coherent representation.

descriptors.title: Numbers to 120
descriptors.description: Recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals, number lines and charts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can name, represent and order numbers to at least 20 (AC9MFN01). They can quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting (AC9MFN03). They have not yet read, written or ordered numbers in the two-digit range up to 120, or used patterns in the number system (tens/ones) to navigate across decades.

nodes.label: Two-digit numeral recognition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write two-digit numerals to at least 99, including numerals that look or sound similar (e.g. 16 and 61).
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable numeral reading is required for Node 2 (hundreds chart navigation) and Node 3 (ordering on a number line) — students who confuse teen and decade numerals produce systematic ordering errors and cannot correctly locate numbers on the chart.
criteria: Reads two-digit numerals to 99 correctly, including commonly confused pairs such as 16 and 61.
Writes the numeral when a two-digit number is stated aloud.

width.minimum: Read and write numerals for numbers 10–99; identify easily confused pairs (e.g. 16/61, 60/16) from a set.
width.typical: Read, write and name two-digit numerals to 99 across a range of representations; practise with commonly confused pairs; use number charts to locate and name numerals.
wider: Explore how two-digit numbers are represented in other numeral systems (Japanese kanji, Chinese characters), comparing the role of position versus special characters for tens.
Investigate how numbers are named and written in different languages — identifying where the spoken form makes the tens-ones structure explicit and where it is less obvious.

modes.reason: Confusion between teen numbers (13–19) and decade multiples (30–90) is common and persistent. Fluency with numeral reading requires deliberate practice with the commonly confused pairs before students can reliably navigate the number line.

nodes.label: Tens and ones structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the tens and ones in a two-digit number and use the hundreds chart to navigate the number system.
criteria: States the number of tens and ones in a given two-digit number.
Locates a two-digit number on the hundreds chart and explains its position in terms of the row (tens) and column (ones).

width.minimum: Identify the number of tens and ones in a two-digit number using a hundreds chart or physical materials; explain the pattern of tens in a hundreds chart.
width.typical: Use a hundreds chart to identify how numbers are structured as tens and ones; colour-code the tens column; use physical materials (MAB blocks, bundled sticks) to build two-digit numbers; explain the pattern of decade numbers.
wider: Collaboratively build a hundreds chart from scrambled numeral cards, discussing how the tens-ones structure organises the grid.
Compare the hundreds chart structure with the counting boards used in other cultural traditions, identifying what structural features are shared.

modes.reason: Students who only encounter the hundreds chart as a static resource often miss the structural logic — that each row is a new ten. Working with multiple representations (chart, physical materials, number line) helps students see the tens-ones pattern as a system property, not a chart property.

nodes.label: Ordering to 120 on a number line
nodes.checkpoint: Students can order a set of numbers to at least 120 and position them on a number line, using patterns in the number system.
criteria: Orders a mixed set of numbers to at least 120 from smallest to largest.
Positions numbers on an empty number line at approximately correct relative locations, using benchmark numbers to reason about placement.

width.minimum: Order a set of five or more two-digit numbers; place numbered cards in correct order on an empty number line.
width.typical: Order numbers to at least 120 using number lines, number tracks and charts; peg numbered cards at relative positions on an empty number line; extend ordering into the range 100–120 using patterns established to 99.
wider: Order numbers written in multiple formats — numerals, words, tally marks — placing them on the same number line and discussing equivalence.
Investigate how numbers beyond 100 are named across different languages and cultures, connecting naming patterns to the ordering structure.

modes.reason: Placing numbers on an empty (unlabelled) number line requires students to reason about relative magnitude — not just sequence. Scaffolding with benchmark numbers (0, 50, 100, 120) before removing them supports the transition from sequential to proportional placement.

descriptors.title: Partition two-digit numbers
descriptors.description: Partition one- and two-digit numbers in different ways using physical and virtual materials, including partitioning two-digit numbers into tens and ones
descriptors.knowledge: Students can partition and combine collections up to 10 using part-part-whole relationships (AC9MFN04). They can represent numbers to at least 20 (AC9MFN01). They have not yet partitioned two-digit numbers systematically into tens and ones, or explored non-standard partitions of two-digit numbers.

nodes.label: Part-part-whole to 10
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and represent all pairs of numbers that combine to make 10, using physical or virtual materials.
nodes.hinge_reason: Number bond fluency to 10 is a direct prerequisite for the bridging-through-10 strategy in AC9M1N04 Node 2 — students who cannot recall combinations to 10 automatically cannot execute the bridge (e.g. knowing that 7 needs 3 to make 10).
criteria: States the missing part when given one part and the whole (e.g. 7 and ___ make 10).
Represents a number combination to 10 using materials or a diagram.

width.minimum: Use ten-frames or physical materials to find at least three pairs that combine to make 10; record the pairs as number combinations.
width.typical: Use virtual ten-frames, physical materials and part-part-whole diagrams to identify all pairs to 10; build fluency with the full set of combinations; explain why 0+10, 1+9, 2+8 … all equal 10.
wider: Explore part-part-whole combinations to 10 using different manipulatives (two-colour counters, interlocking cubes, bead strings), comparing how each makes the structure visible.
Investigate how number bonds to 10 appear in cultural artefacts such as abacus designs and ten-frame tools used in different countries.

modes.reason: Fluency with number combinations to 10 is foundational to all addition and subtraction strategies at this level. Students need practice and precision with these facts — they are building blocks, not concepts that widen significantly.

nodes.label: Standard partition: tens and ones
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a two-digit number into tens and ones using physical materials, and record the partition using numbers.
criteria: Partitions a given two-digit number into the correct number of tens and ones using materials.
Records the partition as a correct number statement connecting the groups to the numeral.

width.minimum: Partition a given two-digit number into tens and ones using physical materials; record as a number statement (e.g. 35 = 3 tens and 5 ones).
width.typical: Partition a range of two-digit numbers into tens and ones using physical and virtual materials; record using number statements; connect the digits in the numeral to the grouped materials; include numbers with zero ones (e.g. 40 = 4 tens).
wider: Use multiple representations of the same partition (MAB blocks, bundled sticks, ten-frames, place-value chart) and compare how each displays the tens and ones.
Investigate how place-value notation for tens and ones functions in other numeration systems — noting what is structurally similar and different.

modes.reason: Students frequently partition into tens and ones correctly with MAB blocks but fail to connect this to the digit positions in the written numeral. Using multiple physical representations alongside the numeral helps students see that the tens digit records the grouped count, not just an arbitrary symbol.

nodes.label: Non-standard partitions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a two-digit number in multiple ways, including non-standard partitions, and record each partition.
criteria: Produces at least two different correct partitions of a given two-digit number.
Verifies each partition by combining the parts and confirming the total.

width.minimum: Find at least two different partitions of a two-digit number (one standard, one non-standard); record each as a number statement.
width.typical: Partition two-digit numbers in multiple ways — standard (tens and ones) and non-standard (e.g. 24 = 10 + 14 = 20 + 4 = 15 + 9); use physical and virtual materials to build and check each partition; record all partitions found.
wider: Systematically find all non-standard partitions of a two-digit number, organising the results in a table and explaining any patterns noticed.
Connect non-standard partitions to addition strategies — identifying which partitions are most useful as 'bridging' strategies for adding numbers within 20.

modes.reason: Students readily find the standard tens-and-ones partition but resist non-standard partitions, often believing only one correct partition exists. Scaffolding with a systematic approach (fix one part, vary the other) supports the reasoning that any partition that totals the original number is valid.

descriptors.title: Quantify sets by skip counting
descriptors.description: Quantify sets of objects, to at least 120, by partitioning collections into equal groups using number knowledge and skip counting
descriptors.knowledge: Students can quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting (AC9MFN03). They can recognise and continue skip counting sequences by twos, fives and tens (AC9M1A01). They have not yet applied skip counting systematically to count large collections beyond 20 by grouping into equal groups.

nodes.label: Group into equal sets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a collection of objects into equal groups of a chosen size, explaining why grouping makes counting more efficient.
criteria: Partitions a collection into equal groups of a stated size with no objects left over from the grouping phase.
Explains why grouping makes counting more efficient than counting one by one.

width.minimum: Group a collection of 20–40 objects into equal groups of 5 or 10; explain why grouping is helpful.
width.typical: Group collections of various sizes into equal groups of 2, 5 or 10; compare different grouping sizes for the same collection; explain the efficiency gained by grouping rather than counting one by one.
wider: Investigate how grouping strategies are used in practical contexts — packaging, stacking, bundling — and discuss what group size is most efficient for different purposes.
Explore grouping practices used historically and in First Nations contexts, comparing the choice of group size to the decimal (base-10) grouping used in the standard system.

nodes.label: Skip count the groups
nodes.checkpoint: Students can skip count a grouped collection to find the total and connect the count to the digit representation of the total.
nodes.hinge_reason: Skip counting fluency is required for Node 3 — students who lose track of the count mid-sequence cannot reliably produce the total needed to connect groups to digit notation. Errors here prevent the place-value connection in Node 3 from working.
criteria: Skip counts correctly across a grouped collection to state the total.
Includes any remaining ungrouped objects in the final count.

width.minimum: Skip count by 5s or 10s to find the total of a grouped collection of at least 50 objects; state the total and connect it to the count of groups.
width.typical: Skip count by 2s, 5s or 10s over grouped collections to find totals to at least 120; include any ungrouped remainder in the count; record the total; connect the number of groups and the group size to the resulting total.
wider: Apply skip counting to count collections of Australian coins by denomination (5c, 10c, $1, $2), connecting skip counting to practical money contexts.
Count the same large collection using different group sizes, comparing the number of groups produced and the skip counting sequence used, and discussing which is most efficient.

modes.reason: Skip counting fluency for groups of 5 and 10 requires practice — the sequence must be automatic enough to apply reliably to counting tasks. Students who lose track mid-sequence need more practice with the sequence itself before applying it to collections.

nodes.label: Connect groups to digits
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect the number of tens groups and ones remainder in a counted collection to the digits in the written numeral.
criteria: After counting a collection by grouping in tens, states the number of tens and ones correctly.
Writes the numeral for the total and explains how the tens digit and ones digit relate to the physical groups.

width.minimum: After counting a collection by tens, state the number of tens groups and any remaining ones; connect these to the digits in the written numeral.
width.typical: Count collections of at least 120 objects by grouping in tens and ones; record the total; explicitly connect the number of tens to the tens digit and the number of ones to the ones digit in the numeral; explain the connection in words.
wider: Count a very large collection (200+ objects) by grouping into hundreds, tens and ones, introducing the idea of three-digit numbers as a natural extension of the grouping strategy.
Record the counting process using a simple place-value chart, reinforcing the connection between the physical groups and the numeral structure.

modes.reason: Students who only count by tens with pre-grouped materials (e.g. MAB blocks) sometimes fail to generalise to ungrouped real-world collections. Counting genuinely ungrouped collections (pencils, seeds, tiles) across different contexts strengthens the connection between the grouping act and the numeral produced.

This node is where grouping, skip counting, and place-value numeral reading come together as a coordinated skill. The three components all need to operate simultaneously — this is the integration point for the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Add and subtract within 20
descriptors.description: Add and subtract numbers within 20, using physical and virtual materials, part-part-whole knowledge to 10 and a variety of calculation strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent practical addition and subtraction situations using materials and counting strategies (AC9MFN05). They can partition and combine collections to 10 using part-part-whole relationships (AC9MFN04). They have not yet applied systematic calculation strategies (counting on, bridging through 10, partitioning) to add and subtract within 20.

nodes.label: Counting-on and counting-back strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add and subtract within 20 using counting-on from the larger number and counting-back strategies, recording with + and − symbols and the equal sign.
nodes.hinge_reason: Counting-on is the baseline strategy required for Node 2 — students who still default to counting-all cannot efficiently apply the bridging-through-10 strategy, which requires holding the first addend as a fixed starting point and partitioning the second.
criteria: Applies counting-on correctly for addition within 20 (starts count at the larger number + 1).
Records the calculation using + or − and = symbols.

width.minimum: Add two numbers within 20 using counting-on; subtract using counting-back; record one calculation using + or − and = symbols.
width.typical: Apply counting-on and counting-back strategies consistently within 20; use physical materials and number lines to represent the strategy; record calculations using + and − symbols and the equal sign; connect materials to symbolic recording.
wider: Compare counting-on with counting-all for the same calculation, articulating why counting-on is more efficient and when each strategy might be preferred.
Use virtual number lines to model counting-on and counting-back, comparing the visual jump with the physical count.

modes.reason: Students transitioning from counting-all to counting-on need practice to make counting-on the default strategy. The key error — starting the count at the first addend rather than the count after it — requires targeted correction and fluency practice.

nodes.label: Bridging through 10
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add numbers within 20 by partitioning one addend to bridge through 10, using part-part-whole knowledge.
nodes.hinge_reason: Bridging through 10 is a prerequisite strategy for two-digit addition in Year 2 — students who cannot apply it within 20 will lack the foundational move required when adding across decade boundaries. It is also required for Node 3 subtraction strategies that use the think-addition approach.
criteria: Partitions one addend correctly to make 10 with the other when adding numbers that cross 10.
Records the bridging chain with correct number sentences showing each step.

width.minimum: Partition one addend to make 10 with the other, then add the remainder; record the bridging strategy as a number sentence (e.g. 7 + 5 = 7 + 3 + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12).
width.typical: Apply bridging through 10 to a range of additions within 20; use physical materials (ten-frames, counters) to model the partition; record the full bridging chain as a number sentence; connect the strategy to part-part-whole knowledge of combinations to 10.
wider: Investigate which additions within 20 can be most efficiently solved by bridging (those that cross 10) versus those best solved by counting-on or using doubles, building a strategic repertoire.
Create story problems that require bridging through 10 and explain why bridging is the most efficient strategy for each.

modes.reason: Bridging through 10 relies on automatic knowledge of number combinations to 10. Students who don't yet know, for example, that 7 + 3 = 10 cannot apply the bridge. Using ten-frames and part-part-whole materials in varied contexts helps students see the bridging move as a general strategy rather than a procedure to memorise.

The bridging chain (7 + 5 = 7 + 3 + 2 = 10 + 2 = 12) is a multi-step reasoning sequence. Students need the full chain made visible before they can apply it independently. Recording each step explicitly is the scaffold.

nodes.label: Subtraction strategies within 20
nodes.checkpoint: Students can subtract within 20 using a range of strategies including counting-back, using related addition facts, and partitioning, choosing strategies based on the numbers involved.
criteria: Solves subtraction problems within 20 using a strategy other than counting-all.
Represents a subtraction story problem using a diagram or Think Board and records it with a correct number sentence.

width.minimum: Subtract within 20 using at least one strategy beyond counting-all; represent using physical materials or a Think Board.
width.typical: Apply counting-back, think-addition (using known addition facts), and partitioning strategies to subtract within 20; represent story problems on a Think Board; use + and − symbols and the equal sign; explain which strategy was chosen and why.
wider: Explore subtraction through creation and performance of addition and subtraction stories in movement contexts — connecting the mathematical operation to narrative and embodied experience.
Compare 'taking away' and 'finding the difference' as two subtraction interpretations, using the same number sentence to represent both situations.

modes.reason: Students often treat subtraction as only 'take away', missing the 'difference' and 'missing addend' interpretations. Varied story contexts are necessary to build the broader concept — the same symbolic subtraction sentence represents multiple real-world situations.

This node integrates counting strategies, part-part-whole knowledge, and symbolic recording into flexible strategy selection. Students need to coordinate all three to solve novel subtraction situations efficiently.

descriptors.title: Model additive problems
descriptors.description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive situations including simple money transactions; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent practical addition and subtraction situations using materials and counting strategies (AC9MFN05). They can add and subtract within 20 using calculation strategies (AC9M1N04). They have not yet used structured mathematical modelling (Think Board, diagrams, multiple representations) to connect real-world additive situations to mathematical representations and calculations.

nodes.label: Interpret the additive situation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the mathematical structure of a practical additive situation — whether it involves joining, separating, or comparing quantities.
criteria: Identifies what is known and what is unknown in an additive story problem.
States whether the situation requires adding or subtracting and gives a reason.

width.minimum: Listen to or read one practical additive story problem and identify: what is known, what is unknown, and whether the situation involves adding or subtracting.
width.typical: Interpret a variety of practical additive story problems (joining, separating, comparing); identify the known and unknown quantities; determine the operation needed; explain the situation in own words before solving.
wider: Interpret additive situations drawn from a range of real-world contexts including shopping, travel, and school events, identifying the mathematical structure in each.
Explore additive situations from First Nations contexts — counting objects significant to Country/Place, sharing within community — and identify the mathematical structure.

modes.reason: Students who only experience one type of additive situation (typically joining/adding) often apply the same operation regardless of the problem structure. Varied contexts are necessary to build the ability to interpret the situation before selecting a strategy.

nodes.label: Represent with diagrams and materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent an additive situation using at least two different representations (e.g. diagram, materials, Think Board) and explain the connections between them.
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to represent a problem situation is a prerequisite for Node 3 — students who cannot connect a story to a representation cannot verify whether their calculation answers the right question or interpret the answer back in context.
criteria: Produces a diagram or materials representation that correctly captures the quantities in the story problem.
Explains the connection between the representation and at least one element of the story (e.g. 'these blocks are the passengers who got on').

width.minimum: Represent one additive problem using physical materials or a diagram; connect the representation to the numbers in the story.
width.typical: Use Think Boards to represent additive problems with pictures, materials, diagrams and number sentences; explain the connections between each representation and the story; include simple money transactions using whole dollar amounts.
wider: Represent the same problem using three different formats (materials, number line, part-part-whole diagram) and compare which representation makes the solution most visible.
Create a class display linking physical representations, diagrams and number sentences for a set of related additive problems.

modes.reason: Moving from a concrete material representation to a diagram to a number sentence is a three-step abstraction that requires explicit scaffolding. Students need the connections between each level made visible before they can coordinate them independently.

nodes.label: Solve and explain
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply a calculation strategy to solve an additive problem and communicate the solution in terms of the original situation.
criteria: States the answer to an additive problem using a correct calculation strategy.
Interprets the answer in terms of the original problem context (e.g. 'There are 14 passengers on the bus now').

width.minimum: Apply a calculation strategy to solve one practical additive problem; state the answer in terms of the problem context.
width.typical: Use calculation strategies to solve a variety of practical additive problems; record the solution as a number sentence; interpret the answer in the context of the original problem; check whether the solution is reasonable.
wider: Solve a sequence of related additive problems (e.g. bus stops, shop transactions) where the output of one problem feeds into the next, building a chained calculation narrative.
Explore and solve open-ended additive problems where there are multiple valid solutions (e.g. 'I spent $10 — what could I have bought?').

modes.reason: Interpreting the situation, choosing a representation, applying a strategy, and communicating the answer in context all need to work together here. This is the integration node for the full modelling cycle — students must coordinate all prior components.

descriptors.title: Model sharing and grouping
descriptors.description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping; represent the situations with diagrams, physical and virtual materials, and use calculation strategies to solve the problem
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent practical equal sharing and grouping situations using materials (AC9MFN06). They can add and subtract within 20 using calculation strategies (AC9M1N04). They have not yet modelled sharing and grouping using structured representations (diagrams, Think Boards) and calculation strategies, or connected equal grouping to the idea of repeated equal quantities.

nodes.label: Distinguish sharing from grouping
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a practical situation involves equal sharing (distributing a total among a known number of recipients) or equal grouping (making groups of a known size).
nodes.hinge_reason: Confusing sharing and grouping structures causes students to misidentify what is known and unknown in Node 2 and Node 3 — they model the wrong situation and apply the wrong solution strategy as a result.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether a described situation involves sharing or grouping.
States what is known and what needs to be found in each situation type.

width.minimum: Describe one sharing situation and one grouping situation; explain what is known and what is unknown in each.
width.typical: Identify and distinguish equal sharing and equal grouping situations from a variety of practical contexts; explain the known and unknown quantities in each type; use materials to model the action in each case.
wider: Compare sharing and grouping situations with the same numbers (e.g. 12 objects shared among 3 vs 12 objects in groups of 3) — identifying what stays the same and what is different in each.
Explore sharing and grouping contexts from everyday community and school life, including contexts drawn from First Nations community practices.

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse sharing and grouping because both involve equal quantities. Varied practical contexts help students focus on the distinction — what is fixed (total, number of groups, or group size) — rather than recognising only one type of situation.

nodes.label: Represent with materials and diagrams
nodes.checkpoint: Students can model an equal sharing or grouping situation using physical materials, a drawing and a number recording, explaining the connections between each.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot represent a sharing or grouping action as a diagram or number record, they cannot apply a calculation strategy in Node 3 — the representation is the bridge between the concrete action and the symbolic solution.
criteria: Produces a physical or drawn representation that correctly shows the equal groups.
Records the result as a number and confirms that all groups are equal.

width.minimum: Model one sharing or grouping problem using physical materials; draw a picture to represent the action; record the result as a number.
width.typical: Model sharing and grouping situations using physical materials and diagrams; include money contexts (sharing coins equally between recipients); use subitising and counting to verify equal groups; draw representations showing the groups clearly; record results.
wider: Represent the same sharing problem using three formats — physical objects, array diagram, number sentence — and explain which representation makes the equal-groups structure most visible.
Model sharing problems with coin collections, sorting by denomination and verifying equal amounts using counting and subitising.

modes.reason: The 'dealing' action students use to share physically does not automatically translate to a diagram or number recording. Explicitly scaffolding the move from action to picture to number is the key teaching investment at this node.

nodes.label: Solve and communicate equal-groups problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply a calculation strategy to solve equal sharing and grouping problems and communicate the solution in terms of the problem context.
criteria: Solves a sharing or grouping problem using a calculation strategy (not trial and error with materials alone).
States the answer in context and confirms that all groups are equal.

width.minimum: Solve one sharing or grouping problem using a calculation strategy; state the answer in terms of the original problem.
width.typical: Solve a variety of sharing and grouping problems using calculation strategies (skip counting, repeated addition, subitising); record solutions; explain the answer in the context of the problem; connect repeated equal groups to the idea that each share is the same.
wider: Connect equal grouping to early multiplicative thinking — representing 'How many wheels on 3 cars?' as both repeated addition (4 + 4 + 4) and as an equal-groups diagram, and describing what is the same in each.
Explore open-ended grouping problems where multiple solutions are possible (e.g. 'Arrange 24 objects into equal groups — how many different ways can you do this?').

modes.reason: Solving equal sharing and grouping problems requires students to interpret the situation, choose an appropriate representation, apply a calculation strategy, and explain the answer in context — all simultaneously. This node is the integration point for the modelling cycle applied to multiplicative-type situations.

descriptors.title: Compare and classify shapes
descriptors.description: Make, compare and classify familiar shapes; recognise familiar shapes and objects in the environment, identifying the similarities and differences between them
descriptors.knowledge: Students can sort, name and create familiar shapes and recognise them in the environment (AC9MFSP01). They have not yet classified shapes by comparing multiple properties simultaneously, nor distinguished between regular and irregular instances of the same shape type.

nodes.label: Classify by shared properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort a collection of shapes into groups based on shared properties and explain what is the same within a group and different between groups.
criteria: Sorts a mixed collection of shapes into groups and names a shared property for each group.
Explains at least one difference between two groups.

width.minimum: Sort a collection of shapes into at least two groups; state one property shared by shapes in each group and one difference between the groups.
width.typical: Classify a collection including circles, ovals, triangles, quadrilaterals and irregular shapes into groups; explain the shared properties within each group; distinguish regular from irregular instances of the same type (e.g. equilateral vs scalene triangles); identify overlapping properties and decide how to handle shapes that could belong to multiple groups.
wider: Explore string games from First Nations Australians (e.g. Karda from the Yandruwandha Peoples), recognising and classifying the shapes made by the string in terms of familiar shape properties.
Investigate shapes found in architecture and design across different cultures, classifying and comparing properties and noting how different traditions use shape differently.
Use dynamic geometry software to manipulate shapes, exploring which properties remain the same and which change as a shape is stretched or rotated.

modes.reason: Students who only sort with clearly regular shapes often overgeneralise (all triangles must have equal sides, all rectangles must be upright). Including irregular instances and shapes in non-standard orientations gives the contexts needed to build a property-based concept of shape type rather than a prototype-based one.

nodes.label: Tactile and environmental recognition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify familiar shapes by touch alone and recognise familiar shapes in objects and structures in the environment.
criteria: Correctly names a shape identified by touch, using a property to justify the identification.
Identifies at least two instances of a named shape in the environment.

width.minimum: Identify a shape from a bag by feel and name it; find at least two instances of a named shape in the classroom environment.
width.typical: Identify a range of shapes by feel (circle, triangle, square, rectangle, oval) and explain the properties used to identify each; recognise familiar shapes in a range of environmental objects; compare 3D objects and identify which 2D shapes are visible on their faces.
wider: Conduct a shape walk in a broader environment (school grounds, local area), photographing or sketching instances of each shape type and creating a class display of shapes found in the environment.
Explore shapes in First Nations Australian art and craft, identifying and classifying the shapes used and connecting them to the shapes found on Country/Place.

nodes.label: Make and compare shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make familiar shapes using materials and compare shapes built from the same materials, explaining the similarities and differences.
criteria: Makes a shape using materials that has the key properties of the named shape type.
Compares two constructed shapes and states at least one similarity and one difference.

width.minimum: Make one familiar shape using materials; compare it with a different shape made from the same number of pieces and state one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Make a variety of familiar shapes using blocks, centi-cubes, or construction materials; compare objects built from the same number of pieces; discuss how the arrangement of pieces produces different shapes; connect 3D constructions to their 2D shape components.
wider: Explore how different arrangements of the same number of centi-cubes produce shapes with different properties (height, width, footprint), connecting construction to spatial reasoning.
Create shapes and patterns inspired by First Nations string game designs, comparing the shapes made in different string configurations.

modes.reason: Making shapes requires students to apply classification knowledge generatively — selecting materials to produce specified properties. Comparing constructed shapes integrates property identification, classification, and spatial reasoning.

descriptors.title: Give and follow directions
descriptors.description: Give and follow directions to move people and objects to different locations within a space
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe position and location of themselves and objects within a familiar space (AC9MFSP02). They have not yet given or followed multi-step directional instructions, created algorithms for movement, or used ordinal and positional language to direct others.

nodes.label: Interpret and follow directions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret and follow a sequence of directional instructions using forwards, backwards, left, right and straight ahead to reach a stated location.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable left/right orientation is a prerequisite for Node 2 (giving directions) and Node 3 (creating algorithms) — students who confuse their own left/right give systematically incorrect directions and produce algorithms that fail when tested.
criteria: Follows a multi-step direction sequence correctly, reaching the target location.
Demonstrates correct understanding of left/right relative to own orientation.

width.minimum: Follow a three-step sequence of directions using at least two directional terms to reach a target location.
width.typical: Interpret and follow multi-step directions using forwards, backwards, straight ahead, left, right; understand that left/right are relative to the mover's orientation; follow directions given by a peer or teacher; reach target locations reliably.
wider: Follow directions that describe a familiar journey using landmark-based language from a First Nations perspective, recognising how directional language is shaped by relationship to Country/Place.
Program a floor robot (Bee-Bot or equivalent) by entering a direction sequence, testing it and debugging when the robot doesn't reach the target.

modes.reason: Left/right confusion is extremely common at Year 1 and requires targeted practice. Students need repeated experience with left/right from their own perspective — and from another person facing them — before they can reliably follow peer-given directions.

nodes.label: Create and give directions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a sequence of directional instructions to move an object or person from one location to another, testing whether the instructions work.
criteria: Creates a direction sequence that successfully moves a person or object to the target location when followed exactly.
Revises the instructions when the target is not reached, identifying the specific instruction that caused the error.

width.minimum: Give a three-step direction sequence to move an object or peer to a new location; check whether the instructions were followed successfully.
width.typical: Create multi-step direction sequences using directional language; give instructions to a peer and observe whether the instructions are followed as intended; revise instructions if the target was not reached; use ordinal and positional language to describe positions within a line or space.
wider: Design a direction puzzle for a peer — writing the instructions on paper — and exchange puzzles, testing and giving feedback on precision.
Create an algorithm for a floor robot to reach a target, iterating the instruction sequence based on observed robot movement.

modes.reason: Writing directions from a giver's perspective requires spatial perspective-taking — imagining the path from the mover's point of view. Students who give ambiguous instructions (e.g. 'go forward a bit') need support in making the algorithm precise enough to be followed without interpretation.

nodes.label: Algorithms for movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a step-by-step algorithm of instructions to move an object or person through a space, recognising that each instruction must be precise and complete.
criteria: Creates a movement algorithm that reaches the target when followed exactly.
Explains why each instruction in the algorithm must be precise.

width.minimum: Create a movement algorithm of at least four steps; explain what an algorithm is (a set of instructions that must be followed exactly).
width.typical: Create and follow movement algorithms; recognise that ambiguous or imprecise instructions cause failure; refine algorithms based on testing; connect the robot role-play to the concept of a precise algorithmic instruction set.
wider: Program a digital floor robot using a sequence of coded direction instructions, comparing the precision required for digital instructions with the precision used in verbal instructions.

Create a direction narrative describing a journey across Country/Place, integrating landmark-based and compass-based directional language, and connecting to First Nations ways of describing movement through space.

modes.reason: Creating a complete, working movement algorithm requires students to coordinate spatial reasoning, directional language, sequence, and precision simultaneously. This is the integration node for the descriptor's full demand — and a genuine early encounter with algorithmic thinking.

descriptors.title: Acquire and record categorical data
descriptors.description: Acquire and record data for categorical variables in various ways including using digital tools, objects, images, drawings, lists, tally marks and symbols
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images (AC9MFST01). They have not yet designed data collection processes, selected from multiple recording formats, or reviewed the effectiveness of their collection method.

nodes.label: Identify categories and plan collection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify categories for a data collection question and plan how to record responses before collecting.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who collect without defined categories produce data that cannot be recorded consistently or compared across responses — this directly undermines Node 2 (recording using consistent formats) and Node 3 (reviewing for completeness and comparability).
criteria: Names the categories that will be used before data collection begins.
Selects a recording format appropriate to the data question.

width.minimum: For a given data question, identify at least two categories and choose a recording format before starting to collect data.
width.typical: Discuss possible data questions of interest; identify appropriate categories for the variable; select a recording format (list, tally, objects, drawings) that matches the context; predict what the data might show; begin collection with the plan in place.
wider: Explore yes/no question trees as a data collection tool (chatbot role-play), planning the category structure before the questions are asked.
Investigate how data categories are structured in First Nations representational systems — examining how different purposes for representing information lead to different categorical frameworks.

modes.reason: Students who jump directly to collecting without planning categories often produce data that cannot be compared or interpreted. Scaffolding the pre-collection step — naming categories, choosing format — is the key teaching move for building statistical thinking.

nodes.label: Record using multiple formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record data for a categorical variable using at least two different recording formats, including at least one involving a mark or symbol system (tally, emoji, sticker).
criteria: Records data accurately in at least two different formats.
Explains what each recording format shows and how it could be used to answer the question.

width.minimum: Record data using one mark-based format (tally marks, stickers or emojis) and one other format (list or drawing).
width.typical: Record data using a range of formats — lists, tally marks, objects, images, drawings and symbols; use digital tools where appropriate (star charts, emoji charts); review recordings and explain what each format shows.
wider: Explore ways of representing data through stories and symbols used by First Nations Australians, comparing these formats with conventional tally and list methods and discussing what different formats communicate.
Compare hand-drawn and digital recording formats for the same data set, discussing the advantages of each.
Create an emoji-based data recording system for a class survey, designing symbols for each category and presenting the result to the class.

modes.reason: Students need to develop a repertoire of recording formats so they can match format to context. Each format (list, tally, drawing, digital) has different affordances — building familiarity with the full set is the goal at this node.

nodes.label: Review and reflect on collection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can review collected data, explain what it shows and suggest how the collection method could be improved next time.
criteria: States at least one finding from the collected data.
Suggests one specific improvement to the collection method or category design.

width.minimum: Review collected data and state one thing the data shows; suggest one change to the collection method.
width.typical: Examine collected data and generate questions it could answer; identify whether the categories were helpful or whether they would be changed; consider whether the recording method captured all relevant responses; describe what was learned from the data.
wider: Compare two data sets collected on the same question using different methods, evaluating which method produced clearer or more useful data.
Investigate a class data question across time (daily mood tracking using emojis) and reflect on how the data changed and what patterns emerged.

modes.reason: Reviewing and reflecting integrates all prior nodes — category design, recording, and data interpretation — into the full statistical enquiry cycle. This is where students move from data producer to data analyst.

descriptors.title: Represent and compare categorical data
descriptors.description: Represent collected data for a categorical variable using one-to-one displays and digital tools where appropriate; compare the data using frequencies and discuss the findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collect, sort and compare data represented by objects and images (AC9MFST01). They can acquire and record data using lists, tallies and symbols (AC9M1ST01). They have not yet represented data in formal one-to-one displays, used frequency counts to compare categories, or discussed findings in terms of most/least frequent categories.

nodes.label: Create one-to-one displays
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent categorical data in a one-to-one display (pictograph or object display) where each item represents exactly one data value.
nodes.hinge_reason: Displays that violate the one-to-one principle cannot be reliably read for frequency comparison in Node 3 — students who use differently-sized symbols or misaligned rows produce displays from which frequency comparisons are invalid.
criteria: Creates a one-to-one display with each data value represented by exactly one object or symbol.
Arranges symbols clearly into categories.

width.minimum: Create one pictograph or object display for a categorical data set; ensure one object or drawing represents one data value.
width.typical: Create pictographs with objects or drawings; discuss category choice; arrange items clearly into categories; reflect on whether the chosen categories were helpful; understand that one symbol represents one data value (one-to-one principle).
wider: Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Kolap from Mer Island), recording outcomes, creating a one-to-one display and discussing what patterns the display shows.
Create digital one-to-one displays using available classroom tools, comparing the digital representation with a hand-drawn pictograph of the same data.

modes.reason: The one-to-one principle (each symbol/object represents exactly one data value) requires careful physical practice to establish. Students who use different-sized symbols or place symbols in non-aligned rows produce displays that cannot be read reliably — precise construction needs explicit reinforcement.

nodes.label: Translate between display formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can translate data between a list or tally and a pictograph, and between a pictograph and a tally, recognising that the same data can be represented in multiple ways.
criteria: Converts a tally chart to a pictograph (or vice versa) with matching totals for each category.
Uses skip counting by fives to read tally marks.

width.minimum: Convert a tally chart into a pictograph (or vice versa) for the same data set; confirm the total count is preserved.
width.typical: Translate between lists, tally charts and pictographs; use skip counting by fives to count tally marks efficiently; explain what each format shows and when each is useful; recognise that all formats represent the same underlying data.
wider: Compare three representations of the same data (list, tally, pictograph) and evaluate which is most useful for answering specific questions about the data.
Represent the same data using both paper-based and digital formats, discussing what is easier and harder to communicate in each.

modes.reason: Translating between formats requires students to track data integrity — the count in each format must match. Scaffolding the translation with a checking step (do the totals match?) builds data discipline and reinforces the idea that the format is a representation of the same underlying information.

nodes.label: Compare frequencies and discuss findings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the frequencies of categories in a data display, identify the most and least frequent categories, and discuss what the data shows.
criteria: Identifies the most and least frequent categories in a data display.
States one finding from the data in terms of the original question.

width.minimum: State which category has the most responses and which has the fewest from a completed display; describe one finding from the data.
width.typical: Compare category frequencies using counting strategies; identify the most and least frequent categories; discuss what the data shows in terms of the original question; address zero-frequency categories (include or omit); explain what the term 'frequency' means.
wider: Investigate class data collected over multiple sessions (e.g. daily mood, weekly weather), comparing frequencies across time and discussing whether the pattern is consistent or variable.
Discuss what additional questions the data raises and plan a follow-up investigation to answer one of them.

modes.reason: Comparing frequencies and discussing findings requires students to read the display, apply counting strategies, interpret the result in the context of the original question, and communicate the finding — the full statistical sense-making cycle operating together.

descriptors.title: Additive patterns
descriptors.description: recognise, describe and create additive patterns that increase or decrease by a constant amount, using numbers, shapes and objects, and identify missing elements in the pattern
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise, continue and create simple repeating patterns with shapes and objects, and skip count in sequences (AC9M1A01, AC9M1A02). They have not yet described the constant additive term in a growing/shrinking pattern or used it to find missing elements.

nodes.label: Recognising the constant term
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the constant amount being added or subtracted in a given additive pattern and describe it.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students can only identify the constant term in number sequences but not in shape or object arrangements, Nodes 2 and 3 are brittle — creating patterns in non-numeric forms and finding missing elements in varied representations both depend on a generalised constant-term concept.
criteria: Identifies the constant term in an additive pattern (e.g. 'adds 2 each time')
Distinguishes between an increasing and a decreasing additive pattern

width.minimum: Examine a given additive number pattern; state the constant term (e.g. 'add 2 each time' or 'subtract 3 each time').
width.typical: Identify the constant term in additive patterns presented as number sequences, shape sequences and object arrangements; describe the pattern in words; recognise patterns increasing and decreasing.
wider: Recognise additive patterns in the built environment (windows per carriage, wheels per car); record results in a table and state the constant term
Recognise additive patterns in First Nations Australians' material culture on Country/Place; represent using drawings, counters and numbers and describe the constant term

modes.reason: Students may recognise the constant term in simple number sequences but fail to identify it in shape or object arrangements, or in decreasing patterns. Multiple context types are needed to build a generalised understanding of 'constant additive term' independent of representation.

nodes.label: Creating additive patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an additive pattern with a specified constant term using materials, shapes or numbers, and describe the rule.
criteria: Creates an additive pattern with the specified constant term
Describes the pattern rule so another person could replicate it

width.minimum: Create one additive pattern (increasing or decreasing) with a given constant term using materials or numbers; describe the rule in words.
width.typical: Create additive patterns using numbers, shapes and objects; describe the rule; write the associated number sequence; connect a material-based pattern to its number sequence.
wider: Use matchsticks or connecting shapes to create a growing pattern (e.g. triangles: 3, 5, 7...); write the number sequence and describe so someone else can replicate it with different materials
Use dynamic digital tools or generative AI to create patterns increasing or decreasing by a constant amount; discuss the instructions given to achieve the output

nodes.label: Finding missing elements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the constant term in an additive pattern to identify missing elements, including non-adjacent missing terms.
criteria: Correctly identifies a missing element in an additive pattern using the constant term
Explains how the constant term was used to find the missing value

width.minimum: Given an additive pattern with one missing element, use the constant term to find the missing value.
width.typical: Identify missing elements in additive patterns in number sequences, tables and object arrangements; use the constant term to work forward or backward; explain the reasoning.
wider: Find missing terms that are not adjacent (e.g. given 1st and 4th terms, find the 2nd and 3rd); explain the strategy
Create a pattern with a deliberately missing element; challenge a partner to identify the rule and find the missing term

descriptors.title: Addition facts to 20
descriptors.description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with addition facts to 20; extend and apply facts to develop related subtraction facts
descriptors.knowledge: Students add and subtract numbers within 20 using part-part-whole knowledge to 10 and a variety of calculation strategies (AC9M1N04). They have not yet established recall-level fluency with all addition facts to 20 or systematically derived the related subtraction facts.

nodes.label: Strategies for facts to 20
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate any addition fact to 20 using at least two strategies (doubles, near doubles, counting on, combinations to 10, bridging to 10) and explain their choice.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with only one strategy (typically counting on) cannot achieve the automaticity required at Node 2 — single-strategy learners plateau at slow reconstruction rather than reaching recall. Node 2 fluency depends on having multiple routes to each fact.
criteria: Applies at least two different strategies to addition facts within 20
Names the strategy and explains the steps

width.minimum: Apply two different strategies to addition facts within 20; explain the steps of each strategy.
width.typical: Apply all five strategy types (doubles, near doubles, counting on, combinations to 10, bridging to 10) across the range of addition facts to 20; choose the most efficient strategy for a given fact; use ten-frames or materials to support reasoning.
wider: Systematically record all partitions of 10 (e.g. 10=10+0, 10=9+1...); explain patterns noticed and how they connect to addition facts
Use a hundreds chart or ten-frame patterns to visualise combinations to 10 and 20; discuss what patterns emerge

modes.reason: Students need to build a range of strategies before moving to recall. A student who knows only one strategy (counting on) is slower and more error-prone at recall than a student with multiple routes to the same fact. Each strategy type needs explicit development.

nodes.label: Recall of addition facts to 20
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recall addition facts to 20 with fluency, without needing to reconstruct each answer from a strategy.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 (deriving subtraction facts) and two-digit addition (AC9M2N04) both require fluent recall under cognitive load. Students still reconstructing addition facts from strategies cannot hold the part-part-whole relationship in working memory while also deriving the inverse.
criteria: Recalls a range of addition facts to 20 correctly without counting-on
Demonstrates fluency (prompt response) across a random selection of facts within 20

width.minimum: Recall a set of addition facts to 20 without reconstructing from counting; respond promptly when presented with random facts within range.
width.typical: Recall all addition facts to 20 fluently; demonstrate proficiency across the full range including facts that students commonly miscalculate (e.g. 7+8, 6+7, 8+9).
wider: Limited width — addition fact recall is a fluency skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extension involves applying recalled facts to multi-digit addition (e.g. 56+37 using 6+7 knowledge) or deriving related subtraction facts, which are addressed in node 3.

modes.reason: Recall requires practise volume, not broader contexts. Students who know strategies but haven't practised to the point of recall are slower and more prone to error under cognitive load. This is a practise node — repeated exposure across varied formats (oral, written, games) builds automaticity.

nodes.label: Related subtraction facts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can derive related subtraction facts from known addition facts (e.g. 8+7=15, so 15-7=8 and 15-8=7) and explain the connection.
criteria: States both related subtraction facts given an addition fact (e.g. from 8+7=15, gives 15-7=8 and 15-8=7)
Explains why the addition and subtraction facts are related using part-part-whole language

width.minimum: Given an addition fact, state the two related subtraction facts and explain why they are related.
width.typical: Derive related subtraction facts systematically from addition facts to 20; use part-part-whole diagrams to show the relationship; apply to solve subtraction problems by recalling the related addition fact.
wider: Partition collections of up to 20 in all possible ways; record all related addition and subtraction facts; explain patterns noticed
Apply related facts to check subtraction answers: 'I can check 15-7=8 by adding 7+8'

modes.reason: The inverse relationship between addition and subtraction is not intuitively obvious to Year 2 students. The reasoning scaffold — 'if the whole is 15 and one part is 7, the other part must be 8' — needs to be made explicit and connected to the part-part-whole model before students can apply it independently.

descriptors.title: Multiplication facts for twos
descriptors.description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for twos; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts using doubling and halving
descriptors.knowledge: Students quantify sets by skip counting (AC9M1N03) and solve sharing/grouping problems (AC9M1N06). They have not yet connected skip counting in twos to multiplication facts or established doubling and halving as inverse operations.

nodes.label: Doubling as multiplication by 2
nodes.checkpoint: Students can double numbers within 20 using materials or mental strategies and connect doubling to multiplying by 2.
criteria: Doubles numbers within 20 correctly using materials or mental strategy
Explains that 'double 6', 'twice 6' and '6 multiplied by 2' mean the same thing

width.minimum: Double at least five numbers within 20 using materials; connect to 'multiply by 2' language.
width.typical: Double numbers within 20 using physical and virtual materials; recognise the relationship between double, twice and multiply by 2; use a hundreds chart to colour doubles and identify the pattern.
wider: Use doubling to establish near doubles: if double 5 is 10, then double 6 is 10+2=12; extend to double 4 is 10-2=8
Investigate doubling patterns on a hundreds chart; describe the pattern of even numbers produced

nodes.label: Recall of twos multiplication facts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recall multiplication facts for twos (2×1 through 2×10) with fluency.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires students to derive division facts from known multiplication facts under the inverse relationship. Students still reconstructing twos facts by counting cannot hold the part-whole structure in working memory simultaneously — fluency at Node 2 is the prerequisite.
criteria: Recalls twos multiplication facts within 2×10 correctly
Responds to randomly ordered twos facts without counting

width.minimum: Recall twos multiplication facts within 2×10 without reconstructing by counting; respond promptly when presented with random facts.
width.typical: Recall all twos multiplication facts fluently; recognise that 2×8 = 8×2 (commutativity); apply to find related facts (e.g. 8 twos uses the same fact as 2 eights).
wider: Limited width — multiplication fact recall for twos is a fluency skill that does not vary meaningfully across contexts. Extension involves applying known twos facts to derive other facts (e.g. 4×3 = double 2×3) or connecting to related division facts, addressed in node 3.

modes.reason: Fluency with twos facts requires practise volume. Games and repeated oral/written practice across different formats build automaticity that supports later work on other multiplication tables.

nodes.label: Halving as division by 2
nodes.checkpoint: Students can halve numbers within 20 and connect halving to dividing by 2, deriving related division facts from known multiplication facts.
criteria: Halves even numbers within 20 correctly
States the related division fact for a given twos multiplication fact
Explains why doubling and halving are inverse operations

width.minimum: Halve at least four even numbers within 20 using materials; state the related division fact.
width.typical: Halve numbers within 20; connect to 'divide by 2' language; derive related division facts from multiplication facts (e.g. 2×7=14, so 14÷2=7); practise doubling and halving games.
wider: Use a doubling and halving game (e.g. virtual dice: choose to double or halve to reach a target number); apply known facts strategically
Investigate: 'If I know 2×9=18, what else do I know?' — list all related facts including division

modes.reason: The inverse relationship between multiplication and division — like that between addition and subtraction — requires explicit reasoning scaffold. Students need to see that 'if 2 groups of 7 make 14, then 14 shared into groups of 2 gives 7' before they can derive division facts independently.

descriptors.title: Measure with informal units
descriptors.description: measure and compare objects based on length, capacity and mass using appropriate uniform informal units and smaller units for accuracy when necessary
descriptors.knowledge: Students order and compare objects by length, mass and capacity using direct comparison and a single informal unit (AC9M1M01, AC9M1M02). They have not yet justified unit choice, compared multiple units, or used smaller units for greater accuracy.

nodes.label: Uniform informal units
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why the informal unit used for measurement must be uniform (identical) and demonstrate what happens when non-uniform units are used.
nodes.hinge_reason: All measurement activity in Nodes 2 and 3 depends on students understanding why unit uniformity is non-negotiable. Students who accept any same-type unit regardless of size will produce measurements in Nodes 2 and 3 that are meaningless — they cannot compare results across objects or justify unit choice.
criteria: Explains that the informal unit must be the same size/mass for measurement to be valid
Demonstrates or explains what goes wrong when non-uniform units are used

width.minimum: Measure the same object with two different-sized informal units; compare results; explain why the units must be the same.
width.typical: Measure objects using uniform informal units across length, capacity and mass; explain why uniformity matters; demonstrate what goes wrong when units differ (e.g. different shoe sizes give different measurements of the same distance).
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' use of body parts (e.g. hands) as uniform informal units; discuss how a standard unit is maintained when different people measure
Investigate First Nations Australians' use of body measurement to understand animal behaviour: e.g. measuring length, width and depth of animal tracks

modes.reason: The need for uniformity is not obvious — students often accept any same-type unit without noticing size differences. Demonstrating failure cases (non-uniform units produce different counts) and then success cases (uniform units produce consistent counts) across multiple contexts makes the principle visible.

nodes.label: Measuring and comparing across attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure and compare objects using appropriate informal units for length, capacity and mass, counting units and recording results.
criteria: Measures an object using informal units for at least two different attributes
Compares two objects for an attribute and states which is longer/heavier/holds more

width.minimum: Measure at least one object using informal units for each attribute (length, capacity, mass); count the units; compare two objects for one attribute.
width.typical: Measure and compare a range of objects using appropriate informal units for length (shorter/longer), capacity (holds more/less) and mass (heavier/lighter); count units; record results; justify unit choice.
wider: Compare the capacity of several containers using sand and a spoon or cup; record results; explain the measurement process including why smaller units give more accurate comparisons
Use balance scales to compare the mass of several objects; count informal units; explain why the unit chosen must have the same mass

nodes.label: Smaller units for accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a smaller informal unit gives greater accuracy and choose a smaller unit when more precision is needed.
criteria: Explains that a smaller informal unit gives a more accurate measurement
Explains why a smaller unit produces a larger count for the same object
Chooses an appropriate unit size for a given measurement task and justifies the choice

width.minimum: Measure one object using a large informal unit; re-measure using a smaller unit; explain why the smaller unit gives a more accurate result.
width.typical: Choose suitable informal units for measuring a range of objects; justify why a shorter unit suits shorter objects or when more accuracy is needed; explain why a smaller unit produces a larger count.
wider: Measure the same length with three different informal units of different sizes; record all three counts; discuss the inverse relationship between unit size and count
Investigate: can you be more accurate with a smaller unit? Measure a short object with a large unit and a small unit; compare and explain

modes.reason: The counterintuitive relationship between unit size and count (smaller unit → larger count for the same length) is a reliable confusion point. Students need to encounter this across multiple measurement contexts — length, capacity, mass — before it generalises.

descriptors.title: Halves, quarters and eighths in context
descriptors.description: identify common uses and represent halves, quarters and eighths in relation to shapes, objects and events
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally explored equal sharing (AC9M1N06). They have not yet identified halves, quarters and eighths in measurement and time contexts or connected the fraction language to real-world uses.

nodes.label: Halves and quarters in shapes and objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and represent halves and quarters of shapes and objects, confirming that parts are equal.
criteria: Folds or cuts a shape into halves with equal parts
Creates quarters from a half by halving again and confirms all four parts are equal

width.minimum: Fold or cut a shape into halves; then into quarters by halving again; confirm all parts are equal.
width.typical: Represent halves and quarters of shapes, paper and food objects by folding or cutting; explain that parts must be equal; connect language (half, quarter) to the fraction symbol and to repeated halving.
wider: Demonstrate how food items (sandwiches, pizzas, cakes) can be cut into halves, quarters and eighths by halving twice; ensure parts are equal
Investigate cup and spoon measures in cooking: what half or quarter of a cup means; compare half-cup to full cup using sand or water
