nodes.label: Halves and quarters in length and position
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use halves and quarters to describe positions and distances in familiar contexts.
criteria: Identifies the halfway point on a given length or distance
Uses the word 'quarter' to describe a position one-quarter of the way along a length

width.minimum: Identify and mark the halfway point on a given length or path.
width.typical: Use halves and quarters to describe lengths, positions and distances; e.g. mark the halfway point in a race, the quarter-way mark, and stand halfway between two objects.
wider: Use halves and quarters to describe positions on a number line, ruler length, or path between two points; relate to fractions of a whole length
Investigate positions on a classroom map or grid using halves and quarters

nodes.label: Halves and quarters in time and events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify halves and quarters of an hour and connect fraction language to real-world time and event contexts.
criteria: Identifies half an hour and a quarter of an hour in a given context
Connects 'half past' and 'quarter past' to the position of the big hand on a clock face

width.minimum: Identify half an hour and quarter of an hour; connect to clock positions (half past, quarter past).
width.typical: Recognise and use halves and quarters in time contexts: half an hour, quarter of an hour, half time and quarters in sporting events; connect to clock language and to the clock face as a circle divided into halves and quarters.
wider: Discuss how sirens in Australian Rules Football represent quarters and half-time; connect to the clock face as a circle divided by quarter-turns
Investigate other events or activities that use halves and quarters of time (e.g. cooking timers, race laps); explain what each fraction refers to

modes.reason: This node brings together the abstract fraction concept (equal parts of a whole) and time as a measurement context. The integration challenge is connecting 'quarter of an hour' to both the numerical fraction (15 out of 60 minutes) and the physical clock face (one quarter of the circle).

descriptors.title: Use calendars
descriptors.description: identify the date and determine the number of days between events using calendars
descriptors.knowledge: Students sequence and describe duration of events and order them using time language (AC9M1M03). They have not yet used a calendar to identify specific dates or calculate the number of days between events.

nodes.label: Reading a calendar
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate a specific date on a calendar and identify what day of the week it falls on.
criteria: Locates a named date on a monthly calendar
Identifies the day of the week for a given date

width.minimum: Locate a given date on a monthly calendar; state the day of the week it falls on.
width.typical: Locate specific dates on a calendar including school events, birthdays, public holidays; identify the day of the week for each; create a class calendar with significant dates entered.
wider: Locate and identify culturally significant dates: ANZAC Day, Easter, Diwali, Ramadan, school holidays; discuss why dates for some events change each year
Create a class calendar; enter student birthdays and upcoming school events; use it to answer questions about upcoming dates

nodes.label: Days between events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine the number of days between two events using a calendar, including events in the same month and across months.
criteria: Counts the number of days between two events in the same month
Determines the date 2 weeks after a given date using a calendar

width.minimum: Count the days between two events in the same month using a calendar.
width.typical: Determine the number of days between events within and across months; use addition to total days across months; locate a date 2 weeks prior to or after a given date.
wider: Model 'How many days are left in this year?' by identifying days remaining in the current month and adding remaining full months; use addition to solve
Investigate how many days are in each month; discuss why some months have different numbers of days

modes.reason: Counting days across a month boundary requires a multi-step reasoning process (days remaining in first month + days in intervening months + days in final month). The reasoning scaffold needs to be made visible and practised before students can apply it independently.

descriptors.title: Read analog clock
descriptors.description: recognise and read the time represented on an analog clock to the hour, half-hour and quarter-hour
descriptors.knowledge: Students sequence events by duration and use time language (AC9M1M03). They have not yet read time on an analog clock or connected clock hand positions to hours, half-hours and quarter-hours.

nodes.label: The two hands and the hour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the hour hand and minute hand on an analog clock, and read times to the hour.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both require students to read specific minute-hand positions (pointing to 6, 3, 9). Students who cannot reliably distinguish the hour and minute hands cannot interpret these positions — every subsequent clock-reading task collapses into guessing.
criteria: Identifies the hour hand and minute hand on an analog clock
Reads and sets the clock to a given time on the hour

width.minimum: Identify the hour and minute hand on a clock; read and show at least three o'clock times.
width.typical: Identify and distinguish the hour and minute hand; explain how long each hand takes to complete one full rotation and what time unit each represents; read and show times on the hour across the full 12-hour cycle.
wider: Create an analog clock from a paper plate; label the numbers, draw both hands; explain the movement of each hand as time passes
Connect clock language to duration: 'It is 3 o'clock — in one hour it will be 4 o'clock; the minute hand goes all the way around'

nodes.label: Half-past
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and show half-past times on an analog clock and explain that half-past means the minute hand is halfway around its cycle.
criteria: Reads a half-past time on an analog clock correctly
Explains that 'half past' means the minute hand is pointing to 6 (halfway around)

width.minimum: Read 'half past' for at least three different hours; explain that the minute hand is pointing to 6.
width.typical: Read and show half-past times for all hours; connect 'half past' language to the minute hand being at the halfway point in its full cycle; relate to half of 60 minutes = 30 minutes.
wider: Connect half past to the clock face divided into halves; discuss why 'half past' means the minute hand has gone halfway around
Relate to M02 — half an hour as half of the clock face circle

nodes.label: Quarter-past and quarter-to
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and show quarter-past and quarter-to times on an analog clock and explain the meaning of each.
criteria: Reads quarter-past and quarter-to times on an analog clock correctly
Explains that 'quarter to 4' means 15 minutes before 4 o'clock
Distinguishes 'quarter past 3' from 'quarter to 4' on the same clock face

width.minimum: Read 'quarter past' and 'quarter to' for at least two different hours each.
width.typical: Read and show quarter-past and quarter-to times; explain the meaning of 'quarter past' (minute hand at 3, 15 minutes into the hour) and 'quarter to' (minute hand at 9, 15 minutes before the next hour); divide the clock face into halves and quarters.
wider: Investigate the clock face divided into four quarters; connect to measures of turn — quarter-past represents a quarter-turn from the top
Compare quarter-past and quarter-to for the same hour; explain how many minutes each represents and why they add to one hour

modes.reason: 'Quarter to' is a persistent difficulty because it references the upcoming hour, not the current one. Students need multiple contexts and explicit attention to the direction of counting to distinguish 'quarter past' (minutes elapsed) from 'quarter to' (minutes remaining).

descriptors.title: Measures of turn
descriptors.description: identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full measures of turn in everyday situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students give and follow directions using positional and movement language (AC9M1SP02). They have not yet identified fractional turns as measures of rotation or connected turns to the concept of angle.

nodes.label: Full and half turns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate a full turn and a half turn in everyday contexts.
criteria: Demonstrates a full turn and a half turn correctly with body or object
Describes both turns in words (e.g. 'a half turn faces you the opposite way')

width.minimum: Demonstrate a full turn and a half turn with their body or an object; describe each in words.
width.typical: Identify, describe and demonstrate full and half turns in everyday contexts: spinning, door handles, tap handles, equipment dials; draw labelled diagrams showing direction and amount of turn.
wider: Identify things that turn in the school environment (handles, dials, switches); demonstrate half and full turns for each; label with arrows showing direction
Connect half and full turns to half-past and o'clock on a clock face

nodes.label: Quarter and three-quarter turns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate quarter and three-quarter turns, including clockwise and anticlockwise directions.
criteria: Demonstrates a quarter turn correctly in a specified direction (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Identifies a three-quarter turn and distinguishes it from a quarter turn
Uses 'clockwise' and 'anticlockwise' correctly to describe direction of turn

width.minimum: Demonstrate a quarter turn clockwise and a quarter turn anticlockwise; identify each correctly.
width.typical: Identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns; use clockwise and anticlockwise language; connect to giving and following directions.
wider: Follow and give movement instructions in a dance or drill: 'quarter turn left, half turn right'; describe the sequence of turns
Program a robot or avatar to navigate a path using quarter, half and three-quarter turns; verify the result

modes.reason: Three-quarter turns and the distinction between clockwise and anticlockwise are common error sources. Physical, embodied demonstration across multiple contexts (body, robot, diagrams) helps students build reliable mental models of rotation direction and amount.

nodes.label: Turns in directions and pathways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give and follow instructions involving quarter, half and three-quarter turns to navigate a space or grid.
criteria: Follows a set of instructions involving quarter, half and three-quarter turns to reach a target
Gives directions involving fractional turns that another person can follow successfully

width.minimum: Follow a set of instructions involving at least two different turns to reach a target position on a grid.
width.typical: Give and follow directions involving quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns to navigate grids, floor mazes or robotic pathways; locate an object in a room using fractional turn instructions.
wider: Investigate clock hands: relate quarter-turns to quarter-hours; explain how the minute hand makes a quarter-turn for every 15 minutes
Create a pathway on a grid that requires a partner to use specific turn instructions; verify the pathway works

descriptors.title: Numbers to 1000
descriptors.description: recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 1000 using physical and virtual materials, numerals and number lines
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 120 using physical and virtual materials, numerals and number lines (AC9M1N01). They have not yet encountered three-digit numbers or the place value structure of hundreds.

nodes.label: Counting into the hundreds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can count forward and backward through hundreds boundaries and recognise that the number sequence continues beyond 120 using the same patterns.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 place value work requires students to treat the hundreds position as a natural extension of the counting sequence. Students who stall or produce errors crossing boundaries (e.g. 199 → 200) cannot form correct three-digit groupings — the counting structure underlies the place value structure.
criteria: Counts forward and backward through a hundreds boundary without error
Identifies the repeating pattern in the number sequence across hundreds

width.minimum: Count forward and backward through at least one hundreds boundary (e.g. 95–105, 195–205) and identify the pattern.
width.typical: Count forward and backward through multiple hundreds boundaries; skip count in tens and hundreds from various starting points; locate approximate positions on a 0–1000 number line.
wider: Skip count in 5s, 10s and 100s from non-zero starting points; record on an open number line and describe the pattern
Investigate how many tens make 100, how many hundreds make 1000; connect to skip counting patterns

nodes.label: Place value to 1000
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read, write and represent three-digit numbers using materials grouped into hundreds, tens and ones, and explain the value of each digit.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who drop or misread zero-placeholder digits (e.g. reading 305 as 35) will produce systematic ordering errors in Node 3 — they cannot correctly compare three-digit numbers if their digit-value interpretation is unreliable.
criteria: Makes a given three-digit number using base-ten materials and states the value of each digit correctly
Writes the numeral for a set of grouped materials including at least one example with a zero digit

width.minimum: Read, write and make a given three-digit number using base-ten materials; explain the value of each digit (e.g. the 3 in 345 means 3 hundreds = 300).
width.typical: Read, write and represent a range of three-digit numbers including those with zeros in tens or ones position; explain each digit's value; match numerals to grouped materials and vice versa.
wider: Collect and group a large quantity of objects (e.g. recycling items) into hundreds, tens and ones; record as a three-digit numeral and explain each group
Represent the same number in multiple ways using materials: e.g. 245 shown as 2 hundreds 4 tens 5 ones, and as 24 tens 5 ones — discuss why both are valid

modes.reason: The meaning of each digit's positional value (especially zero as a placeholder) is a well-known misconception cluster. Representing numbers in multiple physical and symbolic forms helps students see that the digit's position — not just its face value — determines its meaning.

nodes.label: Ordering three-digit numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and order a set of three-digit numbers from smallest to largest (and largest to smallest), justifying their ordering.
criteria: Orders a set of four or more three-digit numbers correctly from smallest to largest
Explains which digit position to compare first when ordering three-digit numbers
Identifies a missing number in a three-digit number sequence

width.minimum: Order a set of at least four three-digit numbers from smallest to largest; explain which digit to compare first.
width.typical: Order sets of three-digit numbers including numbers that share the same hundreds digit; locate numbers on a 0–1000 number line; identify missing numbers in a sequence.
wider: Use hundreds chart puzzles to locate positions and reason about number order using patterns in the number system
Order numbers that look or sound similar (e.g. 808, 880, 818, 881); explain the strategy used to distinguish them
Locate and order numbers on number lines with different intervals (e.g. every 10, every 100)

modes.reason: Numbers that look or sound similar (808 vs 880) are a documented confusion point. Working across multiple ordering contexts — number lines, charts, symbolic sets — helps students build reliable comparison strategies anchored to place value rather than superficial features.

descriptors.title: Partition three-digit numbers
descriptors.description: partition, rearrange, regroup and rename two- and three-digit numbers using standard and non-standard groupings; recognise the role of a zero digit in place value notation
descriptors.knowledge: Students partition one- and two-digit numbers in different ways including into tens and ones (AC9M1N02). They have not yet partitioned three-digit numbers, worked with non-standard groupings, or reasoned about zero as a placeholder.

nodes.label: Standard partitioning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a three-digit number into hundreds, tens and ones using materials and explain the value of each part.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 non-standard regrouping requires students to reason about how many tens are contained in a hundreds group. Students who omit zeros or misread place value cannot perform this reasoning — they cannot regroup what they have not correctly partitioned.
criteria: Partitions a three-digit number into hundreds, tens and ones using materials
Writes the expanded form of a three-digit number including one with a zero digit

width.minimum: Partition at least two three-digit numbers into hundreds, tens and ones using base-ten materials; match to expanded form (e.g. 300 + 40 + 5).
width.typical: Partition a range of three-digit numbers including those with a zero digit; represent as expanded notation; compare the digits of a numeral with grouped materials.
wider: Partition three-digit numbers with zero in different positions (tens, ones, hundreds) and explain why the numeral still has three digits
Use a range of materials (base-ten blocks, bundling sticks, collections of objects) to represent the same number and compare the representations

modes.reason: Zero as a placeholder is a persistent misconception — students may omit zeros or misread 305 as 35. Multiple representations across different contexts (materials, expanded form, numerals) help consolidate the concept that zero holds a position even when no quantity occupies it.

nodes.label: Non-standard regrouping
nodes.checkpoint: Students can rename a three-digit number using non-standard groupings (e.g. 245 as 24 tens and 5 ones) and explain why both representations are equivalent.
criteria: Renames a three-digit number in at least one non-standard way using materials
Explains why the renamed form represents the same quantity as the standard form

width.minimum: Rename one three-digit number in at least one non-standard way using materials; explain why the value is unchanged.
width.typical: Rename two- and three-digit numbers in multiple ways using standard and non-standard groupings; use knowledge of place value to explain equivalence; e.g. 245 as 2 hundreds 45 ones or 24 tens 5 ones.
wider: Find all possible ways to rename a given three-digit number using different groupings; record systematically and look for patterns
Use non-standard partitioning to assist mental addition: e.g. rename 138 as 13 tens and 8 ones to add 40 more

modes.reason: Non-standard regrouping requires students to reason through equivalence explicitly — it is not immediately obvious that 24 tens and 5 ones equals 245. The reasoning scaffold of 'how many tens are in 2 hundreds?' needs to be made visible before students can apply it independently.

descriptors.title: Halves, quarters and eighths
descriptors.description: recognise and describe one-half as one of 2 equal parts of a whole and connect halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informally explored equal sharing (AC9M1N06). They have not yet named halves, quarters or eighths as unit fractions, or connected them through the structure of repeated halving.

nodes.label: One-half as equal parts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and create one-half of a shape, object or collection, explaining that both parts must be equal.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 depend on halving — creating quarters by halving a half, and eighths by halving a quarter. Students who accept unequal parts as halves will produce incorrect quarters and eighths, and the repeated-halving structure breaks completely.
criteria: Creates or identifies one-half of a shape, object or collection with equal parts
Explains that both halves must be equal — not just two parts

width.minimum: Share a collection or fold a shape into 2 equal parts; identify one part as one-half; confirm equality of the two parts.
width.typical: Create halves of shapes, objects and collections using different methods (folding, measuring, sharing); explain 'a half is one part out of 2 equal parts of a whole'; compare halves of different-sized wholes.
wider: Compare half of a set of 12 counters with half of a set of 8 counters — discuss how both are one-half even though they are different amounts
Create halves using measurement contexts: half of a strip of paper, half of a cup of water; explain what 'equal' means in each case

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse half with 'one of two parts' without understanding the equal-parts constraint, and conflate the size of the half with the concept of one-half (e.g. thinking half of 12 is bigger than half of 8, so it's 'more than a half'). Multiple contexts — shapes, objects and collections — help students see that the relationship (1 of 2 equal parts) is what defines one-half, not the size.

nodes.label: Quarters through repeated halving
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create quarters by halving a half, and name each part as one-quarter.
criteria: Creates quarters by halving a half using a material or shape
Names each of the four equal parts as one-quarter and confirms they are equal in size

width.minimum: Fold or divide a shape or object in half, then fold the half in half again; name each of the four equal parts as one-quarter.
width.typical: Create quarters of shapes, objects and collections using repeated halving; demonstrate that a quarter is a half of a half; name parts and compare sizes.
wider: Investigate how food items (sandwiches, pizzas, slices) can be cut into quarters by halving twice; confirm all parts are equal
Explore halves and quarters in real measurement contexts: half a cup, quarter of a metre length, half an hour

nodes.label: Eighths through repeated halving
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create eighths by halving a quarter, explain that an eighth is a half of a quarter, and compare the sizes of halves, quarters and eighths of the same whole.
criteria: Creates eighths by repeated halving and names each part as one-eighth
States that an eighth is smaller than a quarter and a quarter is smaller than a half of the same whole
Explains the relationship: a quarter is a half of a half; an eighth is a half of a quarter

width.minimum: Divide a shape or strip into eighths by repeated halving; name each part as one-eighth; state that an eighth is a half of a quarter.
width.typical: Create and name halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving; compare the size of parts (eighths are smaller than quarters, quarters are smaller than halves); relate number of parts to the size of each part.
wider: Use repeated halving to subdivide shapes in different ways; discuss why the more times you halve, the smaller each part becomes
Divide a shape into 4 equal parts and 8 equal parts; compare one-quarter and one-eighth; connect to the unit fraction rule (4 equal parts → one-quarter; 8 equal parts → one-eighth)

modes.reason: This node brings together halves, quarters and eighths as a connected structure. The key integration is the inverse relationship: more equal parts means each part is smaller. Students need to coordinate the part-count, the name, and the size simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Add and subtract two-digit numbers
descriptors.description: add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers, representing problems using number sentences, and solve using part-part-whole reasoning and a variety of calculation strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students add and subtract numbers within 20 using part-part-whole knowledge to 10 and a variety of calculation strategies (AC9M1N04). They have not yet extended these strategies to two-digit numbers or represented problems as number sentences.

nodes.label: Number sentences for problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent an addition or subtraction situation as a number sentence and explain how each number in the sentence connects to the problem.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both require students to represent problems as number sentences before applying strategies. Students who cannot form a number sentence from a situation have no structure to reason from — strategy selection and application cannot occur.
criteria: Writes a correct number sentence for an addition or subtraction situation
Identifies what each number in the sentence represents in the context

width.minimum: Write a number sentence for a given addition or subtraction situation; identify what each number in the sentence represents.
width.typical: Represent addition and subtraction problems using number sentences and bar models; explain the connection between each number and the situation; recognise that the same situation can be represented as both an addition and subtraction sentence.
wider: Use First Nations Australians' stories and dances to represent addition and subtraction relationships as number sentences; discuss how the two operations balance each other
Write number sentences for situations where one quantity is unknown (missing addend); explain how part-part-whole helps find the missing value

nodes.label: Strategies for two-digit addition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add two-digit numbers using at least two strategies (e.g. bridging tens, partitioning, near doubles) and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Correctly adds two two-digit numbers using a mental strategy
Explains the reasoning steps of the strategy used
Applies at least two different strategies to the same problem type

width.minimum: Add two two-digit numbers using one mental strategy; explain the steps (e.g. partition, bridge to ten, combine).
width.typical: Apply strategies including near doubles, part-part-whole to 10, bridging tens and partitioning to mentally solve two-digit addition problems; use informal jottings to track steps; recognise that zero added leaves a number unchanged.
wider: Apply the associative property to rearrange addends for easier calculation: e.g. 7+8 = 7+(7+1) = (7+7)+1
Use a number line or hundreds chart to solve two-step addition problems; compare results with mental strategies and explain why they give the same answer

modes.reason: At this node students need to build a repertoire of strategies rather than rely on a single approach. Each strategy (bridging, partitioning, near doubles) suits different problem types — building range means students can select flexibly.

nodes.label: Strategies for two-digit subtraction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can subtract one- and two-digit numbers using part-part-whole reasoning and at least one mental strategy, and represent the problem as a number sentence.
criteria: Subtracts a one- or two-digit number from a two-digit number correctly
Represents the subtraction as a number sentence
Explains the strategy steps used

width.minimum: Subtract a one- or two-digit number from a two-digit number using a mental strategy; represent as a number sentence.
width.typical: Apply strategies including counting back, bridging tens and partitioning to subtract one- and two-digit numbers; use informal jottings; connect subtraction to related addition facts (inverse relationship).
wider: Use a physical or mental number line to solve multi-step subtraction problems (e.g. gift card problem: $100 - $38 - $15)
Explore the inverse relationship by writing the related addition fact for a subtraction problem; discuss why knowing one helps you solve the other

modes.reason: Subtraction is more error-prone than addition at this stage because students may revert to counting back from the minuend rather than using efficient strategies. Working across multiple problem contexts — including those where the structure clearly suggests bridging or adding up — helps students see that the choice of strategy depends on the numbers involved.

descriptors.title: Multiply and divide with strategies
descriptors.description: multiply and divide by one-digit numbers using repeated addition, equal grouping, arrays, and partitioning to support a variety of calculation strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving equal sharing and grouping (AC9M1N06). They have not yet formalised arrays or used repeated addition, skip counting and partitioning as multiplication and division strategies.

nodes.label: Equal groups and repeated addition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a multiplication situation as equal groups and as a repeated addition number sentence.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 arrays require students to interpret rows as equal groups and columns as equal groups. Students who cannot form or count equal groups cannot name arrays or use them to find totals — the array concept is built directly on the equal-groups foundation.
criteria: Makes equal groups for a given multiplication situation and counts the total
Writes a repeated addition sentence that matches the situation

width.minimum: Make equal groups for a multiplication situation (e.g. 4 trays of 6); count by repeated addition; write the addition sentence.
width.typical: Represent multiplication situations as equal groups, skip counting and repeated addition; write number sentences; use materials or diagrams to support calculation.
wider: Connect skip counting to repeated addition: e.g. 3, 6, 9, 12 is the same as 3+3+3+3; record both and explain the relationship
Find the total in equal-group problems from everyday contexts (wheels on cars, windows in carriages) by skip counting and repeated addition

nodes.label: Arrays
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make and name arrays for multiplication situations and use them to find totals, including by partitioning the array.
criteria: Makes an array for a given multiplication and names it correctly (e.g. '3 fours')
Uses an array to find the total by skip counting rows or columns
Shows that '3 fours' and '4 threes' give the same total using materials

width.minimum: Make an array for a given multiplication (e.g. 3×4); name it ('3 fours'); find the total by counting rows or skip counting.
width.typical: Make, name and interpret arrays for a range of multiplications; use bar models; demonstrate that different arrays can represent the same product (e.g. '3 fours' = '4 threes'); partition an array to find totals using known facts.
wider: Make different arrays for the same total (e.g. all arrays for 12); name each and connect to multiplication facts; discuss which arrangement is easiest to count
Partition a larger array using subitising and known facts: e.g. 3×5 array seen as 2 fives (10) + one more five (5)

modes.reason: The commutative property of multiplication (3 fours = 4 threes) is a key conceptual hinge that students often miss when working with arrays. Seeing different arrays that produce the same product, and naming them both ways, makes commutativity visible.

nodes.label: Division as sharing and grouping
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve division problems by sharing into equal groups (partition) and by making groups of a given size (quotition), and explain the difference.
criteria: Solves a sharing (partitive) division problem using materials and states the answer
Solves a grouping (quotitive) division problem and explains whether the answer is the number of groups or the group size
Distinguishes between the two division structures when presented with a problem

width.minimum: Solve one partitive division problem (sharing into equal groups) and one quotitive problem (making groups of a given size); find the answer using materials.
width.typical: Solve a range of partitive and quotitive division problems using materials, diagrams and skip counting; use a Think Board to show the situation, operation and answer; interpret whether the answer refers to the number of groups or the size of each group.
wider: Compare partitive and quotitive division for the same numbers: e.g. 12÷3 as 'share 12 into 3 groups' vs '12 into groups of 3' — discuss what the answer means in each case
Explore what happens when sharing doesn't divide evenly; describe the remainder in terms of the situation

modes.reason: The distinction between partitive and quotitive division is a known conceptual difficulty — students often only recognise one structure (usually sharing). Working across both problem types makes the full concept of division legible.

descriptors.title: Model additive and multiplicative problems
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations, including money transactions; represent situations and choose calculation strategies; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
descriptors.knowledge: Students use mathematical modelling to solve practical additive problems including simple money (AC9M1N05) and equal sharing/grouping problems (AC9M1N06). They have not yet modelled situations requiring a deliberate choice between additive and multiplicative strategies, or interpreted and communicated solutions in terms of context.

nodes.label: Identifying the operation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a practical problem situation and identify whether it requires addition, subtraction, multiplication or division, justifying their choice.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 representation and calculation depend on correct operation identification. Students who apply a default operation (usually addition) regardless of problem structure cannot choose appropriate strategies in Node 2 or interpret results meaningfully in Node 3.
criteria: Names the operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication or division) needed for a given practical problem
Justifies the choice by explaining how the operation matches the structure of the situation

width.minimum: Read or hear a practical problem; identify the operation needed; justify why that operation matches the situation.
width.typical: Interpret a range of additive and multiplicative problem situations; identify and justify the appropriate operation; represent the situation with a diagram or number sentence before calculating.
wider: Compare two problems with similar surface features but different operations required; discuss how to tell them apart
Create own problems that require each of the four operations; swap with a partner to identify the operation needed

modes.reason: Selecting the correct operation is the key modelling step at Year 2 and a major source of difficulty. Students often apply a preferred operation (usually addition) regardless of structure. Working across diverse problem contexts — including those where the structure is non-obvious — builds the interpretive skill.

nodes.label: Representing and solving
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical problem using a diagram, number sentence or materials, choose a calculation strategy, and find the answer.
criteria: Represents a practical problem with a diagram or number sentence
Selects and applies a calculation strategy to find the answer

width.minimum: Represent one practical problem with a diagram or number sentence; select a strategy; calculate the answer.
width.typical: Represent a range of practical problems including money transactions using diagrams, number sentences and calculation strategies; select appropriate strategies for the numbers involved; record working.
wider: Model simple money problems with whole dollar amounts using addition, subtraction, multiplication or division: e.g. class contribution problems, purchasing scenarios
Model equal grouping/sharing problems with real contexts: team sizes, food distribution; decide what to do with remainders and justify the decision
Model 'How many days left in this year?' by identifying days remaining in the current month and adding remaining full months using a calendar

modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of practical problem types — money, days, teams, food — to build a repertoire of contexts they can model. Each new context type strengthens transfer of the modelling process.

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret their calculated answer in terms of the original situation and communicate the solution clearly, including the units or context it refers to.
criteria: States the answer to a practical problem in terms of the situation, including appropriate units or labels
Judges whether the answer is reasonable given the original situation

width.minimum: State the answer to a practical problem in terms of the situation (e.g. 'There are 9 dollars each' not just '9').
width.typical: Communicate solutions to practical problems with reference to the situation; explain why the answer is reasonable; consider whether remainders affect the solution (e.g. 'there are 4 full teams with 2 people left over').
wider: Model problems from First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Yangamini); represent the relationship as a number sentence and interpret the solution in context
Solve multi-step problems and communicate each step and the final solution in terms of the original situation

modes.reason: This node brings together identifying the operation, representing the situation, and interpreting the result. The integration challenge is connecting the abstract calculation back to the concrete situation — a step students frequently omit.

descriptors.title: Classify shapes by sides
descriptors.description: recognise, compare and classify shapes, referencing the number of sides and using spatial terms such as "opposite", "parallel", "curved" and "straight"
descriptors.knowledge: Students sort, compare and classify shapes by features using informal language (AC9M1SP01). They have not yet used specific spatial terms (parallel, opposite, curved, straight) or classified shapes by number of sides systematically.

nodes.label: Spatial terms for shape features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the terms straight, curved, parallel and opposite correctly to describe the sides and features of shapes.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 both rely on students using spatial terms to describe classification properties and orientation-invariant features. Students who conflate 'parallel' with 'same length' or cannot identify curved vs straight sides cannot accurately classify shapes or explain why orientation doesn't change type.
criteria: Correctly identifies straight and curved sides in given shapes
Identifies a pair of parallel sides in a polygon and explains what makes them parallel

width.minimum: Identify straight and curved sides on a given shape; identify one pair of parallel sides in a shape where they exist.
width.typical: Use all four terms (straight, curved, parallel, opposite) to describe shape features; identify opposite sides and parallel sides in polygons; distinguish between shapes with and without parallel sides.
wider: Investigate shapes of different sporting fields and label their features using spatial terms: sidelines, parallel lines, curved boundaries
Use digital tools to create and manipulate shapes; drag vertices and describe the effect on side properties using spatial language

modes.reason: 'Parallel' is a new term at Year 2 and students commonly confuse it with 'the same length' or apply it only to horizontal lines. Multiple contexts — different shape orientations, real-world examples, digital tools — help establish the correct concept (same direction, never meeting) across varied representations.

nodes.label: Classifying by number of sides
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort and classify a collection of shapes by number of sides, including identifying and naming triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and hexagons.
criteria: Sorts a collection of shapes by number of sides correctly
Names triangles (3 sides) and quadrilaterals (4 sides) accurately

width.minimum: Sort a set of shapes into groups by number of sides; correctly count sides for each shape.
width.typical: Sort and classify shapes by number of sides; name common polygons (triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon); explain the classification rule; sort in different ways (e.g. by number of sides, by whether all sides are equal).
wider: Sort triangles and other polygons into subgroups; discuss how a triangle can have different side lengths and angles but is always a triangle
Sort quadrilaterals by properties: some have all equal sides, some have parallel opposite sides — investigate which quadrilaterals have both

nodes.label: Orientation invariance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that rotating or flipping a shape does not change its classification, and demonstrate this with examples.
criteria: Identifies a shape in a non-standard orientation as the same shape
Explains that rotating or flipping a shape does not change what type of shape it is

width.minimum: Show that a shape (e.g. triangle, rectangle) is still the same shape when turned upside down or on its side.
width.typical: Manipulate shapes in different orientations; confirm classification is unchanged; explain that shape identity depends on number of sides and properties, not orientation; recognise irregular shapes in the same category as regular ones.
wider: Cut out pictures of shapes in various orientations; sort into categories; explain why each belongs even when not in the 'standard' position
Use a digital tool to rotate and flip shapes; describe what changes (position, orientation) and what stays the same (number of sides, type)

modes.reason: Orientation dependence is a well-documented misconception: students may not recognise a triangle with a vertex pointing down as a triangle, or a square rotated 45° as a square. Multiple orientation contexts make orientation invariance explicit.

descriptors.title: Locate positions in 2D space
descriptors.description: locate positions in two-dimensional representations of a familiar space; move positions by following directions and pathways
descriptors.knowledge: Students give and follow directions in familiar spaces using positional language (AC9M1SP02). They have not yet located positions in 2D map representations or moved through represented spaces by following systematic directional pathways.

nodes.label: Interpreting 2D representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a simple map or diagram of a familiar space and locate key features or positions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 require students to track position on a 2D representation while following or giving instructions. Students who do not understand that a map represents real space from above cannot meaningfully follow pathways on it — they lack the spatial reference frame the tasks require.
criteria: Locates a named feature or position on a simple map of a familiar space
Explains what a map represents (a view of the space from above)

width.minimum: Use a simple classroom map or seating plan to locate a named position or feature.
width.typical: Interpret maps of familiar places (classroom, school grounds); identify positions of key features; use a seating plan to locate a new seat; understand that maps represent real spaces from above.
wider: Discuss why we use maps to give and receive directions and describe spatial relationships; compare the map view to the real space
Use a classroom seating plan to give directions to classmates to find their seats; discuss what information the map provides that spoken directions alone might miss

nodes.label: Following directional pathways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a set of directional instructions (including forward, backward, left, right, and fractional turns) to move through a grid or map.
criteria: Follows a set of movement instructions to reach a target position on a grid
Identifies and corrects an error in a given set of instructions that leads to the wrong position

width.minimum: Follow at least three movement instructions to move from one position to another on a grid.
width.typical: Follow movement instructions on a 4×4 grid or floor mat (forward, turns, backward) to reach a target; use a robotic toy to follow a path on a street scene mat; adjust instructions as needed.
wider: Move through a 2D maze using directional language: clockwise, anticlockwise, quarter turn, take the path to the right
Follow and create instructions for a robotic toy on a floor map; verify the path and adjust instructions when the robot doesn't reach the target

modes.reason: Connecting directional language to 2D representation is a spatial reasoning challenge — students need to interpret their position relative to the map, not just their physical orientation. Multiple grid and map contexts (floor mat, screen, paper) help build this perspective-taking.

nodes.label: Giving directional pathways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can give clear directional instructions to move from one position to another in a 2D representation, considering order, direction and distance.
criteria: Gives a set of directional instructions that successfully moves from one grid position to a target
Identifies why incorrect instructions fail and revises them

width.minimum: Give a set of at least three instructions to move from one grid position to another; verify the instructions lead to the correct target.
width.typical: Give instructions for moving through grids, maps and pathways; consider the order of instructions, direction and distance; test and revise instructions when they don't achieve the intended movement.
wider: Create a movement pathway on a grid that requires a partner to use at least three turns; write the instructions and test them
Use quarter, half and three-quarter turns in directional instructions; connect to M05 turns vocabulary

descriptors.title: Acquire and sort categorical data
descriptors.description: acquire data for categorical variables through surveys, observation, experiment and using digital tools; sort data into relevant categories and display data using lists and tables
descriptors.knowledge: Students acquire and record categorical data using lists, drawings and symbols (AC9M1ST01). They have not yet used surveys, observation experiments, or digital tools as acquisition methods, or sorted data into explicitly defined categories before recording.

nodes.label: Posing a question and choosing a method
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a question about a categorical variable and choose an appropriate method to collect data (survey, observation or experiment).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 collection requires pre-defined categories — students who have not posed a question and selected a method arrive without a category structure or data collection plan, making sorting in Node 2 arbitrary and display in Node 3 meaningless.
criteria: Poses a question about a categorical variable
Chooses an appropriate collection method and gives a reason for the choice

width.minimum: Pose one question about a categorical variable; choose whether to use a survey, observation or experiment to collect data; justify the choice.
width.typical: Pose questions about categorical variables (favourite things, transport to school, rubbish categories); select the most appropriate data collection method for each; discuss how the question shapes the method needed.
wider: Observe events before deciding on data categories: e.g. watch students arriving before deciding on transport categories; discuss how observation helps design better categories
Explore ways First Nations Australians observe, collect, sort and record data; discuss how the purpose of data collection shapes the method used

modes.reason: Matching question type to collection method is not obvious to Year 2 students. The reasoning scaffold — 'Can I ask people directly? Do I need to watch? Do I need to do a test?' — needs to be made explicit and practised across multiple question types.

nodes.label: Collecting and sorting into categories
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect data and sort it into relevant, mutually exclusive categories.
criteria: Collects data using a survey, observation or digital tool
Sorts all collected data into defined categories with no item left unsorted

width.minimum: Collect data using one method; sort responses into at least three categories; confirm that each response belongs to exactly one category.
width.typical: Collect data through surveys, observation or digital tools; define categories before collecting; sort responses; use counting strategies to determine totals per category.
wider: Use familiar software or AI tools to construct a survey; collect class data; sort and interpret responses; consider whether questions need modifying for reuse
Investigate 'How much rubbish is really rubbish?' by gathering and categorising objects: throw away, recycle, reuse; decide whether the data answers the question

nodes.label: Displaying in lists and tables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can display sorted categorical data in a list or table and use it to answer questions about most/least popular categories.
criteria: Displays sorted data in a list or table
Correctly identifies the most and least common category from the table
States the total count for at least one category

width.minimum: Transfer sorted data into a list or table; identify the most common and least common category.
width.typical: Record data in well-organised lists and tables; use counting strategies to find totals per category; answer questions from the table (most popular, least popular, how many in a category, total respondents).
wider: Compare different ways of recording the same data (list vs table vs tally); discuss which is easier to read and why
Investigate whether the question asked was clear enough; modify a survey question and discuss how the data collected might change

descriptors.title: Compare graphical representations
descriptors.description: create different graphical representations of data using software where appropriate; compare the different representations, identify and describe common and distinctive features in response to questions
descriptors.knowledge: Students represent and compare data using picture graphs and simple tables (AC9M1ST02). They have not yet created multiple different graphical representations of the same dataset or compared their common and distinctive features.

nodes.label: Creating a second representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the same dataset in two different ways (e.g. picture graph and column graph) and confirm both show the same data.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 comparison is structurally impossible without two complete representations of the same dataset. Students who cannot produce the second representation cannot engage with the comparison at all.
criteria: Creates two different representations of the same dataset
Confirms both representations show the same value for each category

width.minimum: Create two different representations of the same small dataset; confirm both show the same totals for each category.
width.typical: Create two different graphical representations (from: picture graph, column graph, dot plot, tally chart, list); use digital tools where appropriate; confirm both represent the same data; add appropriate titles and category labels.
wider: Use digital tools including AI to create picture graphs with one-to-one correspondence; decide on appropriate title and whether categories suit the context
Represent country-of-birth data for the class using two different representations; compare and discuss

nodes.label: Comparing common and distinctive features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what is the same and what is different about two graphical representations of the same data.
criteria: Identifies at least one common feature between two representations of the same data
Identifies at least one distinctive feature between the two representations
Confirms both representations show the same data despite looking different

width.minimum: Identify at least one feature that is the same and one that is different between two representations of the same data.
width.typical: Compare two representations of the same data; identify common features (same categories, same totals, same data); identify distinctive features (different visual form, different ease of reading, different scale or layout); describe each representation's information and how easy or hard it is to interpret.
wider: Compare a picture graph and column graph of the same data; describe how they look different but represent the same information; discuss which is easier to read and why
Compare three representation types for the same data (e.g. tally chart, picture graph, column graph); rank from easiest to hardest to interpret and justify

modes.reason: Students often assume different-looking representations show different data. Working across multiple dataset types and multiple representation pairs builds the understanding that the form is independent of the data — the same data can look many different ways.

descriptors.title: Addition and subtraction as inverse operations
descriptors.description: recognise and explain the connection between addition and subtraction as inverse operations, apply to partition numbers and find unknown values in number sentences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, describe and create additive patterns using numbers, shapes and objects; identify missing elements in sequences (AC9M2A01). They have not yet formally articulated the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction or applied it to find unknowns in number sentences.

nodes.label: Inverse relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain, using a part-part-whole model or bar model, why addition and subtraction are inverse operations.
nodes.hinge_reason: Conceptual understanding of the inverse relationship is the foundation for Nodes 2 and 3 — systematic partitioning and finding unknowns both require students to understand why an inverse operation works, not merely remember which operation to apply. Students who only have mechanical fact-family recall cannot flexibly solve unknowns in varied positions.
criteria: Students can write all four related facts in an addition/subtraction fact family for a given set of three numbers.
Students can explain why addition and subtraction are inverse operations using a diagram or model.

width.minimum: Use a part-part-whole diagram for one set of related addition and subtraction facts (e.g. 16+8=24, 24-8=16, 24-16=8), explaining the connection.
width.typical: Represent multiple sets of related addition and subtraction facts using part-part-whole diagrams, bar models and number lines; explain the inverse relationship for each.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian stories and dances that represent balance and transformation, connecting to the concept of inverse operations
Investigate how the inverse relationship extends to multiplication and division — introducing the structural pattern across operation families

modes.reason: Students often accept the fact families mechanically without understanding why they work. Multiple representations (part-part-whole, bar model, number line, story context) help students see the structural reason rather than memorise pairs.

nodes.label: Partitioning using inverse operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the inverse relationship to partition numbers in multiple ways and record all related facts.
criteria: Students can generate multiple partitions of a given number and write the related addition and subtraction facts.
Students can explain the relationship between the partitions and the fact family.

width.minimum: Given a total of 24, find at least three different part-part-whole partitions and write all related addition and subtraction facts for each.
width.typical: Systematically partition numbers using part-part-whole models; record complete fact families; explain how partitioning relates to the inverse operation.
wider: Explore how many ways a given number can be partitioned, connecting to combinatorics thinking (e.g. 'How many ways can 12 be split?')
Apply systematic partitioning to problem-solving: 'The answer is 30 — what could the question be?' using both addition and subtraction

modes.reason: Systematic exploration of all partitions for a number builds fluency with fact families and prepares students for algebraic thinking by demonstrating that a number has multiple equivalent decompositions.

nodes.label: Finding unknowns in number sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can find the unknown value in addition and subtraction number sentences using the inverse operation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Finding unknowns in number sentences is directly applied in AC9M3N06 mathematical modelling — practical problems frequently require students to find a missing value from a number sentence. Students who cannot apply the inverse operation to unknowns in varied positions will be unable to solve formulated problems where the unknown is not in the most familiar position.
criteria: Students can find the unknown in a number sentence where the unknown is in any position.
Students can explain which inverse operation they used and why.

width.minimum: Solve three number sentences with unknowns in different positions (e.g. □+8=24, 24-□=8, □-8=16) using the inverse operation, showing reasoning.
width.typical: Solve a range of number sentences with unknowns in any position, using inverse operations; represent the strategy clearly including with a calculator check.
wider: Explore unknowns in word problems where the unknown position varies — 'Peter had some money, spent $375, now has $158; how much did he start with?'
Connect number sentences with unknowns to algebraic equations — introducing box/variable notation as a preview of formal algebra

modes.reason: Unknown-in-different-positions problems require students to reason about the structure of the equation, not just apply a procedure. Explicit scaffolding of 'which operation undoes the given one?' prevents random guessing.
Finding unknowns integrates the inverse relationship and partitioning ideas — students who have understood nodes 1 and 2 can approach unknowns flexibly; those who haven't will guess.

descriptors.title: Mental strategies from known facts
descriptors.description: extend and apply knowledge of addition and subtraction facts to 20 to develop efficient mental strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recall and demonstrate proficiency with addition facts to 20 and related subtraction facts (AC9M2A02). They have not yet applied these facts systematically as a foundation for mental computation with larger numbers.

nodes.label: Extending known facts to larger numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a known fact (e.g. 6+7=13) to derive related calculations (e.g. 16+7=23, 60+70=130) by recognising the place value extension.
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising the place value extension from basic facts is the conceptual engine behind all mental strategies in Node 2 — students who do not see why facts extend cannot select appropriate strategies (bridging, partitioning, compensation all rely on this principle) and will revert to counting-based approaches with larger numbers.
criteria: Students can state a related larger-number calculation from a given basic fact and explain the connection.
Students can use a known addition fact to derive a larger-number subtraction fact.

width.minimum: Given three known facts, generate two related larger-number calculations for each and explain the connection.
width.typical: Apply the extension pattern across a range of addition and subtraction facts to 20; derive mental calculation results for two- and three-digit extensions.
wider: Explore how the extension principle works for subtraction facts as well — connecting 13-7=6 to 130-70=60, 1300-700=600
Investigate how doubles facts (6+6, 7+7) extend to particularly efficient mental strategies for near-doubles in large numbers

modes.reason: Students who know 6+7=13 often cannot see why 16+7=23 without re-counting. Seeing the extension pattern across multiple fact families — and across both addition and subtraction — resolves this.

nodes.label: Choosing efficient mental strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and apply an efficient mental strategy (bridging, partitioning, compensation) for a given computation with larger numbers.
criteria: Students can calculate a two- or three-digit addition or subtraction mentally using at least one named strategy.
Students can name the strategy they used and explain why they chose it.

width.minimum: Calculate three two-digit additions mentally using a named strategy; explain the strategy chosen for each.
width.typical: Apply bridging through tens, partitioning and compensation strategies across a range of additions and subtractions; choose the most efficient strategy for each.
wider: Compare two strategies applied to the same problem to determine which is more efficient and why (e.g. bridging vs compensation for 78+24)
Investigate when compensation produces an estimate rather than an exact answer, and when it produces an exact result

modes.reason: Mental strategy fluency is built through practice. Once students know the strategies, repeated application in varied contexts is what makes them genuinely 'mental' rather than laboured.
The descriptor calls for a repertoire of strategies. Students need enough practice with each strategy (bridging, partitioning, compensation) to have genuine choice.

descriptors.title: Multiplication facts 3, 4, 5 and 10
descriptors.description: recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10; extend and apply facts to develop the related division facts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts for twos; extend and apply facts to develop related division facts (AC9M2A03). They have not yet developed automatic recall of 3, 4, 5 and 10 times tables.

nodes.label: Building the 3, 5 and 10 times tables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate and explain the pattern in the 3, 5 and 10 multiplication facts using skip-counting, grouping or repeated addition.
nodes.hinge_reason: Pattern-grounded understanding of the 3, 5 and 10 tables is required for Node 2 (building the 4 times table via doubling) and Node 3 (fluent recall and division derivation) — students with only fragile rote recall will be unable to derive unknown facts under pressure or use the doubling strategy for the 4s, creating gaps that propagate into AC9M3N04 calculation tasks.
criteria: Students can state any multiplication fact for 3, 5 or 10 within the expected range.
Students can describe a pattern in the 5 or 10 times table using mathematical language.

width.minimum: Use skip-counting or repeated addition to generate the complete 3 and 5 times tables; identify and describe one pattern in each.
width.typical: Generate the 3, 5 and 10 times tables using multiple representations (skip-counting, arrays, repeated addition); identify and describe the patterns (e.g. multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5).
wider: Explore how the 10 times table connects to place value and the decimal system — explaining why multiplying by 10 shifts digits left
Investigate multiplication patterns using a calculator or spreadsheet, generating lists of multiples and describing emerging patterns

modes.reason: Students who learn times tables purely through rote recall without pattern understanding often have fragile recall under pressure. Seeing the structural pattern (multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5; 3s have a digit sum pattern) builds durable recall.

nodes.label: Building the 4 times table and deriving related facts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recall the 4 times table and explain its relationship to the 2 times table (doubling).
nodes.hinge_reason: The 4 times table and the doubling derivation strategy are both required for Node 3 fluency — students who have not built the 4s cannot complete the full set of recall targets. Additionally, the doubling reasoning scaffold is the key mechanism preventing rote overload at Node 3.
criteria: Students can state any multiplication fact for 4 within the expected range.
Students can derive a division fact from a known multiplication fact for any of 3, 4, 5 or 10.

width.minimum: Generate the 4 times table using doubling from the 2 times table; state three related division facts.
width.typical: Build the 4 times table using doubling; practise recall across all facts; derive the related division facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10.
wider: Explore how the 4 times table connects to the 8 times table through another doubling step
Apply 4 times table facts to solve real-world problems involving groups of 4 (seasons, legs of animals, corners of squares)

modes.reason: The 4=2×2 doubling derivation is a reasoning scaffold that connects the new table to already-known facts. Making this reasoning explicit prevents students from treating the 4 times table as an entirely new memorisation task.

nodes.label: Fluency and division fact extension
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recall multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10 with proficiency and immediately state the related division facts.
criteria: Students can state any multiplication fact for 3, 4, 5 or 10 without hesitation.
Students can immediately state the two related division facts for any given multiplication fact.

width.minimum: Recall any multiplication fact for 3, 4, 5 or 10 and immediately state both related division facts.
width.typical: Demonstrate fluent recall across all 3, 4, 5 and 10 times tables; derive and use related division facts in calculation contexts.
wider: Systematically explore algorithms using the multiplication facts — e.g. finding all numbers up to 100 that are divisible by 3, 4, 5 or 10
Investigate commutativity across tables: use 4×7=28 to derive 7×4, connecting to less-familiar combinations

modes.reason: Fact fluency is the explicit goal — 'recall and demonstrate proficiency' requires automaticity, which is built through practice after understanding. Students who understand patterns but hesitate under time pressure need consolidation not more breadth.

descriptors.title: Metric units and estimation
descriptors.description: identify which metric units are used to measure everyday items; use measurements of familiar items and known units to make estimates
descriptors.knowledge: Students can measure and compare objects based on length, capacity and mass using appropriate uniform informal units and smaller units for greater accuracy (AC9M2M01). They have not yet named or used metric units, or connected informal measurement to the metric system.

nodes.label: Naming metric units for everyday attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can match metric units (mm, cm, m, km; mL, L; g, kg) to appropriate everyday measurement contexts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct unit identification is the prerequisite for AC9M3M02 (measuring with instruments) — students who cannot match the attribute to the appropriate unit cannot select the right instrument or interpret the measurement result correctly.
criteria: Students can identify the appropriate metric unit for a given everyday measurement context.
Students can explain why a particular unit is appropriate for a given attribute.

width.minimum: Sort six everyday items into groups by measurement attribute and name the appropriate metric unit for each attribute.
width.typical: Examine packaging and real-world items; match measurement attributes (length, capacity, mass) to appropriate metric units; explain why a given unit is appropriate or inappropriate.
wider: Investigate how metric units on product packaging represent different scales — e.g. comparing 500mL and 2L containers, 50g and 1kg packets
Explore the structure of the metric system — prefixes milli-, centi-, kilo- — as a pattern that applies across all measurement attributes

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse units across attributes (e.g. using kilograms for length) or fail to distinguish between units within an attribute (cm vs m). Exposure across varied real-world items resolves this more effectively than explicit rules.

nodes.label: Using benchmarks to estimate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use familiar measurement benchmarks to estimate an unknown quantity and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Students can state an estimate for a measurement and identify the benchmark they used.
Students can explain why their estimate is reasonable in relation to the benchmark.

width.minimum: Use one benchmark item (e.g. 1L milk carton, 1kg of flour) to estimate the measurement of two other items; explain reasoning.
width.typical: Apply benchmark items across length, mass and capacity estimation contexts; explain reasoning referencing the benchmark; compare estimate to measured value.
wider: Estimate measurements in natural and outdoor contexts — tree heights, distances across the playground, capacity of a bucket — connecting to First Nations Australian knowledge of country
Investigate estimation error: which types of estimation (length, mass, capacity) produce more accurate results and why

modes.reason: Students who estimate only in classroom contexts with familiar items often cannot transfer the skill to outdoor or less familiar contexts. Varied real-world estimation contexts — including First Nations country-based examples — establish estimation as a generalised skill rather than a classroom exercise.

descriptors.title: Measuring with instruments
descriptors.description: measure and compare objects using familiar metric units of length, mass and capacity, and instruments with labelled markings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify which metric units are used to measure everyday items and use benchmarks to make estimates (AC9M3M01). They have not yet used measuring instruments with labelled metric markings to produce precise measurements.

nodes.label: Reading labelled markings on instruments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read a measurement from a ruler, measuring jug or scales by identifying the value at a marked graduation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Instrument reading is a prerequisite for Node 2 measurement and comparison tasks — students who can only read at labelled marks will produce incorrect measurements for the majority of real measurements that fall between graduations, undermining all subsequent comparison work.
criteria: Students can read a measurement from a marked instrument and state the value with its unit.
Students can interpret the meaning of the lines on a measuring instrument.

width.minimum: Read three measurements from two different instruments (e.g. ruler and measuring jug), identifying the unit and the value shown.
width.typical: Read measurements from rulers, measuring jugs and kitchen/bathroom scales across length, capacity and mass; interpret labelled and unlabelled graduations.
wider: Investigate how to interpolate between unlabelled graduations (e.g. a ruler with only every 5cm marked) using reasoning about equal divisions
Explore how precision varies with instrument choice — comparing a measuring jug marked in 100mL vs one marked in 10mL

modes.reason: Students often read only at labelled marks and cannot interpret positions between graduations. Exposure to varied instruments with different graduation densities resolves this.

nodes.label: Measuring and comparing across attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure objects for length, mass and capacity using appropriate instruments and compare results using metric language.
criteria: Students can use an appropriate instrument to measure an object for length, mass or capacity.
Students can compare two measurements using correct metric units and comparison language.

width.minimum: Measure and record two objects for each of length, mass and capacity; make at least one comparison statement for each attribute.
width.typical: Measure a range of objects across all three attributes; compare using metric units and comparative language; connect measurements to real-world context.
wider: Conduct a measurement investigation comparing objects across contexts (e.g. science measurement tasks) and discuss why precision matters in the context
Investigate what happens when you measure the same object with different instruments — exploring measurement variation and its sources

modes.reason: Cross-attribute measurement integrates reading skill (node 1) with instrument selection (from AC9M3M01) and the comparison of results. Students who struggle here often have a gap in instrument reading or unit identification.

descriptors.title: Formal time units
descriptors.description: recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time including days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare the duration of events
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and read time on an analog clock to the hour, half-hour and quarter-hour (AC9M2M04). They have not yet worked with the full hierarchy of time units (days, hours, minutes, seconds) or used these relationships to estimate and compare durations.

nodes.label: Relationships between time units
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state the relationships between days, hours, minutes and seconds and use these to convert between adjacent units.
nodes.hinge_reason: Time unit relationships are the prerequisite for Node 2 duration estimation and comparison — students who do not know that 1 hour = 60 minutes cannot estimate whether an event will take 'about 45 minutes' or convert between units when comparing durations. The non-decimal relationships are error-prone and must be secure before application.
criteria: Students can state the number of seconds in a minute, minutes in an hour, and hours in a day.
Students can convert a given duration between adjacent time units.

width.minimum: State the number of hours in a day, minutes in an hour, and seconds in a minute; convert two given time quantities (e.g. '3 hours = ? minutes').
width.typical: Apply the full hierarchy of time unit relationships; convert across adjacent units in both directions; explain why the relationships have the values they do (history of 60-based time).
wider: Explore why different cultures have used different time unit systems — e.g. ancient Egyptian hours, Indigenous seasonal calendars
Investigate how digital devices represent time and compare digital time displays with the unit relationships

modes.reason: Time unit relationships (60 seconds, 60 minutes, 24 hours) are non-decimal and must be memorised. Practice with varied conversion problems is more effective than broadening context here.

nodes.label: Estimating and comparing durations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate the duration of familiar events in appropriate units and compare durations using the time unit relationships.
criteria: Students can estimate the duration of a familiar event in an appropriate unit and explain the choice.
Students can compare two durations and state which is longer, converting to a common unit if needed.

width.minimum: Estimate the duration of three everyday events in appropriate units and justify the unit choice; compare two durations expressed in different units.
width.typical: Estimate and measure durations of a range of events; compare using time unit relationships; connect to planning contexts (e.g. planning a party schedule).
wider: Design a daily timetable or sequence of events, applying duration estimation and addition with time units
Investigate how estimating time relates to First Nations Australian seasonal calendars and duration of events on Country

modes.reason: Students who estimate time only in structured classroom contexts (sand timers, countdowns) often cannot apply duration reasoning to open-ended real-world planning. Timetable design and culturally situated time-keeping contexts extend the skill.

descriptors.title: Analog and digital clocks to the minute
descriptors.description: describe the relationship between the hours and minutes on analog and digital clocks, and read the time to the nearest minute
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and use the relationship between formal units of time (AC9M3M03) and can read analog time to the quarter-hour from Y2. They have not yet read analog or digital clocks to the nearest minute, or described the relationship between the hour and minute hands at all positions.

nodes.label: Minute hand and its relationship to hours
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the minute hand relates to hours on an analog clock — one full revolution = one hour = 60 minutes.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that the hour hand moves continuously (not in jumps) is required for accurate time reading in Node 2 — students with the 'static hour hand' misconception will misread times near the hour boundary and produce systematic errors across all to-the-minute readings.
criteria: Students can explain that one full revolution of the minute hand equals 60 minutes (one hour).
Students can describe where the hour hand points for a given time to the half-hour.

width.minimum: Explain the minute hand's full circuit using a clock face: state how many minutes elapse per full revolution and connect to the hour hand's movement.
width.typical: Describe the relationship between the hour and minute hands across several different times; explain how the hour hand moves as the minute hand completes revolutions.
wider: Explore how the 12-hour clock requires am/pm distinction — investigating how digital clocks encode this and why it matters
Compare 12-hour and 24-hour clock formats, connecting to contexts like train timetables and digital devices

modes.reason: The inter-relationship between both hands is not intuitively obvious — the hour hand continuously moves, not in jumps. Explicit scaffolding of 'where is the hour hand when the minute hand is at 30 minutes?' prevents the common misconception that the hour hand is static.

nodes.label: Reading time to the nearest minute
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and record time to the nearest minute on both analog and digital clocks.
criteria: Students can read an analog clock to the nearest minute.
Students can write the digital equivalent of a given analog time and vice versa.

width.minimum: Read four times shown on analog clocks to the nearest minute; record each in both analog description and digital notation (e.g. 3:47).
width.typical: Read and record times to the nearest minute on analog and digital clocks across a range of times; set a digital device to a specified time; explain the reasoning.
wider: Convert between 12-hour digital notation and analog time descriptions, including am/pm
Use time to the nearest minute for duration calculations — e.g. a program starts at 2:15 and runs for 35 minutes; when does it end?

modes.reason: Reading to the nearest minute requires precision and benefits from practice across a range of clock positions, particularly near the hour where the relationship between the minute numbers (5, 10...) and the 1-minute subdivisions is confusing.

descriptors.title: Angles as turns
