descriptors.description: identify angles as measures of turn and compare angles with right angles in everyday situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full measures of turn in everyday situations (AC9M2M05). They have not yet formally defined these turns as angles or compared general angles to a right angle benchmark.

nodes.label: Angle as a measure of turn
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that an angle measures the amount of turn between two directions, and identify quarter, half and full turns as angles.
nodes.hinge_reason: The 'angle as turn' definition is the conceptual foundation for Node 2 — students who retain the 'angles are static corners' misconception cannot reliably classify angles relative to a right angle benchmark, because they have no dynamic reference point for what a right angle represents as a turn.
criteria: Students can identify a right angle in an everyday context and explain it as a quarter turn.
Students can physically demonstrate a quarter, half and full turn and name each as an angle.

width.minimum: Demonstrate quarter and half turns physically; identify these as angles and connect them to the corner of a square (right angle) and a straight line.
width.typical: Connect quarter turn to right angle, half turn to straight angle, and full turn to 360°; identify these angles in everyday objects and situations.
wider: Explore how turns are used in navigation and robotics — programming a simple floor robot to make quarter, half and three-quarter turns
Investigate how First Nations Australian dances and ceremonies use directional turns, connecting to angle measurement

modes.reason: Students often see angles only as static corners in shapes and miss the dynamic 'turn' definition. Encountering angles in movement contexts (physical turns, robotics, dance) establishes the measure-of-turn concept more broadly.

nodes.label: Comparing angles with right angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify everyday angles as equal to, greater than, or less than a right angle.
criteria: Students can classify an angle as less than, equal to, or greater than a right angle.
Students can identify right angles in everyday environments using a right angle tester.

width.minimum: Identify three everyday angles (doors, corners, open books) as greater than, less than, or equal to a right angle; justify each classification.
width.typical: Compare a range of everyday angles with a right angle benchmark using a right angle tester; classify as acute (less than), right (equal to) or obtuse (greater than).
wider: Explore how right angles are used in construction and design — identifying right angles in building structures and why they are important
Introduce informal angle language (acute, obtuse) as natural extensions of the 'less than right angle / greater than right angle' description

descriptors.title: Money values and representation
descriptors.description: recognise the relationships between dollars and cents and represent money values in different ways
descriptors.knowledge: No direct predecessor identified in the progression map at Y3. Students have used money in additive modelling contexts at Y2 (AC9M2N06) but have not yet formally studied the dollar-cent relationship or represented money values in multiple ways.

nodes.label: Dollar and cent relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state that 100 cents = $1 and use this to convert between dollar and cent representations.
nodes.hinge_reason: The dollar-cent conversion with place value grounding is required for Node 2 and for AC9M3N06 financial modelling tasks — students who have only a mechanical rule (not a place value understanding) produce systematic errors in mixed notation and in making-change calculations.
criteria: Students can convert a cents amount to dollars and cents (e.g. 375¢ = $3.75).
Students can convert a dollar amount to cents (e.g. $4.20 = 420¢).

width.minimum: Convert three money amounts between cents and dollars; explain the relationship (100 cents = $1).
width.typical: Convert money amounts between cents and dollars in both directions; explain the place value connection — dollars are units, cents are hundredths.
wider: Investigate how different countries use different currencies and coin systems, comparing structures
Connect the dollar-cent relationship to the decimal place value system — setting up understanding of decimal notation for money amounts

modes.reason: The 100-based relationship between dollars and cents requires explicit connection to place value — students who understand this as a conversion rule without place value grounding often make errors in mixed notation (e.g. writing $1.50 as $1.5 or $150).

nodes.label: Representing money values in different ways
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a given money amount using different combinations of coins and notes, and identify equivalent representations.
criteria: Students can show two different ways to represent the same money amount using coins and notes.
Students can identify which combination of coins/notes is more efficient for a given amount.

width.minimum: Represent one money amount using two different combinations of coins and notes; confirm both are equivalent.
width.typical: Represent money amounts using multiple coin and note combinations; find the most efficient representation; connect to making change.
wider: Explore cashless payment contexts — how digital transactions represent money without physical coins, and what stays the same
Investigate how First Nations Australian communities have engaged with exchange and value systems, and how these compare to the dollar-cent system

modes.reason: Students often have only one mental model of a money amount (e.g. always thinking of it as a sum of the smallest coins). Seeing equivalent representations across varied combinations builds flexibility and prepares for making change.

descriptors.title: Numbers beyond 10 000
descriptors.description: recognise, represent and order natural numbers using naming and writing conventions for numerals beyond 10 000
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, represent and order numbers to at least 1000 using physical and virtual materials, numerals and number lines (AC9M2N01). They have not yet worked with numbers beyond the thousands range, or applied naming and writing conventions to numbers in the ten-thousands and beyond.

nodes.label: Place value to ten-thousands
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the value of each digit in a five-digit number, naming the ten-thousands place.
nodes.hinge_reason: Place value understanding of five-digit numbers is the prerequisite for all downstream nodes — naming conventions (Node 2), number line placement (Node 3) and ordering (Node 4) all require students to correctly identify digit values. Students who have not resolved the extension pattern will produce systematic errors in every subsequent node.
criteria: Students can state the value of a specified digit in any five-digit number (e.g. the digit 4 in 24 381 is worth 4000).
Students can correctly partition a five-digit number into its place value components.

width.minimum: Identify place value of each digit in a given five-digit number using a place value chart.
width.typical: Represent five-digit numbers using physical or virtual materials (MAB/base-ten blocks); identify and state the value of any digit in a five-digit number.
wider: Explore numbers up to 100 000, extending place value understanding across six-digit numbers
Compare First Nations Australian counting and number systems with the Hindu-Arabic place value system, examining structural differences

modes.reason: Students often over-rely on the ones/tens/hundreds pattern and struggle to extend the logic to ten-thousands. Encountering the pattern across multiple five-digit numbers — including those with internal zeros — helps resolve this rather than re-explaining the same example.

nodes.label: Naming conventions for large numerals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read aloud and write in words any natural number in the ten-thousands range, applying Australian naming conventions correctly.
criteria: Students can correctly write in words any numeral in the ten-thousands range, including those with zero digits.
Students can correctly write the numeral when given a number in words.

width.minimum: Read and write in words at least five different numerals in the ten-thousands range, including at least one with a zero digit.
width.typical: Read, write and say numbers in the ten-thousands fluently across varied examples; correctly handle zero as a placeholder in naming (e.g. 40 305 = 'forty thousand, three hundred and five').
wider: Research how large numbers are named differently across languages and cultures (e.g. lakh system in South Asian languages vs. thousands system)
Explore naming conventions for numbers into the hundred-thousands, generalising the pattern

modes.reason: Naming conventions require fluency through repeated practice. Zero-placeholder cases cluster errors; targeted practice with a range of examples is more effective than broadening context.

nodes.label: Representing large numbers on number lines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can place and read numbers beyond 10 000 on a number line, making reasonable estimates of unmarked positions.
criteria: Students can place given five-digit numbers at approximately correct positions on a number line.
Students can estimate the value of a position on a number line and justify their estimate using a benchmark.

width.minimum: Place three given five-digit numbers on a number line with marked endpoints; read one number from an indicated position.
width.typical: Place and estimate positions of five-digit numbers on number lines with varying scales; explain reasoning for estimates using benchmark numbers (e.g. 50 000 as midpoint).
wider: Use interactive digital number lines to explore scale across orders of magnitude — from thousands to millions
Investigate how population data for Australian towns and cities can be ordered on a number line, connecting to real-world context

nodes.label: Ordering and comparing large numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can order a set of natural numbers beyond 10 000 from smallest to largest and compare any two using < > = symbols.
criteria: Students can correctly order a set of five-digit numbers from smallest to largest.
Students can use < > = to compare any two natural numbers and explain the comparison using place value.

width.minimum: Order four five-digit numbers from smallest to largest, using place value reasoning to justify order.
width.typical: Compare and order sets of five-digit numbers using place value; apply < > = to pairs of large numbers; explain reasoning referencing digit positions.
wider: Order and compare real-world data sets beyond 10 000 (populations, distances, prices) and reason about what the differences mean in context
Investigate how ordering conventions differ when numbers represent different quantities (e.g. ordering temperatures vs. distances)

modes.reason: Ordering integrates all prior nodes — place value understanding, naming and number line positioning all contribute to correct ordering. Students who struggle here often have a gap in one of the component understandings.

descriptors.title: Unit fractions
descriptors.description: recognise and represent unit fractions including 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and 1/10 and their multiples in different ways; combine fractions with the same denominator to complete the whole
descriptors.knowledge: Students can partition, rearrange, regroup and rename two- and three-digit numbers using standard and non-standard groupings (AC9M2N02). They have not yet worked formally with unit fractions as named quantities or combined fractions with the same denominator.

nodes.label: What a unit fraction means
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a unit fraction represents one equal part of a whole divided into equal parts, and identify the denominator's role.
nodes.hinge_reason: The equal-parts definition and the denominator's role are prerequisite for Node 2 (counting multiples) and Node 3 (combining to whole). Students who conflate 'equal' with 'same shape' will miscount parts and misapply combining — the misconception propagates into every subsequent fraction task.
criteria: Students can identify and name the unit fraction represented when a shape or set is divided into equal parts.
Students can explain what the denominator of a unit fraction tells us about the whole.

width.minimum: Fold or partition a shape into equal parts and identify one part as 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 or 1/10, explaining what the denominator tells us.
width.typical: Partition shapes, lengths and sets into equal parts; name each part as a unit fraction; explain that the denominator names the number of equal parts.
wider: Explore how fractions are represented in First Nations Australian sharing and distribution practices, comparing with symbolic fraction notation
Investigate fractions in other cultural contexts — e.g. how recipes in different cultures use fractional measures

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse 'equal parts' with 'same shape parts'. Seeing unit fractions across varied representations — area models, length models, set models — resolves this more effectively than re-teaching with a single model.

nodes.label: Multiples of unit fractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and represent multiples of unit fractions (e.g. 2/3, 3/4, 4/5) and locate them on a number line.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the numerator as a count is directly required for Node 3 — combining fractions to complete the whole requires students to count parts toward the total. Students who conflate numerator and denominator roles will be unable to reason about what is missing from the whole.
criteria: Students can correctly name and write a fraction from a shaded area model or marked number line.
Students can represent a given fraction (e.g. 3/5) on a number line or area model.

width.minimum: Shade or mark three different multiples of a unit fraction on area models and a number line (e.g. 2/4, 3/5).
width.typical: Represent multiples of halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and tenths using area models, number lines and sets; name fractions correctly using numerator and denominator.
wider: Explore fractions beyond one whole (e.g. 5/4, 7/3) as natural extensions of the multiple pattern on a number line
Investigate how tenths connect to decimal notation, using number lines to show both representations

modes.reason: Students benefit from explicit scaffolding of the numerator as a count — 'we are counting how many parts of size 1/4'. This framing prevents confusion between numerator and denominator roles and makes the multiple structure legible.

nodes.label: Combining fractions to complete the whole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine fractions with the same denominator to make a whole, and identify the missing part to complete a whole.
criteria: Students can identify the fraction needed to complete a whole when given a partial fraction.
Students can combine fractions with the same denominator and explain when the result equals one whole.

width.minimum: Given a fraction, identify the complementary fraction needed to complete the whole (e.g. if 3/5 is shaded, 2/5 remains); demonstrate with at least two different denominators.
width.typical: Combine fractions with the same denominator to make a whole across halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and tenths; represent using models and number sentences.
wider: Connect combining fractions to addition number sentences (e.g. 3/5 + 2/5 = 5/5 = 1), bridging to formal fraction addition
Apply fraction combination to real-world division contexts — e.g. sharing food, measuring ingredients

modes.reason: This node integrates the unit fraction meaning (node 1) with multiple counting (node 2) into the completing-the-whole concept. Students who struggle here typically have a gap in one of the prior nodes.

descriptors.title: Addition and subtraction with place value
descriptors.description: add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value to partition, rearrange and regroup numbers to assist in calculations without a calculator
descriptors.knowledge: Students can add and subtract one- and two-digit numbers using part-part-whole reasoning and a variety of calculation strategies (AC9M2N04). They have not yet applied place value partitioning and regrouping to three-digit calculations without a calculator.

nodes.label: Partitioning for addition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition two- and three-digit numbers to add by place value (e.g. 245 + 132 = 200+100 + 40+30 + 5+2).
criteria: Students can partition both addends by place value and combine to find the sum.
Students can record the partitioned addition strategy clearly.

width.minimum: Add at least two pairs of three-digit numbers by partitioning into hundreds, tens and ones, recording the working.
width.typical: Apply place value partitioning to add a range of two- and three-digit number pairs; connect to informal written layout.
wider: Explore different partitioning strategies — e.g. partitioning one number only, or using non-standard partitions like 245 = 200+45
Apply partitioning addition to multi-step problems and real-world contexts involving distances or quantities

nodes.label: Regrouping in addition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise when regrouping (carrying) is needed in addition and apply it correctly across hundreds, tens and ones.
nodes.hinge_reason: Regrouping in addition is a prerequisite for decomposition in Node 3 subtraction — students who have not generalised regrouping across place value positions cannot reliably apply the inverse procedure (decomposition/borrowing) and will produce systematic errors in subtraction.
criteria: Students can identify when regrouping is needed in an addition calculation.
Students can correctly apply regrouping and produce the correct sum.

width.minimum: Solve at least three addition problems requiring at least one regrouping step, explaining where the regrouping occurs.
width.typical: Add two- and three-digit numbers across a range of problems requiring regrouping at tens and/or hundreds; explain the regrouping action using place value language.
wider: Use base-ten blocks or virtual manipulatives to model the physical exchange that underlies regrouping, connecting the model to the written procedure
Investigate what happens when regrouping is needed at multiple places simultaneously

modes.reason: Regrouping is a common error site — students who see it only in columns of the same type (tens only) often fail to generalise. Encountering it at hundreds, tens and ones across varied problems resolves the confusion.

nodes.label: Subtraction using place value
nodes.checkpoint: Students can subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value partitioning, including cases requiring decomposition.
nodes.hinge_reason: Subtraction with decomposition feeds directly into AC9M3N06 mathematical modelling problems and AC9M3N05 estimation-checking tasks — students who cannot reliably subtract with decomposition cannot complete multi-step problems or check the reasonableness of results in subsequent standards.
criteria: Students can subtract a three-digit number from a three-digit number using at least one place value strategy.
Students can correctly apply decomposition where required and produce the correct difference.

width.minimum: Subtract two pairs of three-digit numbers using place value partitioning; at least one problem requires decomposition (borrowing).
width.typical: Apply place value strategies — partitioning, rearranging, decomposition — to subtract across a range of two- and three-digit problems; choose the most efficient strategy.
wider: Compare different subtraction strategies (partitioning, counting on/back, compensation) for the same problem, evaluating efficiency
Apply subtraction to financial contexts — e.g. calculating change from $100 in real-world purchase scenarios

modes.reason: Subtraction with decomposition is the highest-error node in this descriptor — the 'borrowing' action is procedurally error-prone. Students who understand the place value rationale through multiple representations (models and written) make fewer errors than those who memorise procedure.
Once the decomposition concept is understood, students also benefit from practice to build fluency and reduce procedural errors in multi-step problems.

descriptors.title: Multiplication and division strategies
descriptors.description: multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers, representing problems using number sentences, diagrams and arrays, and using a variety of calculation strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can multiply and divide by one-digit numbers using repeated addition, equal grouping, arrays and partitioning (AC9M2N05). They have not yet extended multiplication to two-digit numbers, or represented multiplicative problems using formal number sentences and arrays systematically.

nodes.label: Multiplication representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a multiplication situation as an array, a repeated addition and a number sentence, connecting all three.
nodes.hinge_reason: Array and number sentence representations are the entry point for Node 2 strategies (partitioning, doubling use arrays as structural models) and Node 3 (division connected to multiplication via arrays). Students who cannot flexibly move between representations cannot access the strategy-building and inverse-relationship work in subsequent nodes.
criteria: Students can draw an array for a given multiplication number sentence.
Students can write a multiplication number sentence for a given array or equal groups scenario.

width.minimum: Represent one multiplication fact in three ways: array, repeated addition, and number sentence. Explain the connection between representations.
width.typical: Represent a range of multiplication situations using arrays, repeated addition and number sentences; explain how all three representations show the same quantity.
wider: Explore commutativity through arrays — rotating an array shows the same product, connecting 3×4 and 4×3 as the same area
Investigate multiplication in First Nations Australian contexts such as equal-sharing of resources or pattern-based counting

modes.reason: Students who see multiplication only as repeated addition often struggle to transition to arrays and then to formal strategies. Connecting across representations early prevents this bottleneck.

nodes.label: Multiplication strategies for one- and two-digit numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can multiply a one-digit number by a two-digit number using at least one efficient strategy (e.g. partitioning, doubling).
criteria: Students can calculate a one-digit by two-digit product using at least one named strategy.
Students can explain the strategy they used and why it works.

width.minimum: Calculate at least three products involving a two-digit number using a chosen strategy, recording working.
width.typical: Apply and compare partitioning, doubling-and-halving and repeated addition strategies to multiply one-digit by two-digit numbers; choose an efficient strategy for a given problem.
wider: Explore the area model as a visual representation of two-digit multiplication (e.g. 4×23 as a 4×20 + 4×3 rectangle)
Investigate patterns in multiplication tables, using the area model to explain why the pattern holds

modes.reason: Building a repertoire of strategies — partitioning, doubling, using known facts — is the explicit goal of this descriptor. Students need to have encountered enough strategy examples to make genuine choices.

nodes.label: Division as the inverse of multiplication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a division problem using a number sentence and array, and connect it to the related multiplication fact.
criteria: Students can write a division number sentence for a sharing or grouping problem.
Students can use a multiplication fact to solve a related division problem.

width.minimum: Solve two division problems by connecting to a known multiplication fact; represent each as a number sentence.
width.typical: Solve a range of division problems by relating them to multiplication; represent using diagrams, number sentences and sharing/grouping models.
wider: Explore the distinction between sharing (partitive) and grouping (quotitive) division contexts, recognising both produce the same calculation
Investigate remainders — what happens when division does not produce a whole number result

modes.reason: Students often treat division as a separate topic from multiplication. Seeing division in both sharing and grouping contexts, each connected to multiplication arrays, resolves this fragmentation.

descriptors.title: Estimation
descriptors.description: estimate the quantity of objects in collections and make estimates when solving problems to determine the reasonableness of calculations
descriptors.knowledge: No direct predecessor in progression map. Students have worked with counting and place value but have not yet developed explicit estimation strategies or used estimation to check reasonableness of calculations.

nodes.label: Estimation strategies for collections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate the quantity of objects in a collection using a benchmark or grouping strategy, and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Students can estimate the size of a collection and name the strategy they used.
Students can compare their estimate to the actual count and reflect on its reasonableness.

width.minimum: Estimate the quantity in one collection of 20–100 objects using a stated strategy (chunking or benchmark); compare estimate to actual count.
width.typical: Estimate quantities across collections of varying sizes using chunking, anchoring and benchmarking strategies; reflect on accuracy of estimates.
wider: Estimate quantities in real-world contexts — number of seeds in a fruit, tiles on a floor, students in an assembly — and discuss sources of estimation error
Explore estimation contexts used in First Nations Australian land management practices (e.g. estimating quantities of food resources)

modes.reason: Students need a small repertoire of strategies (chunking, anchoring, benchmarking) to make estimation portable across contexts. Teaching one strategy and moving on limits applicability.

nodes.label: Estimation to check reasonableness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate the answer to an addition or subtraction problem before calculating, and use the estimate to judge whether their calculated answer is reasonable.
criteria: Students can make a prior estimate for a calculation problem and state a reasonable range.
Students can identify a calculated answer as reasonable or unreasonable based on their estimate and explain why.

width.minimum: For two calculation problems, make a prior estimate and then check whether the calculated answer is in the right range; explain the judgment.
width.typical: Apply estimation to check reasonableness of addition, subtraction and simple multiplication calculations; explain how to recognise an unreasonable answer.
wider: Apply estimation-before-calculation as a regular habit across multiplicative problems, discussing when estimation is more efficient than exact calculation
Investigate how rounding strategies affect estimation accuracy — comparing rounding to nearest 10 vs nearest 100

modes.reason: The reasoning chain 'estimate first → calculate → compare → judge' needs explicit scaffolding. Without it, students often treat estimation as an add-on rather than a checking tool.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations including financial contexts; formulate problems using number sentences and choose calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve practical additive and multiplicative problems, including money (AC9M2N06). They have not yet systematically formulated problems as number sentences for three-digit calculations, or applied modelling across both additive and multiplicative situations with explicit interpretation.

nodes.label: Formulating problems as number sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can translate a practical additive or multiplicative situation into a number sentence, identifying the operation needed.
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct problem formulation is the entry gate to the modelling cycle — students who cannot identify the operation from a practical situation cannot progress to Node 2 (strategy selection) or Node 3 (interpretation). An incorrectly formulated number sentence invalidates the entire calculation and interpretation that follows.
criteria: Students can write a number sentence that correctly represents a practical problem.
Students can identify which operation the problem requires and justify the choice.

width.minimum: Translate one word problem (additive) and one word problem (multiplicative) into number sentences, identifying the operation and unknown.
width.typical: Formulate a range of practical problems as number sentences, selecting the appropriate operation; include problems with an unknown in different positions.
wider: Formulate problems involving two-step operations (e.g. buy three items, pay with $20, how much change) — bridging to multi-step modelling
Explore how the same real-world situation can be formulated differently depending on what question is asked

modes.reason: Students often confuse problem type when surface features change (e.g. money vs distance vs quantities). Encountering formulation across varied contexts builds the generalised skill of identifying the underlying operation.

nodes.label: Choosing and applying calculation strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate calculation strategy for a given problem and apply it, including using digital tools where appropriate.
criteria: Students can select and apply a calculation strategy appropriate to the problem.
Students can identify when a digital tool is appropriate and use it to check or calculate.

width.minimum: Solve two practical problems using different calculation strategies; for one, justify why the chosen strategy was appropriate.
width.typical: Apply a range of strategies (mental, written, digital) to practical problems; choose based on number size and context; explain strategy choice.
wider: Compare the efficiency of mental, written and digital strategies across a range of problem types, developing judgment about when each is appropriate
Investigate financial decision-making contexts where different strategies have real implications (e.g. comparison shopping)

modes.reason: Strategy choice requires a repertoire — students need exposure to multiple strategies across enough problem types to develop genuine selection judgment.

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a calculated answer in terms of the original situation and communicate the solution with appropriate units and context.
criteria: Students can explain what their calculated answer means in terms of the original situation.
Students communicate solutions with appropriate labels and in sentences connected to the problem context.

width.minimum: Solve one practical problem and write a sentence that interprets the answer in terms of the situation (e.g. 'The total cost is $48, which means...').
width.typical: Solve and interpret a range of practical problems; communicate solutions referencing original context, including appropriate units (e.g. dollars, metres, items).
wider: Present solutions to multi-step problems with complete reasoning, including estimation check, calculation and interpretation
Explore how the same numerical answer can mean different things in different contexts (e.g. 24 apples vs $24 vs 24 minutes)

modes.reason: Interpretation integrates formulation, strategy and calculation into a complete modelling cycle. Students who struggle with interpretation often have a weak connection between the number sentence and the real-world situation it represents.

descriptors.title: Algorithms and number patterns
descriptors.description: follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions to investigate numbers; describe any emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: No direct predecessor in the progression map. Students have worked with number patterns informally through addition and multiplication, but have not yet explicitly followed or created step-by-step algorithms to generate or investigate number sequences.

nodes.label: Following an algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a given step-by-step algorithm involving a sequence of operations and produce the correct numerical output.
nodes.hinge_reason: Precise algorithm execution and systematic recording are prerequisite for Node 2 (creating algorithms) and Node 3 (describing patterns) — students who skip steps or fail to record outputs cannot produce the data needed to create or observe patterns. The skill of tracking state is the foundation the whole standard rests on.
criteria: Students can follow a step-by-step algorithm and produce correct outputs for given inputs.
Students can record their steps clearly showing how they reached the output.

width.minimum: Follow one provided algorithm (3–5 steps) applied to at least three different starting numbers; record each output.
width.typical: Follow several algorithms of varying complexity involving addition, subtraction and multiplication steps; record outputs systematically in a table.
wider: Follow algorithms that include decision points ('if the result is even, do X; if odd, do Y') and trace the different paths
Investigate the Collatz sequence or similar number algorithms as examples of algorithmic thinking applied to number investigation

modes.reason: Following an algorithm precisely requires students to track state across steps — a reasoning demand that benefits from explicit scaffolding of how to record intermediate results without losing place.

nodes.label: Creating algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a simple algorithm (sequence of steps) to generate or investigate a number sequence.
criteria: Students can write a step-by-step algorithm that generates the intended output.
Students can test their algorithm with at least two starting values and check whether it produces the expected result.

width.minimum: Create an algorithm with at least three steps that, when applied to a starting number, generates a number sequence; test it with two starting values.
width.typical: Create algorithms to generate or transform number sequences; test and refine algorithms when outputs are unexpected; represent algorithms as numbered steps.
wider: Express algorithms as flowcharts with decision branches, extending beyond linear step sequences
Create algorithms to model real-world processes (e.g. a savings algorithm: 'start with $10, add $5 each week, stop when you reach $50')

nodes.label: Describing emerging patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe a pattern they observe in the outputs of an algorithm, including whether it continues, repeats or terminates.
criteria: Students can describe a pattern in the outputs of an algorithm using mathematical language (e.g. increasing by, repeating every).
Students can predict a future value in the sequence and justify the prediction based on the pattern.

width.minimum: Apply an algorithm to generate at least six outputs and write one sentence describing a pattern they notice.
width.typical: Generate sequences from algorithms and describe patterns in terms of structure (growing, repeating, alternating); predict future values; explain why the pattern occurs.
wider: Connect algorithmic patterns to algebraic thinking — expressing patterns as rules (e.g. 'each term is 3 more than the previous')
Investigate whether changing one step of an algorithm changes the pattern — comparing two algorithms that differ by one step

modes.reason: Pattern description integrates algorithm following, output generation and mathematical observation. Students who can follow but not describe are missing the investigative dimension the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Chance language and reasoning
descriptors.description: identify practical activities and everyday events involving chance; describe possible outcomes and events as 'likely' or 'unlikely' and identify some events as 'certain' or 'impossible' explaining reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Probability is introduced at Year 3 — no direct Y2 predecessor. Students have informal everyday language about likelihood but have not yet applied a formal likelihood vocabulary or reasoned about certainty and impossibility.

nodes.label: Identifying chance events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between events that definitely happen, definitely don't happen, and might happen, and connect these to everyday experiences.
nodes.hinge_reason: A working understanding of what makes an event a chance event (outcome not predetermined) is the conceptual foundation for Node 2 — students who cannot distinguish chance events from certain/impossible ones cannot apply likely/unlikely language correctly or reason about possible outcomes.
criteria: Students can classify an event as certain, impossible or a chance event.
Students can explain what makes an event a chance event (we don't know in advance what will happen).

width.minimum: Classify three everyday events as certain, impossible or involving chance; justify each classification.
width.typical: Identify and classify a range of everyday events using certain/impossible/chance; explain what makes an event a chance event (outcome is not predetermined).
wider: Explore how chance appears across different everyday contexts — weather forecasting, games, sport outcomes, natural events
Investigate how different cultures have explained unpredictable events, and how the concept of probability developed as a mathematical way of reasoning about uncertainty

modes.reason: Students often have narrow intuitions about what counts as a 'chance event' (e.g. only games with dice). Broad contextual exposure — weather, sport, nature — establishes that chance is a property of situations, not just games.

nodes.label: Likely, unlikely and explaining reasoning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe outcomes of chance events as likely or unlikely and explain their reasoning with reference to the possible outcomes.
criteria: Students can describe an outcome as likely or unlikely and explain their reasoning.
Students can identify all possible outcomes for a simple chance event.

width.minimum: For two chance events, describe the most likely outcome and explain why, referencing what outcomes are possible.
width.typical: Apply likely/unlikely language to a range of chance contexts; explain reasoning by considering all possible outcomes and comparing their chances.
wider: Introduce an informal probability scale from impossible to certain, placing events at approximate positions and justifying placement
Explore situations where 'equally likely' applies — fair coins, fair spinners — and contrast with situations where outcomes are not equally likely

modes.reason: The reasoning chain 'what outcomes are possible? → which seems to happen more often? → therefore it is likely/unlikely' needs explicit scaffolding. Without it, students assert likelihood based on gut feeling rather than structured analysis of outcomes.

descriptors.title: Conducting chance experiments
descriptors.description: conduct repeated chance experiments; identify and describe possible outcomes, record the results, recognise and discuss the variation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify chance events and describe outcomes as likely, unlikely, certain or impossible (AC9M3P01). They have not yet conducted repeated experiments, recorded results systematically, or observed and discussed variation in outcomes.

nodes.label: Identifying and recording possible outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can list all possible outcomes for a simple chance experiment before conducting it, and set up a recording method.
nodes.hinge_reason: A complete pre-experiment outcomes list and recording table are prerequisites for Node 2 (systematic data collection) and Node 3 (recognising variation) — students who skip this step produce incomplete or unstructured data that cannot support the variation discussion the descriptor requires.
criteria: Students can list all possible outcomes for a given chance experiment.
Students can construct a recording table for results before beginning the experiment.

width.minimum: Before an experiment (e.g. flipping a coin, spinning a spinner), list all possible outcomes and design a tally or frequency table to record results.
width.typical: List all possible outcomes for varied experiments (coins, spinners, dice, coloured counters); create appropriate recording tables; explain why listing outcomes before experimenting is useful.
wider: Explore experiments with more than two outcomes (e.g. a four-section spinner) and identify how the number of possible outcomes affects likelihood
Compare the number of possible outcomes across different experiments and predict which would show more variation

modes.reason: Listing outcomes before experimenting is a reasoning discipline that doesn't come naturally — students typically want to start and record as they go. Explicit scaffolding of 'predict, then test' establishes the experimental structure the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Conducting repeated trials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can conduct a repeated chance experiment, recording each result accurately and producing a complete data set.
criteria: Students can conduct an experiment and record every outcome without omission.
Students can produce a complete tally or frequency table for their trial results.

width.minimum: Conduct one experiment with at least 20 trials, recording each outcome in a tally table.
width.typical: Conduct repeated experiments across varied tools (coins, spinners, dice); record all outcomes systematically; work in a consistent, organised way across the full trial sequence.
wider: Increase trial numbers (20 vs 50 vs 100 trials) and compare whether results look more or less consistent as the number of trials increases
Conduct the same experiment across multiple groups and pool results — experiencing the effect of larger sample sizes

nodes.label: Recognising and discussing variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe variation in their results — acknowledging that outcomes differ across trials and that results may differ from what was expected.
criteria: Students can describe at least one way their results varied from what they expected.
Students can explain that variation in a chance experiment is normal, not a mistake.

width.minimum: After conducting an experiment, make one statement about variation: identify that results varied and that they may not match the expected outcome.
width.typical: Describe and discuss variation in results: compare actual frequencies with expected outcomes; explain why a fair coin does not always land heads exactly half the time; compare results with other groups.
wider: Investigate what happens to variation as sample size increases — running 20 trials vs 100 trials and comparing how close results are to expected frequencies
Connect to statistical investigation (AC9M3ST03): design an experiment to test a question about likelihood, using results to make a claim

modes.reason: The concept of variation — that results differ from expectations due to chance, not error — is a key probabilistic insight. Students who conduct only one experiment often think their result is 'wrong'. Comparing results across groups and experiments makes variation legible as a feature of chance, not a mistake.

descriptors.title: Objects, features and suitability
descriptors.description: make, compare and classify objects, identifying key features and explaining why these features make them suited to their uses
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, compare and classify shapes referencing the number of sides and using spatial terms such as opposite, parallel, curved and straight (AC9M2SP01). They have not yet connected shape features to purpose/use, or made and compared 3D objects with feature identification.

nodes.label: Identifying key features of objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name the key geometric features (faces, edges, vertices, curves) of common 3D objects.
criteria: Students can identify and correctly count faces, edges and vertices of a given 3D object.
Students can classify objects using geometric feature language (faces, edges, vertices).

width.minimum: Identify and count faces, edges and vertices for two 3D objects (e.g. cube, triangular prism); describe one key feature of each.
width.typical: Compare and classify a range of 3D objects by their geometric features; use formal language (prism, pyramid, cylinder, cone, sphere); describe similarities and differences.
wider: Investigate geometric features in natural objects — crystals, shells, seeds — connecting geometry to natural structures
Explore how First Nations Australians use geometric patterns and three-dimensional forms in art, architecture and tools

nodes.label: Features and suitability for purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the geometric features of an object make it suited to its everyday use.
criteria: Students can name at least one key feature of an object and explain how that feature suits its purpose.
Students can compare two objects and explain why one is better suited to a given use based on its geometric features.

width.minimum: Explain why the features of one common object (e.g. a cylinder can, a rectangular box) make it suited to its use.
width.typical: Compare several everyday objects and explain how their geometric features (shape, faces, stability, capacity) relate to their purpose; evaluate alternative designs.
wider: Design and make a 3D object for a specific purpose, explaining feature choices — connecting to Design Technologies
Investigate how architectural and engineering structures use specific geometric features for strength, stability or visual effect

modes.reason: Explaining suitability requires connecting geometry knowledge (node 1) with functional reasoning about the world. Students who can identify features but cannot explain their purpose haven't yet made the geometric-functional connection.

descriptors.title: Mapping and location
descriptors.description: interpret and create two-dimensional representations of familiar environments, locating key landmarks and objects relative to each other
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate positions in two-dimensional representations of a familiar space and move positions by following directions and pathways (AC9M2SP02). They have not yet created their own two-dimensional maps or described the relative positions of multiple landmarks simultaneously.

nodes.label: Interpreting 2D maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a 2D map to locate key landmarks and describe their positions relative to each other using directional and spatial language.
criteria: Students can locate a specified landmark on a 2D map.
Students can describe the position of one landmark relative to another using spatial language.

width.minimum: Use a given 2D map to locate three landmarks and describe the position of two relative to a third using spatial language.
width.typical: Interpret a range of 2D maps (classroom, school grounds, local area); locate landmarks and describe relative positions using compass directions, grid references and spatial language.
wider: Interpret aerial photographs and compare them with drawn maps — exploring what information each representation emphasises
Explore how First Nations Australians represent country in maps, artworks and stories, comparing with Western mapping conventions

modes.reason: Students often interpret maps of only one type (school grounds) and cannot transfer spatial reasoning to other contexts. Encountering varied representations — including aerial photos and First Nations maps — broadens the concept of what a map is.

nodes.label: Creating 2D maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a 2D representation of a familiar environment that shows the key landmarks and their relative positions.
criteria: Students can create a 2D map of a familiar space with landmarks placed in approximately correct relative positions.
Students can explain why they placed a landmark where they did in relation to another landmark.

width.minimum: Create a simple map of a familiar space (e.g. classroom or bedroom) showing at least four landmarks in approximately correct relative positions.
width.typical: Create 2D maps of familiar environments with an appropriate key, scale indication and correct relative positions of landmarks; evaluate maps against the actual environment.
wider: Create maps of the school grounds or local area using grid references, comparing the map with a digital satellite view
Use digital mapping tools to create and annotate maps, discussing the conventions used by digital platforms

descriptors.title: Data collection and recording
descriptors.description: acquire data for categorical and discrete numerical variables to address a question of interest or purpose by observing, collecting and accessing data sets; record the data using appropriate methods including frequency tables and spreadsheets
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create different graphical representations using software and compare representations of data (AC9M2ST02). They have not yet explicitly acquired data through observation and collection for named variable types, or used frequency tables as a systematic recording method.

nodes.label: Categorical and numerical variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between categorical and discrete numerical variables and identify each in a given investigation context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Variable type identification is a prerequisite for Node 2 (appropriate recording method) and AC9M3ST02 (selecting appropriate graph types) — students who cannot classify variables will choose inappropriate recording and representation methods, undermining the entire investigation.
criteria: Students can classify a variable as categorical or discrete numerical and justify the classification.
Students can give an example of each variable type from everyday contexts.

width.minimum: Given two example investigations, identify whether the variable is categorical or discrete numerical and explain the difference.
width.typical: Identify the variable type in a range of investigation contexts; explain what values the variable could take; propose questions of interest for each variable type.
wider: Explore how the same real-world phenomenon can be measured as either categorical or numerical depending on the question asked (e.g. 'What colour is your hair?' vs 'How many siblings do you have?')
Investigate how variable type determines which graphical representations are appropriate

modes.reason: The categorical/numerical distinction requires a conceptual framework — it is not intuitively obvious. Explicit scaffolding of 'what type of values does this variable take?' provides the decision procedure students need.

nodes.label: Collecting and recording data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect data through observation or survey for a question of interest and record it in a frequency table or spreadsheet.
criteria: Students can collect data for a question of interest and record all responses without omission.
Students can construct a frequency table showing tally marks and totals for a collected data set.

width.minimum: Collect data from at least 10 observations for one variable and record in a frequency table; explain what the tally marks represent.
width.typical: Collect, tally and record data for categorical and discrete numerical variables using frequency tables and spreadsheets; ensure data is complete and correctly recorded.
wider: Access an existing data set (e.g. class or school data, weather records) and record a subset in a frequency table — practising data acquisition from secondary sources
Investigate how data collection methods affect what you can and cannot find out (e.g. observation vs survey vs measuring)

descriptors.title: Graphical representations
descriptors.description: create and compare different graphical representations of data sets including using software where appropriate; interpret the data in terms of the context
descriptors.knowledge: Students can acquire and record data for categorical and discrete numerical variables (AC9M3ST01). They have not yet created multiple representations of the same data set for comparison, or explicitly interpreted representations in context.

nodes.label: Creating graphical representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create at least two types of graphical representation (e.g. picture graph, bar graph) for the same data set.
criteria: Students can create a correctly labelled bar graph or picture graph from a frequency table.
Students can include a title, axis labels, and a consistent scale in their graph.

width.minimum: Create one bar graph or picture graph from a provided frequency table; include title, labels and scale.
width.typical: Create two or more different graph types (picture graph, bar graph, dot plot) from the same data set, including using software where appropriate; ensure all components are correctly labelled.
wider: Create graphical representations using digital tools (spreadsheet graphing functions) and compare the software output with hand-drawn versions
Explore a wider range of graph types relevant to the data (e.g. line graph for numerical data over time) and discuss when each type is appropriate

nodes.label: Comparing representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare two graphical representations of the same data and explain what each makes easier or harder to see.
criteria: Students can identify a feature of the data that is more clearly shown in one graph type than another.
Students can explain which graph is more useful for a specific question about the data.

width.minimum: Compare two representations of the same data and state one thing that is easier to see in each.
width.typical: Compare the features of different graph types for the same data set; explain which representation better answers specific questions about the data.
wider: Investigate how the same data can be made to look different by changing scale or graph type — discussing misleading representations
Explore how media and advertising use graphical representations and whether they are honest depictions of the data

modes.reason: Comparison requires holding two representations in mind simultaneously and reasoning about their relative affordances. This is the integrative move of the descriptor — students who can create graphs but not compare them haven't reached the full demand.

nodes.label: Interpreting in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret what a graphical representation shows and answer questions about the data in terms of the original context.
criteria: Students can read values from a graph accurately.
Students can make a statement about what the data shows that connects back to the original question of interest.

width.minimum: Answer three questions about a provided graph that require reading values and making a simple interpretation statement about the context.
width.typical: Interpret data in graphs by identifying patterns, most/least common values, and making statements connected to the original question of interest.
wider: Formulate additional questions that the data set could answer, and identify questions it cannot answer — developing question-data alignment thinking
Connect interpretation to decision-making: 'What would you do based on this data?' — applying data reasoning to real choices

descriptors.title: Guided statistical investigations
descriptors.description: conduct guided statistical investigations involving the collection, representation and interpretation of data for categorical and discrete numerical variables with respect to questions of interest
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collect data and create graphical representations (AC9M3ST01, AC9M3ST02). They have not yet completed a full investigation cycle end-to-end under teacher guidance.

nodes.label: Posing investigable questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a question of interest that can be investigated by collecting data, and state the variable(s) involved.
nodes.hinge_reason: An investigable question with a clearly identified variable is the entry point for the investigation cycle in Node 2 — a question that cannot be answered by data collection, or where the variable is undefined, means the student cannot proceed to collection or interpretation meaningfully.
criteria: Students can state a question that can be answered by collecting data.
Students can identify the variable in their question and its type (categorical or discrete numerical).

width.minimum: With teacher guidance, formulate one question of interest that can be investigated using data; identify the variable and its type.
width.typical: Formulate and refine questions of interest; identify relevant variables and their types; explain how data could be collected to answer the question.
wider: Compare several possible questions about the same context and evaluate which can be answered with available data
Explore questions of community or social relevance — e.g. questions about their school or local environment — connecting statistics to purposeful inquiry

modes.reason: Posing an investigable question requires understanding what makes a question answerable with data. The reasoning scaffold 'what would I need to collect to answer this?' needs to be made explicit.

nodes.label: Conducting the investigation cycle
nodes.checkpoint: Students can complete a guided investigation cycle: collect data, represent it graphically, and make an interpretive statement about the results.
criteria: Students can collect data, create a graph and make an interpretive statement as a connected investigation.
Students can explain how their interpretation relates back to the original question of interest.

width.minimum: With teacher guidance, complete one investigation: collect data for a given question, create one graph, and write one sentence interpreting the result.
width.typical: Complete a guided investigation from question through data collection, representation and interpretation; compare results with classmates; discuss what the data shows.
wider: Conduct two investigations on similar questions with different groups/samples and compare findings — introducing the idea that data varies
Contribute findings to a class investigation combining data from multiple groups — experiencing aggregated data as more informative than individual samples

modes.reason: The investigation cycle integrates all prior statistics nodes. Students whose component skills are individually solid often still struggle with the cycle as a whole — the integration of posing, collecting, representing and interpreting requires coordination that needs guided practice.

descriptors.title: Unknown values in equations
descriptors.description: Find unknown values in numerical equations involving addition and subtraction, using the properties of numbers and operations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise addition and subtraction as inverse operations and find unknown values in basic number sentences (AC9M3A01). They have not yet applied equivalence reasoning to equations with unknowns on either side, or used properties such as commutativity across multi-addend equations.

nodes.label: Equation as balance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that an equation means both sides have the same value, using a balance model.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who read the equals sign as 'write the answer here' cannot engage with Node 4's relational thinking tasks — finding unknowns in equations of the form a + b = □ + c requires understanding equality as balance, not as a command to compute.
criteria: Students can explain that both sides of an equation must have the same value
Students can identify whether a given equation is true or false and justify using a balance model

width.minimum: Use a balance scale or diagram to represent one equation; explain what the equals sign means in terms of balance.
width.typical: Represent a range of true and false equations using balance scales and informal units; explain why 7 + 8 = 6 + 9 is true and 5 + 4 = 10 is false using balance reasoning.
wider: Create families of equivalent addition sentences that have the same total, using balance reasoning to verify
Investigate whether equations with three addends can be balanced in different ways (e.g. 2+2+3 = 2+3+2 = 3+2+2)

modes.reason: The equals sign is commonly misread as 'the answer comes next' rather than as a relational symbol meaning balance. Exposure to equations with expressions on both sides (e.g. 6+8 = □+10) is the resolution — single-answer-format equations reinforce the misconception.

nodes.label: Inverse relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to find an unknown in a number sentence.
criteria: Students can write the related subtraction sentence to solve an unknown-addend equation
Students can use a part-part-whole diagram to represent an unknown-addend problem and identify which part is missing

width.minimum: Solve one unknown-addend problem (e.g. 27 + □ = 63) by applying subtraction as the inverse operation; explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Use part-part-whole diagrams and bar models to represent and solve unknown-addend and unknown-total problems; explicitly articulate the inverse relationship (e.g. □ = 63 − 27 because subtraction undoes addition); apply to two-digit and three-digit problems.
wider: Investigate how the same bar model can generate multiple related equations (a+b=c, c−a=b, c−b=a), building fluency with the full fact family
Solve multi-step problems where two unknowns are constrained by the same equation structure

modes.reason: Students benefit from repeated practice deriving related subtraction facts from addition facts and vice versa. The connection between the inverse operation and the unknown position needs to become automatic before applying it to larger numbers.

nodes.label: Commutativity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use commutativity to reason about equivalent expressions and simplify calculation.
criteria: Students can show using materials or a number line that the order of addends does not change the sum
Students can use commutativity to reorder a multi-addend sum into a more convenient calculation

width.minimum: Demonstrate with materials or a number line that 5+2 = 2+5; use commutativity to find an easier calculation order for one multi-addend sum.
width.typical: Use number lines and materials to demonstrate commutative property; apply to multi-addend expressions (2+2+3 = 3+2+2); use commutativity to identify efficient calculation orders.
wider: Investigate which operations are commutative and which are not — testing subtraction and discussing why a−b ≠ b−a in general
Explore how commutativity of addition can simplify mental computation by choosing an easier order (e.g. reordering addends to make tens)

nodes.label: Relational thinking — find unknowns in equivalent sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can find unknown values in equations where both sides contain expressions (e.g. 6 + 8 = □ + 10), using relational thinking.
criteria: Students can find the unknown in an equation where both sides contain an expression (e.g. 6 + 8 = □ + 10)
Students can explain whether a given equation is true or false using relational reasoning (e.g. describing common differences on a number line)

width.minimum: Find the unknown in one equation of the form a + b = □ + c by reasoning about what value makes both sides equal; explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Use relational thinking, balance models and number lines to find unknowns in equivalent number sentences; explain whether equations involving addition and subtraction are true by reasoning about the common difference or equivalent sums; apply to two-digit examples (e.g. 27 − 14 = 17 − 4).
wider: Generate families of equivalent equations starting from a known sum (e.g. all the equations equivalent to □ + □ = 14) and explore what patterns emerge
Investigate number sentences where the unknown appears on the left side (□ − 6 = 9) and compare the reasoning required to when it appears on the right

modes.reason: Students who only practise equations with the unknown on the right (a + b = □) do not develop relational thinking. Equations with expressions on both sides (a + b = □ + c) are the breadth that forces the shift from procedural calculation to equivalence reasoning.

The step from 'calculate both sides' to 'use the structure of the equation to find the unknown without calculating' requires explicit scaffolding — e.g. 'what do I need □ to be so that this side matches that side?' Teachers invest in making this reasoning move visible.

descriptors.title: Multiplication facts to 10×10
descriptors.description: Recall and demonstrate proficiency with multiplication facts up to 10 x 10 and related division facts; extend and apply facts to develop efficient mental strategies for computation with larger numbers without a calculator
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recall multiplication facts for 3, 4, 5 and 10 and apply to develop related division facts (AC9M3A03). They have not yet extended this to all facts up to 10×10, and have not yet applied known facts to derive efficient strategies for multi-digit computation.

nodes.label: Patterns in the multiplication table
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain patterns in the 10×10 multiplication table using arrays.
criteria: Students can use an array to represent a multiplication fact and explain the corresponding division facts
Students can identify at least two patterns within the multiplication table (e.g. even multiples, commutativity)

width.minimum: Use arrays to show the pattern in one row of the multiplication table (e.g. multiples of 6); explain the related division facts from the same array.
width.typical: Use arrays on grid paper to develop and explain patterns across the 10×10 table; identify commutativity visually (e.g. 4×7 = 7×4 from the same array); use arrays to explain corresponding division facts.
wider: Explore the symmetry of the full 10×10 table and explain why half the facts mirror the other half (commutativity as a structural property)
Identify which products appear most and least frequently in the table, and explain why some products (e.g. 12, 24) have many factor pairs

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate visual and structural understanding of the table — not just memorise isolated facts. Building a repertoire of array-based representations helps students derive unfamiliar facts from known structural relationships.

nodes.label: Derivation strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can derive unknown multiplication facts from known facts using doubling, halving, and adding/subtracting one group.
criteria: Students can derive at least one unfamiliar multiplication fact using a named strategy (doubling, near-multiple, distributive), explaining each step
Students can state the related division fact for any multiplication fact they can recall or derive

width.minimum: Use one derivation strategy (e.g. doubling: ×3 facts doubled give ×6 facts) to establish at least one unfamiliar multiplication fact; record and explain the connection.
width.typical: Use and explain multiple derivation strategies including doubling, halving, near-multiples (e.g. ×9 = ×10 minus one group), and distributive property (e.g. ×7 = ×2 + ×5) to establish facts for 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9; connect each derived fact to its related division fact.
wider: Compare multiple derivation paths for the same fact (e.g. 6×7 via 2+5 decomposition vs 3×7 doubled) and discuss which is most efficient for quick recall
Investigate the distributive property visually — using arrays to show that 6×7 = 6×(2+5) = 6×2 + 6×5, and connecting this to the area model

modes.reason: Students who know only one derivation path for each unfamiliar fact are brittle — they need a repertoire of strategies to handle different contexts quickly. Building multiple pathways to the same fact strengthens the mental network supporting recall.

nodes.label: Recall fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recall multiplication and division facts up to 10×10 with increasing automaticity.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot recall facts with automaticity must use working memory for recall during Node 4's extension tasks — applying facts to larger numbers — leaving insufficient capacity to track the place-value reasoning simultaneously. Fluency at this node is a prerequisite for efficient mental computation.
criteria: Students can recall multiplication facts up to 10×10 without needing to derive each one
Students can quickly state the related division fact for any multiplication fact they know

width.minimum: Recall all facts for two or more fact families (e.g. 4s and 8s) with reasonable speed; identify related division facts.
width.typical: Demonstrate increasing automaticity with all multiplication facts up to 10×10 and their related division facts; use varied retrieval practice (games, timed recall, mixed fact families).
wider: Design an instructive card game that embeds multiplication and division fact recall in a game format — drawing on game design principles to make retrieval practice engaging
Investigate which fact families students find hardest to recall and use targeted strategies to address those specifically

modes.reason: Automaticity requires repeated retrieval practice distributed over time. This is a consolidation-heavy node — fluency does not come from understanding alone, and consistent low-stakes practice is the primary intervention for students who are slow but accurate.

nodes.label: Apply to larger numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can extend and apply multiplication and division facts to compute with larger numbers mentally.
criteria: Students can use a known multiplication fact to solve a related computation with multiples of 10
Students can explain the place-value reasoning connecting the known fact to the larger problem

width.minimum: Use one known fact (e.g. 6×7=42) to solve one related larger problem mentally (e.g. 6×70, 60×7); explain the place-value reasoning used.
width.typical: Apply multiplication facts and place value to solve a range of mental computation problems with larger numbers (e.g. 4×30, 7×80, 560÷7); explain the strategy; select efficient strategies based on the numbers involved.
wider: Investigate how knowledge of factors supports estimation for larger products (e.g. knowing 8×7=56 means 8×70≈560 and 80×70≈5600)
Apply fact-based strategies to multi-step problems, identifying where each step uses a known fact as a building block

modes.reason: The extension from known facts to larger numbers requires explicit place-value reasoning — students need to articulate 'I know 6×7=42, and 6×70 is 10 times larger, so 420.' Without this scaffolding, students resort to repeated addition for larger multiples.

descriptors.title: Measure with scaled instruments
descriptors.description: Interpret unmarked and partial units when measuring and comparing attributes of length, mass, capacity, duration and temperature, using scaled and digital instruments and appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can measure with familiar metric units using instruments with labelled markings (AC9M3M02) and read analog clocks to the nearest minute (AC9M3M04). They have not yet interpreted readings that fall between labelled markings on scaled instruments, or measured duration on clocks without marked minutes.

nodes.label: Reading between the marks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read a measurement from a scaled instrument where the value falls between two marked units, identifying the unit each mark represents.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify what each subdivision represents on an unfamiliar instrument cannot meaningfully select or use instruments in Node 2's multi-attribute measurement tasks — they will record incorrect values or avoid instruments where the reading falls between marks.
criteria: Students can read a measurement from a scaled instrument where the value falls between two marked units
Students can explain what the unmarked subdivisions on a given instrument represent

width.minimum: Read one measurement from a scaled instrument (e.g. kitchen scale) where the value falls between two marked values; explain what each marking on the scale represents.
width.typical: Interpret partial and unmarked units on analog scales across at least two different attributes (e.g. mass on a kitchen scale, volume in a measuring jug); explain what unit the subdivisions represent; record values using appropriate units.
wider: Make a scaled measuring instrument from scratch (e.g. a measuring cup using a known container and subdivisions), explaining how they determined where to place each marking
Compare analog and digital instruments measuring the same attribute — discussing what information each provides and how to handle a digital reading between whole-unit increments

modes.reason: Students who only practise with fully marked instruments may not recognise what unmarked subdivisions represent. Reading across different instruments (scales, measuring jugs, thermometers) where subdivision sizes differ builds the generalised skill of 'determine the scale unit before reading'.

nodes.label: Measurement across multiple attributes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure and compare across all five attributes using appropriate instruments and units, recording measures with decimal notation where appropriate.
criteria: Students can select and use an appropriate scaled instrument and unit for a given measurement task
Students can record a measurement in decimal notation where the value falls between whole units

width.minimum: Measure one object or event using a scaled instrument for at least two different attributes; record with appropriate units.
width.typical: Measure length, mass, capacity, temperature and duration using scaled instruments; select the appropriate instrument and unit for each attribute; record measures using decimal notation (e.g. 5.25 m, 2.5 kg, 28.5°C); compare measurements made with different instruments.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Ranger Groups and other groups use scaled instruments to monitor and care for Country/Place — comparing traditional and contemporary measurement tools for environmental monitoring

Design and conduct a measurement investigation requiring at least three different attributes (e.g. measuring conditions for a plant growth experiment), explaining why each instrument and unit was selected

descriptors.title: Perimeter and area
descriptors.description: Recognise ways of measuring and approximating the perimeter and area of shapes and enclosed spaces, using appropriate formal and informal units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can measure with metric units and informal units for length and area (AC9M3M02). They have not yet formally distinguished perimeter from area or applied area measurement using arrays of unit squares.

nodes.label: Perimeter — boundary as length sum
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that perimeter is the total length of the boundary and measure it by adding side lengths.
criteria: Students can measure the perimeter of a polygon by measuring and summing its sides
Students can explain what perimeter measures (the total length of the boundary)

width.minimum: Measure the perimeter of one polygon by measuring and adding side lengths; explain what perimeter means.
width.typical: Measure perimeters of various shapes including rectangles and irregular shapes; use string or rope for curved boundaries; compare perimeters using suitable units; explain that perimeter is the sum of side lengths forming the boundary.
wider: Create rectangles with the same perimeter on grid paper and investigate whether all have the same shape — introducing the non-uniqueness of perimeter
Measure perimeters of real enclosed spaces (garden beds, classroom floor sections) using string, comparing the practicality of different measurement approaches

nodes.label: Area — space enclosed by boundary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure area by covering a shape with unit squares and counting, including partial units at edges.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate perimeter and area arrive at Node 3 unable to measure or distinguish the two attributes simultaneously — the core task of that node. The confusion must be resolved in Node 2 before meaningful comparison is possible.
criteria: Students can measure the area of a shape by covering with unit squares, including partial units
Students can explain what area measures and distinguish it from perimeter

width.minimum: Cover one rectangle with unit squares (no gaps or overlaps) and count to find the area; explain what area measures.
width.typical: Measure and compare areas using arrays of paper tiles or mosaic squares; handle partial units at irregular edges by combining halves and parts; demonstrate using one tile repeatedly rather than tiling the whole shape; explain that area is the space enclosed by the boundary.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Ranger Groups measure areas of land for fire management decisions, contextualising area measurement within caring for Country/Place
Measure areas of irregular shapes (leaves, handprints) using square grids and discuss how to handle partial squares systematically — developing an approximation strategy

modes.reason: Perimeter-area confusion is persistent — students may measure the squares around the edge of a shape (perimeter) when asked for area, or count only internal squares without accounting for boundary ones. Measuring both attributes for the same shape, and discussing what each counts, is the resolution.

nodes.label: Distinguishing and comparing perimeter and area
nodes.checkpoint: Students can measure and compare both perimeter and area for the same shapes, clearly distinguishing the two attributes.
criteria: Students can measure both the perimeter and area of a given shape and record each with appropriate units
Students can explain the difference between perimeter and area and describe a context where each is the relevant measurement

width.minimum: Measure both the perimeter and area of one shape; explain the difference between the two measurements.
width.typical: Measure and compare perimeter and area across a range of shapes; explain that two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas; choose appropriate units for each attribute; recognise that more accurate area measures require attention to partial units.
wider: Explore the paddock problem: create rectangles with the same perimeter on grid paper and compare their areas — discovering that perimeter does not determine area
