Investigate real-world contexts where perimeter and area are both relevant (fencing vs carpeting a room) and discuss which measurement is needed for each purpose

modes.reason: The perimeter-area confusion is one of the most robust misconceptions in primary measurement. Contexts where both are measured for the same shape — and where they give different information — are the most effective resolution. The paddock problem (same fence length, different enclosed area) is particularly powerful.

descriptors.title: Duration with am and pm
descriptors.description: Solve problems involving the duration of time including situations involving 'am' and 'pm' and conversions between units of time
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use relationships between days, hours, minutes and seconds to estimate and compare duration (AC9M3M03) and read analog and digital clocks to the nearest minute (AC9M3M04). They have not yet worked with am/pm notation in duration problems or converted between units of time to solve problems.

nodes.label: am and pm notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and write times using am and pm notation and explain what each represents.
criteria: Students can correctly read and write times using am and pm notation
Students can explain which part of the day am refers to and which pm refers to

width.minimum: Read and write at least three times in am and pm notation; explain what am and pm mean.
width.typical: Read and write times in am and pm notation across the full day; recognise that noon and midnight are the transition points; represent a day's schedule using both am and pm times; explain which times fall in am and which in pm.
wider: Investigate the history and purpose of the am/pm convention — comparing with 24-hour time and discussing when each is more useful (transport timetables, clocks, scheduling)
Connect am/pm notation to a world map context: exploring what time it is in different time zones while it is 10:00 am in Sydney

nodes.label: Duration calculations spanning am and pm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the duration between two times, including cases where the start and finish times span the am/pm boundary.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who subtract times directly as whole numbers (e.g. 2:30 pm − 10:45 am = 8:15, missing the carry) produce systematically incorrect duration values. This error propagates directly into Node 3 conversion problems and any real-world timetabling context in this standard.
criteria: Students can calculate the duration between two times that span noon or midnight
Students can express duration in appropriate units (hours and minutes, or minutes and seconds)

width.minimum: Calculate the duration between two times that are both am or both pm; state the answer in hours and minutes.
width.typical: Calculate duration between two times including cases that span the noon or midnight boundary; use number line or bridging strategies (e.g. count to the hour, then add remaining minutes); apply to real contexts (movie duration, bus journey, flight times).
wider: Create a timetable for a real or imagined event (athletics carnival, sports day) involving activities across am and pm, ensuring durations are correctly calculated and times are consistent
Investigate flight duration problems including departure and arrival in different time zones — discussing why the quoted duration and the difference in times might not match

modes.reason: Duration calculations spanning the noon boundary require students to bridge through 12:00 — a reasoning scaffold (how long to noon? how long after noon?) prevents common errors from subtracting times directly as if they were whole numbers.

nodes.label: Converting units of time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert between units of time and apply conversions to solve practical problems.
criteria: Students can convert a duration between seconds, minutes and hours
Students can apply a unit conversion to solve a practical time problem

width.minimum: Convert one duration between units (e.g. express 90 minutes as 1 hour and 30 minutes); use this to solve one practical problem.
width.typical: Convert between seconds, minutes and hours; apply conversions to solve practical duration problems; create timetables requiring unit conversions; apply to real contexts (exercise routines, activity schedules).
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' explanations of time through cultural accounts about cyclic phenomena — sun, moon and stars as time-keeping systems — and discuss how cyclical models of time differ from linear duration measurement
Design a full-day schedule for an event, converting between units throughout and checking all times are consistent with am/pm notation

descriptors.title: Angle types
descriptors.description: Estimate and compare angles using angle names including acute, obtuse, straight angle, reflex and revolution, and recognise their relationship to a right angle
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify angles as measures of turn and compare them with right angles (AC9M3M05). They have not yet classified angles using formal names (acute, obtuse, straight, reflex, revolution) or estimated angle sizes.

nodes.label: Classify angles by name
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex or revolution.
criteria: Students can correctly classify a given angle as acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex or revolution
Students can explain the relationship of each angle type to a right angle

width.minimum: Identify at least four angle types from examples using a right-angle template; name each correctly.
width.typical: Classify angles in the environment and in geometric shapes using angle names; use a right-angle template to compare; explain the relationship of each type to a right angle (e.g. acute < 90°, obtuse > 90° but < 180°).
wider: Systematically classify all interior angles of a set of polygons (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon) and record findings — noticing which shapes contain which angle types
Identify angle types in the built environment using photographs — classifying roof pitches, door hinges, ramp gradients by angle type

nodes.label: Estimate and compare angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate whether angles are smaller or larger than a right angle and compare angles using a right-angle template.
criteria: Students can use a right-angle template to classify and compare angles in the environment
Students can order a set of angles from smallest to largest using a right-angle reference

width.minimum: Use a right-angle template to compare at least three angles in the environment; order them from smallest to largest.
width.typical: Estimate and compare angles in shapes and in the environment using a right-angle template; create a right-angle template and use it systematically; use tools like spirit levels and set squares to determine perpendicularity; classify angles in the environment.
wider: Use spirit levels and set squares as construction tools — investigating how right angles are used in building and carpentry, and why perpendicularity matters practically
Investigate how dynamic geometry software visualises angle measurement, exploring the relationship between rotation and angle size

descriptors.title: Decimals — tenths and hundredths
descriptors.description: Recognise and extend the application of place value to tenths and hundredths and use the conventions of decimal notation to name and represent decimals
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, represent and order natural numbers and understand place value for hundreds, tens and ones (AC9M3N01, AC9M3N02). They have not yet extended place value beyond the ones place to fractional parts of a whole.

nodes.label: Tenths as place value
nodes.checkpoint: Students can partition a whole into ten equal parts and represent one or more tenths using decimal notation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not anchor the place value meaning of tenths enter Node 2 treating decimal digits as whole numbers, making the multiplicative structure of hundredths (tenth of a tenth) inaccessible. The misconception propagates through all decimal comparison and notation work in this standard.
criteria: Students can represent a given number of tenths using a bar model or number line and write the decimal notation
Students can explain what the digit after the decimal point represents (tenths)

width.minimum: Divide a bar model into 10 equal parts; name and write the decimal for 2 or more of those parts (e.g. 0.3); explain what the digit after the decimal point represents.
width.typical: Use bar models, number lines and materials to represent tenths; name and write decimals to tenths; explain the value of each digit; connect to the counting sequence (0.1, 0.2, … 0.9, 1.0).
wider: Connect tenths to measurement: represent 1.5 metres on a ruler and explain what the 5 tenths means in centimetres
Use base-ten materials (one flat = whole, one long = tenth, one unit = hundredth) to build tenths and make explicit the multiplicative relationship

modes.reason: Common misconception: students treat 0.3 as 'three' rather than 'three-tenths', particularly when comparing (thinking 0.8 > 0.15 is uncertain because '15 is bigger than 8'). Exposure to tenths in multiple representations — bar, number line, measurement — addresses this by anchoring the place value meaning.

nodes.label: Hundredths and multiplicative structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent hundredths and explain the multiplicative relationship between ones, tenths and hundredths.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not grasp the 1:10:100 multiplicative chain treat decimals as paired whole numbers, producing systematic errors in decimal comparison, ordering, and all subsequent decimal operations. This misconception is the most consequential in the decimal number system.
criteria: Students can represent a decimal to hundredths using materials and identify the value of each digit
Students can rename a decimal in multiple ways (e.g. 0.25 as twenty-five hundredths or two-tenths and five-hundredths)

width.minimum: Use materials to show that one tenth divided into 10 equal parts gives hundredths; write one decimal to hundredths (e.g. 0.25) and explain the value of each digit.
width.typical: Use materials (bundles, decipipes, grid squares) to show the multiplicative chain: 1 whole = 10 tenths = 100 hundredths; rename decimals (e.g. 0.25 as two-tenths and five-hundredths or twenty-five hundredths); connect to measurement (e.g. 1.75 units = 1 unit and 75 hundredths).
wider: Explore the multiplicative chain using base-ten materials where the flat = 1, long = 0.1, unit = 0.01 — physically building the relationship and testing equivalences
Investigate how hundredths appear in money: why does $2.75 have 75 hundredths and what is the hundredths place in 'seventy-five cents'?

modes.reason: The multiplicative structure (tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) is the conceptual hinge — students who miss this treat decimals as two separate whole numbers either side of a dot. Varied representations (materials, measurement, money) that all show the same 1:10:100 chain are the resolution.

nodes.label: Decimal notation conventions and contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name, write and read decimals to hundredths in money and measurement contexts, explaining how notation conventions differ.
criteria: Students can correctly read a decimal in money notation and in measurement notation, noting the different conventions
Students can explain that the digits after the decimal point represent tenths and hundredths in both money and measurement

width.minimum: Write at least one decimal value in both money notation and measurement notation; read each aloud correctly (e.g. $2.75 as 'two dollars seventy-five', 2.75 m as 'two point seven five metres').
width.typical: Connect decimal notation to both money and metric measurement contexts; explain the similarities and differences in how each is read (money vs measurement conventions); recognise that in both, the digits after the decimal point represent tenths and hundredths of the unit.
wider: Compare how decimals are read across different real-world contexts (sporting scores, scientific measures, GPS coordinates) and discuss why different conventions exist
Investigate how currency decimals connect to hundredths: 75 cents is 75 hundredths of a dollar — verify this by counting coins and connecting to decimal notation

descriptors.title: Odd and even numbers
descriptors.description: Explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can skip count by twos, fives and tens (AC9M1A01) and understand equal sharing and grouping (AC9M1N06). They have not yet formally explained the odd/even distinction or the patterns that emerge when combining odd and even numbers through operations.

nodes.label: Identify odd and even
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether any whole number is odd or even using the ones digit.
criteria: Students can identify any given whole number as odd or even using the ones digit
Students can explain why the ones digit determines whether a number is even

width.minimum: Identify whether given numbers are odd or even using the ones digit rule; explain why numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 are even.
width.typical: Identify odd and even numbers using the ones digit rule; explain the connection to equal sharing (even numbers can be shared equally between 2 without a remainder); verify using materials for smaller numbers; apply the rule to larger numbers without materials.
wider: Investigate whether the ones digit rule holds for numbers in the hundreds and thousands — testing cases and explaining why the ones digit determines divisibility by 2 regardless of the other digits
Follow an algorithm (flowchart) to classify a set of numbers as odd or even, connecting the mathematical property to computational thinking

nodes.label: Patterns with operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the patterns that result from adding, subtracting and multiplying odd and even numbers.
criteria: Students can predict the odd/even result of a calculation before computing it, using a named pattern
Students can explain why at least one odd/even pattern holds using the equal-sharing definition

width.minimum: Verify one addition pattern with examples (e.g. even + even = even) using materials or calculation; explain why the pattern holds.
width.typical: Investigate and explain patterns for all combinations of odd and even numbers across addition, subtraction and multiplication (e.g. odd + odd = even, odd × even = even); use pattern knowledge to check the reasonableness of arithmetic answers.
wider: Systematically generate and verify the complete set of odd/even patterns for addition, subtraction and multiplication, and explain the reasoning behind each pattern using the equal-sharing definition
Investigate whether the patterns extend to division — exploring which combinations of odd/even divisor and dividend always/sometimes/never produce whole-number quotients

modes.reason: Students need to move beyond pattern recognition to explanation — 'odd + odd = even because when you pair up all the unpaired ones from each odd number, they make a pair.' Scaffolding the reasoning from the equal-sharing model to the pattern generalisation requires explicit structure.

descriptors.title: Equivalent fractions and decimals
descriptors.description: Find equivalent representations of fractions using related denominators and make connections between fractions and decimal notation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/10) and their multiples (AC9M3N02) and can recognise halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving (AC9M2N03). They have not yet found equivalent fractions using related denominators or connected fractions to decimal notation.

nodes.label: Equivalent fractions — same quantity, different names
nodes.checkpoint: Students can find at least two equivalent fractions for a given fraction using related denominators, and explain what makes them equivalent.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who retain the larger-denominator misconception cannot meaningfully engage with Node 2 — the fraction–decimal connection requires understanding that 1/4 and 2/8 name the same quantity, and that the decimal equivalent belongs to the quantity, not to one particular fraction name.
criteria: Students can find at least two fractions equivalent to a given fraction using materials or diagrams
Students can explain that equivalent fractions name the same quantity using a model

width.minimum: Use paper folding or materials to show that 1/2 = 2/4; identify one other equivalent pair (e.g. 2/4 = 4/8); explain that the fractions name the same quantity.
width.typical: Use folding, area models and collections to find and verify equivalent fractions within families (halves/quarters/eighths, thirds/sixths, fifths/tenths); extend fraction families (e.g. 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12); explain equivalence using the idea of 'same portion of the whole'.
wider: Generate complete fraction families for halves/quarters/eighths and thirds/sixths using paper folding, and represent the full family on a number line to show all names for the same position
Explore capacity subdivisions (half cup = two-quarter cups = four-eighth cups) to ground equivalence in measurement and cooking contexts

modes.reason: Misconception: students believe a fraction with a larger denominator is always a larger fraction. Experiencing equivalent fractions across multiple representations (area, length, set models) builds the understanding that the denominator names the size of each part, not the value of the fraction.

nodes.label: Fraction–decimal connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect familiar fractions to their decimal equivalents using measurement models.
criteria: Students can identify the decimal equivalent of at least 1/4, 1/2 and 1/10 using a measurement model
Students can explain the connection between a fraction and its decimal equivalent (e.g. 1/4 is 25 hundredths of the unit)

width.minimum: Find 1/4 of a metre and connect to 0.25 m; or find 1/10 of a metre and connect to 0.10 m. Explain the connection using a ruler or number line.
width.typical: Connect fractions of measurement units to their decimal equivalents across multiple cases (1/4 m = 0.25 m = 25 cm; 1/10 m = 0.10 m = 10 cm; 1/2 m = 0.5 m); use array diagrams to show the relationship between fractions and division (e.g. 1/4 of 12 = 12÷4 = 3); represent equivalent fractions and decimals on the same number line.
wider: Investigate fraction-decimal equivalents in capacity and mass measurement contexts, generating a reference table of common equivalents (1/4 kg = 0.25 kg, 1/2 litre = 0.5 litres)
Use array diagrams to explore the relationship between fractions, multiplication and division, building towards understanding fractions as division

modes.reason: Connecting fractions to decimals is often presented abstractly. Using measurement contexts (rulers, measuring jugs) where both notations are genuinely used makes the connection meaningful and durable. Students who only see the symbolic transformation (1/4 → 0.25) frequently cannot recall or reconstruct it.

descriptors.title: Fractions on number lines
descriptors.description: Count by fractions including mixed numerals; locate and represent these fractions as numbers on number lines
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise unit fractions and their multiples and combine fractions with the same denominator (AC9M3N02). They have not yet counted past one whole using fractions or represented mixed numerals on number lines.

nodes.label: Counting past one whole with fractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can count by fractions past one whole and name mixed numerals in the counting sequence.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat fractions as labels rather than quantities cannot meaningfully engage in Node 2 — converting between mixed numerals and improper fractions requires understanding that the fraction count continues across whole-number positions, not that it resets.
criteria: Students can continue a fraction counting sequence past one whole, correctly naming each mixed numeral
Students can locate at least three fractions including one mixed numeral on a number line

width.minimum: Count by quarters from zero to at least two wholes, naming each step (one-quarter, two-quarters, three-quarters, one-whole, one-and-one-quarter…); represent on a number line.
width.typical: Count by halves, quarters and thirds; name fractions in the counting sequence including mixed numerals; recognise when different counting sequences land at the same position (e.g. 2/4 = 1/2); use physical objects to ground the count.
wider: Use parallel number lines for halves, quarters and thirds simultaneously, investigating which fraction counts coincide and explaining the equivalence
Extend counting to sixths and eighths, connecting to the fraction families from AC9M4N03

modes.reason: A common error is treating fractions on the number line as labels rather than quantities — placing 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 without understanding that 4/4 = 1 and that counting continues beyond. Parallel number lines showing multiple fraction sequences make the continuity of the counting sequence across one whole visible.

nodes.label: Mixed numerals and improper fractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert between mixed numerals and improper fractions and represent both on a number line.
criteria: Students can convert a mixed numeral to an improper fraction and explain the reasoning
Students can locate a mixed numeral on a number line by correctly subdividing the unit intervals

width.minimum: Convert one mixed numeral to an improper fraction (e.g. 1 and 1/4 = 5/4) and represent it on a number line; explain the conversion.
width.typical: Convert between mixed numerals and improper fractions in both directions; represent on number lines; explain the connection (e.g. 1 and 3/4 = 7/4 because there are 4 quarters in a whole and 3 more); count in tenths and recognise that 10 tenths = 1.
wider: Investigate conversion using physical objects (e.g. cutting oranges into quarters — 7 quarter-pieces = 1 and 3/4 oranges = 7/4 oranges) to ground the abstract conversion in a countable context
Use number lines to explore the relationship between tenths, halves, quarters and fifths — identifying positions that can be named by multiple fractions

modes.reason: The conversion algorithm (multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator) is easily memorised without understanding. Scaffolding the reasoning through the counting sequence or physical partitioning ensures students can reconstruct the conversion from understanding rather than recall a procedure.

descriptors.title: Multiply and divide by powers of 10
descriptors.description: Solve problems involving multiplying or dividing natural numbers by multiples and powers of 10 without a calculator, using the multiplicative relationship between the place value of digits
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and represent numbers beyond 10 000 and understand place value conventions (AC9M3N01); they can multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers (AC9M3N04). They have not yet applied the multiplicative structure of place value to multiply or divide by 10, 100 or 1000.

nodes.label: Multiplying by 10 — digit movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain and demonstrate that multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who hold the 'add a zero' model enter Node 2 with a rule that fails for ×100 and ×1000 edge cases and entirely for decimals. The digit-movement model is the prerequisite conceptual frame for generalising to all powers of 10.
criteria: Students can multiply a two- or three-digit number by 10 without a calculator and explain the digit movement
Students can explain why the rule works using place value language (not just 'add a zero')

width.minimum: Use materials or a place value chart to show that 34 × 10 = 340; explain why each digit moves one place to the left.
width.typical: Use place value charts, numeral expanders or sliders to demonstrate multiplying by 10 across multiple examples; explain why digits move left (each place becomes ten times larger); generalise the pattern.
wider: Use numeral expanders or sliders to make visible the digit movement interpretation — physically sliding digits left and discussing whether 'adding a zero' captures the same idea or misrepresents it
Connect multiplication by 10 to metric unit conversions (e.g. 3 m × 10 = 30 dm or 3.0 m = 30 dm) — applying the pattern to measurement

modes.reason: Common misconception: 'multiply by 10 means add a zero.' This works for whole numbers but breaks down for decimals (0.3 × 10 ≠ 0.30). The correct conceptual model — digits move left — is the hinge. Seeing the pattern in place value charts, sliders and measurement contexts prevents the 'add a zero' shortcut from calcifying.

nodes.label: Dividing by 10 and extending to 100 and 1000
nodes.checkpoint: Students can multiply and divide by 10, 100 and 1000 using the place value relationship, and solve related problems.
criteria: Students can multiply and divide a number by 10, 100 and 1000 without a calculator
Students can solve a practical problem by identifying that ×10 or ÷10 is needed and applying it correctly

width.minimum: Divide one number by 10 using a place value chart and explain the digit movement; solve one multiplication problem involving 100.
width.typical: Use place value charts to demonstrate multiplication and division by 10, 100 and 1000; generalise the pattern (number of places = number of zeros); apply to solve computation problems without a calculator; use digital tools to check and extend the pattern.
wider: Investigate the pattern using a spreadsheet: enter numbers and apply ×10, ×100, ×1000 formulas, record results in a place value table and generalise the pattern from 100 terms
Apply the place value pattern to multi-step problems involving metric conversions (e.g. how many millimetres in 4.5 metres?)

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of related problems they can solve using this rule — not just ×10 but ×100, ÷10, ÷100, and related combinations. A narrow exposure to ×10 alone leaves gaps when ×100 and ×1000 appear.

descriptors.title: Efficient addition and multiplication strategies
descriptors.description: Develop efficient strategies and use appropriate digital tools for solving problems involving addition and subtraction, and multiplication and division where there is no remainder
descriptors.knowledge: Students can add and subtract two- and three-digit numbers using place value (AC9M3N03) and multiply and divide one- and two-digit numbers (AC9M3N04). They have not yet developed efficient strategies for multi-digit multiplication or applied digital tools strategically.

nodes.label: Efficient addition and subtraction strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply and explain at least two efficient strategies for multi-digit addition or subtraction.
criteria: Students can apply at least two different efficient strategies for multi-digit addition or subtraction
Students can explain why a chosen strategy is efficient for a given pair of numbers

width.minimum: Apply one strategy beyond the standard algorithm (e.g. compensation, near-hundreds) to solve one addition or subtraction problem; explain why this approach is efficient.
width.typical: Develop, apply and explain multiple efficient strategies for addition and subtraction (partitioning, compensation, near-numbers, constant difference for subtraction); select strategies based on the numbers involved; use digital tools to verify.
wider: Compare the efficiency of different strategies for the same problem type (e.g. 497 + 348: partition vs compensation) and build a decision rule for when each strategy is more efficient
Apply strategies to multi-step problems where an efficient approach for each sub-step reduces overall cognitive load

modes.reason: Efficient computation requires a repertoire of strategies, not a single approach. Students who know only one method (e.g. always partition) are less flexible than those who can select from compensation, near-hundreds or constant difference depending on the numbers.

nodes.label: Multiplication strategies for larger numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply area model or partitioning strategies to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number.
criteria: Students can multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number using a partitioning strategy, recording each step
Students can explain the connection between their calculation and the area model or array

width.minimum: Use place value partitioning to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number (e.g. 34 × 6 = 30×6 + 4×6); record and explain the steps.
width.typical: Develop and apply efficient strategies for multiplication including area models, partitioning and the distributive property; extend to two-digit by two-digit multiplication using arrays or area models; use digital tools to check solutions.
wider: Use an area model to connect multiplication of two-digit numbers to the distributive property — showing how the grid squares represent the partial products
Investigate which strategies are most efficient for different types of multiplication problems (e.g. near-doubles, using known facts as anchors for derived facts)

modes.reason: Area models and partitioning require students to keep track of partial products — the reasoning scaffold (recording each step, labelling which part of the grid corresponds to which calculation) is necessary to prevent errors that accumulate from informal mental approaches.

nodes.label: Division without remainders
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve division problems without remainders using known multiplication facts and sharing/grouping strategies.
criteria: Students can solve a division problem without a remainder using an appropriate strategy
Students can explain whether they are finding the number of groups or the size of each group

width.minimum: Solve one division problem without a remainder using known multiplication facts or equal sharing (e.g. 48 ÷ 6 by thinking 'what times 6 equals 48?').
width.typical: Solve division problems without remainders using inverse multiplication, grouping and sharing; represent with arrays; use digital tools to check; select efficient strategies based on the size of numbers and available facts.
wider: Investigate the two meanings of division (equal sharing vs equal grouping) using the same problem, and discuss when each interpretation is more natural in context
Connect division to fraction notation — 12 ÷ 4 = 1/4 of 12 = 3 — building the fraction-as-division understanding

descriptors.title: Estimation and rounding
descriptors.description: Choose and use estimation and rounding to check and explain the reasonableness of calculations including the results of financial transactions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can estimate quantities in collections and assess reasonableness of calculations (AC9M3N05). They have not yet applied rounding systematically to calculations or used estimation in financial contexts.

nodes.label: Rounding to convenient numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can round numbers to the nearest 10 or 100 and explain the rounding rule.
criteria: Students can round any two- or three-digit number to the nearest 10 and 100
Students can explain which way a number rounds and why

width.minimum: Round one number to the nearest 10 and one to the nearest 100; explain the rule for deciding which way to round.
width.typical: Round two- and three-digit numbers to the nearest 10 or 100; explain the midpoint rule (5 rounds up); apply to prices and measurements; recognise that rounding to a closer power of 10 gives a more accurate estimate.
wider: Investigate rounding in different directions (always up, always down, round-half-up) and discuss when each is appropriate — e.g. always rounding up when budgeting to avoid overspending
Explore how the choice of rounding precision (to nearest 10 vs nearest 100) affects the usefulness of an estimate for different purposes

nodes.label: Estimation as a check
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use estimation to determine what range a calculation answer should fall within, and identify unreasonable answers.
criteria: Students can estimate the result of a calculation and state a bounding range
Students can identify an unreasonable answer using estimation and explain why it is unreasonable

width.minimum: Estimate the result of one calculation by rounding and determine a bounding range (the answer will be between ___ and ___); identify whether a given answer is reasonable.
width.typical: Use rounded estimates to determine a range for calculation results; identify whether computed answers are reasonable; explain the effect of rounding both numbers up, both down, or one each way on the estimate; apply to multi-step calculations.
wider: Investigate the accumulated effect of rounding in multi-step calculations — when does rounding at each step compound into a significant error?
Compare estimation strategies for the same problem: front-end estimation vs rounding vs compatible numbers, and discuss which gives a closer estimate

modes.reason: Students need the reasoning scaffold 'what am I over-counting and what am I under-counting when I round?' to develop the habit of predicting estimate direction. Without this, estimation remains a ritual rather than a genuine check on reasonableness.

nodes.label: Estimation in financial contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply estimation and rounding to financial transactions and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Students can estimate a total cost by rounding prices and explain whether the estimate is an overestimate or underestimate
Students can justify a rounding direction decision in a financial context (e.g. round up to avoid overspending)

width.minimum: Estimate the total cost of two or three items by rounding prices; explain whether the estimate is likely to be above or below the actual total.
width.typical: Use rounded amounts to complete an estimated budget for a shopping trip or event; explain why overestimating is appropriate when budgeting; apply estimation to check financial calculations for reasonableness.
wider: Plan a complete budget for a class event or excursion, using estimation throughout and justifying all rounding decisions in terms of the financial context
Investigate how supermarket price rounding (everything to the nearest 5 cents in cash transactions) is applied and calculate the cumulative effect on a shopping basket

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling — additive and multiplicative
descriptors.description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations including financial contexts; formulate the problems using number sentences and choose efficient calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve additive and multiplicative problems including financial contexts (AC9M3N06). They have not yet formulated multi-step problems requiring selection between operations, or interpreted solutions in complex financial contexts.

nodes.label: Formulate — represent the situation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical problem using a diagram (part-part-whole, bar model, array) and write a number sentence that matches the structure.
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect formulation propagates through all subsequent modelling phases — an incorrect number sentence produces a correct calculation of the wrong thing. Students who cannot identify problem structure from context cannot meaningfully engage in Nodes 2 or 3.
criteria: Students can represent a practical problem using a diagram and write a matching number sentence
Students can identify what is known and what is unknown in the problem structure

width.minimum: Represent one additive or multiplicative practical problem using a bar model or array; write the corresponding number sentence; identify what is known and what is unknown.
width.typical: Represent a range of additive and multiplicative problems using appropriate diagrams; write number sentences that reflect the problem structure (not just the calculation); identify the operation from the structure (additive: part or whole missing; multiplicative: groups or per-group missing); explain how each number in the sentence connects to the situation.
wider: Compare two different representations of the same problem (e.g. bar model vs array) and discuss how each makes different aspects of the structure visible
Analyse word problems by identifying the structural type before selecting a representation — building the habit of problem analysis before calculation

modes.reason: Students who encounter only additive problems may default to addition for all problems. Exposure to a wide range of problem types — missing part, missing whole, equal groups (number of groups missing), equal groups (per-group missing), comparison — is needed to develop appropriate operation selection. Phase collapse if this node is thin: students formulate incorrectly in all downstream modelling phases.

nodes.label: Solve — choose efficient strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can choose and apply an efficient calculation strategy for the operation identified in formulation.
criteria: Students can solve the formulated problem using an appropriate and efficient strategy
Students can explain why the strategy was appropriate for the numbers involved

width.minimum: Select and apply an appropriate strategy for one additive and one multiplicative calculation; explain why the strategy was chosen.
width.typical: Select efficient strategies for addition, subtraction and multiplication based on the numbers involved; use digital tools where appropriate to support calculations; explain strategy choices; apply known facts and properties to larger numbers.
wider: Compare multiple strategies for the same calculation and justify which is most efficient for those specific numbers
Investigate when digital tools are the most efficient approach and when mental strategies are faster

nodes.label: Interpret and communicate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a solution in terms of the original situation and communicate it clearly.
criteria: Students can state the answer to a practical problem in terms of the situation, including appropriate units
Students can explain whether the answer is reasonable and what it means in the original context

width.minimum: State the answer to one problem in terms of the situation (not just the number); explain what the answer means.
width.typical: Interpret answers in context across a range of problem types (including where remainders must be handled contextually, or where the answer needs units); communicate solutions in full sentences referencing the situation; evaluate whether the answer is reasonable.
wider: Solve multi-step modelling problems where each step requires interpretation before the next can be formulated — building the full modelling cycle iteratively
Present solutions to financial problems using appropriate financial language and conventions, considering who the audience is and what information they need

modes.reason: The interpret-and-communicate phase requires students to coordinate formulation, calculation and contextual reasoning simultaneously. The quality of interpretation reveals whether the full modelling cycle was understood or whether the problem was treated as a calculation exercise.

descriptors.title: Algorithms with addition and multiplication
descriptors.description: Follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions that use addition or multiplication to generate sets of numbers; identify and describe any emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can follow and create algorithms to investigate numbers and describe emerging patterns (AC9M3N07). They have not yet used multiplication as the operation in an algorithm or represented algorithms as formal flowcharts.

nodes.label: Follow a step-sequence algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow a given algorithm using addition or multiplication to generate a number sequence.
criteria: Students can correctly follow a multi-step algorithm to generate the next several terms of a sequence
Students can identify and describe at least one pattern in the generated sequence

width.minimum: Follow a written algorithm (list of steps) using multiplication by a constant to generate at least 5 terms of a sequence; identify one pattern in the sequence.
width.typical: Follow algorithms using both addition and multiplication to generate sequences; record results systematically; identify and describe emerging patterns including recognising that sequences can be extended indefinitely.
wider: Compare sequences generated by an additive algorithm (start at 1, add 3 each time) and a multiplicative algorithm (start at 1, multiply by 3 each time) — contrasting linear vs exponential growth visually
Use a calculator to follow algorithms and extend sequences, verifying patterns across many terms

nodes.label: Represent algorithms as flowcharts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent an algorithm as a flowchart using standard symbols for steps and decisions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot decompose an algorithm into sequential and conditional steps cannot meaningfully create their own algorithms in Node 3 — creation requires the same decomposition skill that following and representing flowcharts develops.
criteria: Students can create a basic flowchart representing an addition or multiplication algorithm
Students can trace a flowchart to generate the first several terms of a sequence

width.minimum: Represent one algorithm as a basic flowchart with at least one step and one decision node; explain what each symbol represents.
width.typical: Create flowcharts representing multiplication-based algorithms; use the flowchart to trace and verify sequence generation; explain how the decision node determines when to stop the sequence.
wider: Represent the same algorithm in two forms (written steps and flowchart) and compare — discussing which is clearer for different purposes
Design a flowchart that generates multiples of a given number and test it with classmates — debugging the flowchart where the output is incorrect

modes.reason: Flowcharts require students to decompose an algorithm into explicit sequential and conditional steps. The reasoning scaffold — 'what happens at each step, and what decision is being made?' — must be made explicit before students can create their own flowcharts accurately.

nodes.label: Create algorithms and identify patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an algorithm using addition or multiplication and identify patterns in the generated sequence.
criteria: Students can design an algorithm that generates a specified type of sequence (e.g. multiples of 4)
Students can identify and describe a pattern in a sequence they have generated and explain how the algorithm produces it

width.minimum: Create one algorithm (specifying starting value and operation) to generate a number sequence; identify and describe an emerging pattern.
width.typical: Create multiplication and addition algorithms; use digital tools (spreadsheets) to generate long sequences; identify patterns including multiples, geometric growth, and patterns in the ones digit; describe patterns in words and explain how the algorithm produces them.
wider: Use a spreadsheet with a 'fill down' formula to generate 100 terms and investigate patterns that only become apparent over many terms (e.g. repeating units digits in multiples)
Create and compare algorithms that produce the same sequence through different rules, investigating whether the same pattern can have different generating algorithms

descriptors.title: Likelihood and chance events
descriptors.description: Describe possible everyday events and the possible outcomes of chance experiments and order outcomes or events based on their likelihood of occurring; identify independent or dependent events
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe outcomes as likely, unlikely, certain or impossible with reasoning (AC9M3P01). They have not yet ordered events by likelihood on a scale, or identified independent and dependent events.

nodes.label: Ordering events by likelihood
nodes.checkpoint: Students can order a set of events from least likely to most likely and justify their reasoning.
criteria: Students can order a set of events from least likely to most likely
Students can justify their likelihood ordering using reasoning about the situation

width.minimum: Order at least three familiar events from least likely to most likely; explain the reasoning for the order.
width.typical: Order events by likelihood using a continuum from impossible to certain; explain reasoning; recognise that likelihood judgements may differ between people depending on their context and experience; use likelihood language consistently.
wider: Investigate how early warning systems use likelihood ordering as a fundamental component of AI decision-making — connecting mathematical probability reasoning to real-world alert systems
Discuss how predictive text uses likelihood to suggest words, and how the suggestion changes as more letters are revealed — making the probabilistic reasoning visible

nodes.label: Reasoning from composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the composition of a set (e.g. contents of a bag) to compare the likelihood of different outcomes.
criteria: Students can correctly predict which outcome is more likely given the composition of a set, with reasoning
Students can explain why the composition affects likelihood

width.minimum: Predict which outcome is more likely from two scenarios with different set compositions (e.g. two bags with different numbers of red and white balls); explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Compare likelihood of selecting different outcomes based on the relative frequencies in a set; explain that more of a certain item means greater likelihood of selecting it; apply to multiple scenarios; connect to the idea that certain outcomes (both at once) are impossible.
wider: Investigate dependent event chains in school contexts: given a high chance of a storm on Friday, what happens to the chance of the outdoor activity? Building multi-step conditional reasoning
Explore impossible event pairs (mutually exclusive outcomes — it cannot be hot and cold at the same time; a card cannot be both red and a spade) and connect to logical reasoning

modes.reason: Common misconception: the gambler's fallacy — believing that after a long run of heads, a tail is now 'due.' Students who encounter multiple independent event contexts (each coin toss is fresh) rather than only dependent contexts are less likely to develop this misconception.

nodes.label: Independent and dependent events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify independent events (where one outcome does not affect another) and dependent events (where it does).
criteria: Students can identify whether a given pair of events is independent or dependent and explain the reasoning
Students can explain why the outcome of one independent event does not change the probability of the next

width.minimum: Identify one pair of events as independent (e.g. two separate coin tosses) and one pair as dependent (e.g. chance of outdoor activity depending on weather); explain the difference.
width.typical: Identify and explain independent and dependent events from everyday and school contexts; explain that for independent events, a previous outcome does not change the probability of the next; provide examples of each type.
wider: Design and investigate a set of dependent events from a school context — mapping how one event's probability depends on a prior outcome, building a causal chain
Investigate the gambler's fallacy: given 5 heads in a row, is a tail more likely next? Examining why the answer is 'no' for independent events and connecting to the independent event definition

modes.reason: Independent vs dependent is a conceptual hinge: students who treat all chance events as independent will make errors in contexts where events genuinely are linked (weather affecting outdoor plans, selecting from a set without replacement). Exposure to clearly dependent contexts alongside clearly independent ones is the resolution.

descriptors.title: Repeated chance experiments
descriptors.description: Conduct repeated chance experiments to observe relationships between outcomes; identify and describe the variation in results
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments, record results and discuss variation (AC9M3P02). They have not yet investigated the relationship between theoretical likelihood and experimental outcomes across a larger number of trials, or connected chance experiments to AI applications.

nodes.label: Plan and conduct chance experiments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select a chance device, conduct a repeated experiment and record outcomes systematically.
criteria: Students can conduct a repeated chance experiment at least 10 times and record outcomes in an organised format
Students can identify all the possible outcomes for their experiment

width.minimum: Conduct a chance experiment at least 10 times using one device (coin, dice or spinner); record outcomes in a table.
width.typical: Conduct repeated experiments using coins, dice, spinners and card draws; record outcomes systematically; use both physical and virtual random generators; connect to the idea that AI systems use random generators to train algorithms.
wider: Investigate two simultaneous coins — recording outcomes systematically (HH, HT, TH, TT) and comparing observed frequencies after many trials
Conduct the same experiment using a physical device and a virtual one, comparing the distributions and discussing whether the digital tool produces 'random' results in the same way

nodes.label: Identify and describe variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe variation in experimental results and discuss what causes it.
criteria: Students can describe the variation in their experimental results
Students can explain that variation is expected in chance experiments and is not an error

width.minimum: Identify variation in results across repeated trials; describe one pattern or departure from an expected pattern.
width.typical: Compare results across multiple repetitions of the same experiment; identify and describe variation; discuss why results vary (chance); compare results with predictions; discuss how results change as the number of trials increases.
wider: Play strategic games (Noughts and Crosses, First to 20) and investigate whether the order of play affects the chance of winning — distinguishing games of pure chance from games with strategic elements
Pool class results from the same experiment to produce a combined dataset, comparing individual variation with the combined distribution and discussing what changes with more trials

modes.reason: Students often expect experimental results to exactly match the theoretical probability (e.g. exactly 5 heads in 10 tosses). Encountering variation across multiple independent trials — and pooling class results to see the distribution stabilise — builds understanding of probability as a long-run tendency.

descriptors.title: Composite shapes from familiar shapes
descriptors.description: Represent and approximate composite shapes and objects in the environment, using combinations of familiar shapes and objects
descriptors.knowledge: Students can make, compare and classify objects by key features (AC9M3SP01). They have not yet formally decomposed complex shapes into familiar components or used this decomposition to represent real-world objects.

nodes.label: Identify components of composite shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the familiar shapes that make up a composite shape or object.
criteria: Students can identify and name the familiar shapes that make up a given composite shape
Students can re-create the composite using those component shapes

width.minimum: Identify the familiar shapes within one composite shape; list the components.
width.typical: Identify familiar 2D shapes within composite designs (logos, natural objects, architectural features); identify the 3D objects that make up a complex object; re-create identified components using physical or virtual materials.
wider: Analyse logos or graphic designs to identify all geometric components, discussing how designers use primitive shapes to create recognisable images
Deconstruct cartoon characters or illustrations into their geometric components, listing all shapes present

nodes.label: Construct and approximate composite shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine familiar shapes to construct or approximate composite shapes and real-world objects.
criteria: Students can combine at least two familiar shapes to construct or represent a composite shape
Students can explain which familiar shapes were combined and how they fit together

width.minimum: Construct one composite shape using at least two familiar shapes; explain which shapes were combined.
width.typical: Use physical or virtual materials to construct composite shapes approximating real objects; use cube grids to model 3D objects; draw cartoon animals or objects using geometric primitives; create simple logos using combinations of shapes.
wider: Design a logo using graphic design software, combining geometric shapes purposefully and explaining how each shape contributes to the overall design
Build virtual 3D environments using cube-based software, making decisions about how to approximate curved surfaces and organic shapes with cubes and explaining the limitations of the approximation

descriptors.title: Grid reference systems
descriptors.description: Create and interpret grid reference systems using grid references and directions to locate and describe positions and pathways
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and create 2D representations of familiar environments (AC9M3SP02). They have not yet used formal grid reference systems to precisely locate and communicate positions.

nodes.label: Reading grid references
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate a position on a grid reference map using a letter-number grid reference.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who have not automatised the letter-then-number convention will systematically locate the wrong positions in Node 2, making direction-writing and pathway descriptions incoherent. The convention must be reliable before students can produce usable grid-reference directions.
criteria: Students can correctly locate a position on a grid map using a grid reference
Students can write the grid reference for a specified location on a grid map

width.minimum: Locate one position on a grid map using a grid reference (e.g. C3); explain how grid references work.
width.typical: Interpret grid reference maps of familiar locations; locate multiple positions; follow directions to trace pathways; recognise that the letter (column) comes before the number (row) in a grid reference.
wider: Compare a grid reference map without the grid overlay to one with it, investigating how the grid increases precision in locating and describing positions
Recognise that spreadsheets use a grid reference system (column letter + row number) and locate and enter data in spreadsheet cells

modes.reason: Students frequently reverse column and row (reading row first, then column), or confuse the region vs intersection interpretation of a grid reference. Consistent practice with correctly formatted references (letter then number) until the convention is automatic prevents downstream confusion in map reading.

nodes.label: Creating and describing with grid references
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write directions using grid references and directional language to guide someone from one location to another.
criteria: Students can write clear directions using grid references to guide movement from one location to another
Students can create a grid reference map of a familiar space with at least four labelled locations

width.minimum: Write a set of directions using grid references to guide someone from one location to another on a familiar map.
width.typical: Interpret and create grid reference maps; write directions combining grid references and directional language; use grids to enlarge images proportionally; use grid references to describe positions and pathways in different contexts.
wider: Simulate a robotic or autonomous vehicle moving through a grid environment using grid references and directional instructions — connecting grid navigation to real automation applications
Use a grid overlay to enlarge a piece of artwork, systematically applying the grid reference to transfer each section proportionally

descriptors.title: Line and rotational symmetry
descriptors.description: Recognise line and rotational symmetry of shapes and create symmetrical patterns and pictures, using dynamic geometric software where appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full measures of turn (AC9M2M05) and make and classify shapes (AC9M3SP01). They have not yet formally investigated rotational symmetry or created symmetrical patterns.

nodes.label: Line symmetry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe lines of symmetry in shapes and pictures.
criteria: Students can identify and draw at least one line of symmetry for a given shape
Students can explain what a line of symmetry means (the two halves match when folded)

width.minimum: Identify at least one line of symmetry in a given shape; explain what makes it a line of symmetry.
width.typical: Identify all lines of symmetry in a range of shapes; create symmetrical shapes and patterns using paper folding, mirrors or software; recognise asymmetric shapes; explain what a line of symmetry means in terms of reflection.
wider: Investigate lines of symmetry in cultural artefacts from diverse traditions (Islamic geometric art, Aboriginal dot paintings, Central Asian textiles), documenting how many lines of symmetry each pattern has
Explore symmetry in the natural environment on Country/Place — investigating flowers, plants and landscapes and discussing how First Nations peoples observe symmetry in nature

nodes.label: Rotational symmetry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify rotational symmetry in shapes and describe the order of rotation.
criteria: Students can test a shape for rotational symmetry by tracing and rotating, and identify one rotation that maps the shape onto itself
Students can distinguish between line symmetry and rotational symmetry for a given shape

width.minimum: Test one shape for rotational symmetry by tracing and rotating; identify whether the shape has rotational symmetry and name one rotation that maps it onto itself.
width.typical: Test and record which rotations produce the same image for a range of shapes; identify the order of rotational symmetry; use dynamic geometry software to test rotational symmetry; connect rotational symmetry to the turn measures from earlier years.
wider: Investigate rotational symmetry in tessellations using dynamic geometric software or generative AI tools — exploring how symmetry constraints produce different families of tessellating patterns
Compare line and rotational symmetry across the same set of shapes, building a systematic record of which shapes have each type and both

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse line symmetry with rotational symmetry. A structured investigation comparing both attributes for the same shapes — explicitly asking 'does this shape map onto itself under rotation?' vs 'does it map onto itself under reflection?' — makes the distinction clear.

descriptors.title: Many-to-one data displays
descriptors.description: Acquire data for categorical and discrete numerical variables to address a question of interest or purpose, using digital tools; represent data using many-to-one pictographs, column graphs and other displays or visualisations; interpret and discuss the information that has been created
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collect categorical and discrete numerical data and record using frequency tables (AC9M3ST01). They have not yet used many-to-one displays where one symbol represents multiple data points.

nodes.label: Many-to-one representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain and interpret many-to-one pictographs and column graphs where one symbol or unit represents more than one data point.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not apply the key when reading many-to-one displays will systematically misinterpret data in Node 3 — constructing displays with an inappropriate key value, or interpreting their own display by counting units rather than applying the scale. The key-first habit must be in place before construction.
criteria: Students can read the key of a many-to-one display and use it to accurately interpret the data
Students can explain what one symbol or column unit represents in a given display

width.minimum: Interpret one many-to-one pictograph; identify the key value (what one symbol represents); answer one question about the data.
width.typical: Interpret many-to-one pictographs and column graphs, including reading the key value, answering questions and identifying the most/least common categories; explain why reading the key before making judgements is essential; distinguish many-to-one from one-to-one displays.
wider: Investigate how digital platforms generate word clouds, quizzes and graphical summaries from collected poll data — connecting data representation to real AI-powered tools
Compare many-to-one representations with different key values for the same data set, discussing how the choice of scale affects readability and impression

modes.reason: Students who only work with one-to-one displays may misread many-to-one displays by counting symbols without applying the key. Encountering multiple displays with different key values — including poorly chosen scales — develops the habit of reading the key first.

nodes.label: Acquire and record data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can acquire data for a question of interest using appropriate methods and record using digital tools.
criteria: Students can collect data for a question of interest and record it in an organised format
Students can identify whether their variable is categorical or discrete numerical

width.minimum: Collect data for one question using observation or a simple survey; record in a tally chart or digital table.
width.typical: Acquire data through surveys, observations, experiments and repeated chance trials; record using tally charts, digital tables and spreadsheets; use digital tools for data organisation; collect data across categorical and discrete numerical variables.
wider: Use secondary data about fire burns to construct data displays that assist First Nations Ranger Groups and other groups to care for Country/Place
Co-create an online poll and explore how the platform generates graphical summaries of the responses, comparing the automated display with a student-made column graph of the same data

nodes.label: Construct and interpret displays
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a many-to-one display and interpret and discuss the information it reveals.
criteria: Students can construct a many-to-one display using a digital tool, including an appropriate key
Students can interpret their display by identifying and discussing at least two features of the data

width.minimum: Construct one many-to-one column graph or pictograph from collected data using a digital tool; identify and discuss one feature of the data.
width.typical: Construct many-to-one pictographs and column graphs using digital tools; interpret displays by describing the distribution and identifying patterns; discuss what the data shows in relation to the original question; make at least one inference beyond the immediate data.
wider: Construct displays of science experiment data and interpret them in terms of the scientific investigation — connecting statistics to cross-curriculum science inquiry
Acquire and graph data from repeated chance experiments, comparing column graphs across multiple trials and connecting the statistical variation to probability concepts

modes.reason: Constructing and interpreting a data display is an integration task — students coordinate data collection, representation decisions, key value choices, and interpretation simultaneously. The quality of the interpretation reveals whether the full statistical inquiry cycle is understood.

descriptors.title: Comparing data displays
descriptors.description: Analyse the effectiveness of different displays or visualisations in illustrating and comparing data distributions, then discuss the shape of distributions and the variation in the data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and compare different graphical representations (AC9M3ST02). They have not yet analysed the relative effectiveness of different displays or discussed distribution shape and variation.

nodes.label: Comparing display types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare two or more data displays of the same data and identify differences in what each communicates effectively.
criteria: Students can compare two displays of the same data and describe at least one advantage of each for a specific purpose
Students can suggest at least one question that can be answered by a given display

width.minimum: Compare two different displays of the same dataset; identify one way each display is more or less useful for answering a particular question.
width.typical: Compare student-generated and digital displays of the same data; describe similarities and differences; comment on usefulness for different questions; interpret representations from media where symbols represent one-to-many relationships.
wider: Evaluate data representations from news sources or online media, asking 'what questions can this display answer?' and 'what information does it obscure or distort?'
Investigate how AI developers use data visualisation as a step in data preparation, connecting data analysis to real-world AI applications

nodes.label: Distribution shape and variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss the shape of a data distribution and describe the variation in the data.
criteria: Students can describe the overall shape of a distribution using informal language
Students can identify and describe the variation in a data set (whether values are spread out or clustered)

width.minimum: Describe one feature of a distribution's shape (e.g. which category has the most data, whether values are spread out or clustered).
width.typical: Discuss the shape of distributions using informal language (spread out, clustered, even); identify the highest and lowest frequency categories; describe variation — how much the values differ; comment on what the distribution suggests about the original question.
wider: Compare distributions from two different data sets on the same question (e.g. survey results from two different classes) and describe the differences in shape and variation
Investigate what happens to a distribution when the sample size changes — collecting data in two rounds and comparing the distributions

modes.reason: Discussing distribution shape requires students to move beyond individual data points to see the aggregate pattern. The reasoning scaffold — 'look at the whole shape first, then describe where the data clusters' — must be made explicit to shift from point-by-point reading to pattern recognition.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations
descriptors.description: Conduct statistical investigations, collecting data through survey responses and other methods; record and display data using digital tools; interpret the data and communicate the results
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct guided statistical investigations involving collection, representation and interpretation of data (AC9M3ST03). They have not yet independently designed survey instruments or accessed data from online sources.

nodes.label: Pose and plan
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a statistical question and plan how to collect relevant data.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who collect data without verifying it can answer their question arrive at Node 3 with data that cannot support a meaningful interpretation. The investigation cycle breaks at the communication phase when the collected data and the original question are misaligned.
criteria: Students can pose a clear statistical question and identify what data is needed to answer it
Students can create a survey question that will produce data relevant to their question

width.minimum: Pose one statistical question and identify what data needs to be collected to answer it; describe how the data will be collected.
width.typical: Pose and refine statistical questions for different contexts; identify the most appropriate data collection method (survey, observation, secondary data); create survey questions that will produce useful data; plan the investigation before collecting.
wider: Investigate a consumer context (e.g. product placement in supermarkets) by identifying exactly what questions need to be answered and what data is needed — distinguishing relevant from irrelevant information
Compare what different types of data sources (own survey vs secondary data) can and cannot tell you about the same question

modes.reason: Students often jump to data collection without asking whether the planned data can actually answer their question. The planning scaffold — 'what question am I asking? what data answers it? how will I collect that data?' — is the key reasoning move that separates purposeful investigation from accidental data gathering.

nodes.label: Collect and record
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect data using surveys or digital sources and record it systematically using digital tools.
criteria: Students can collect and record data systematically using a digital tool
Students can identify whether their data is fit-for-purpose for answering the original question

width.minimum: Collect data using one method (survey or online source); record the data in a digital table or spreadsheet.
width.typical: Collect data through surveys, observation and digital sources; record using digital tables, tally sheets or spreadsheets; access online databases or query interfaces where appropriate; organise data for analysis.
wider: Access and retrieve data from an online query interface (weather records, Google Trends) to investigate a question that cannot be answered by a class survey
Compare data from a class survey with secondary data from an online source about the same question, noting similarities and differences

nodes.label: Interpret and communicate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret data from their investigation and communicate findings in terms of the original question.
criteria: Students can state at least one finding from their investigation in terms of the original question
Students can communicate results to an audience using appropriate language and a clear data display

width.minimum: Identify one finding from a data display and communicate it in a sentence that references the original question.
width.typical: Interpret data displays and describe the main findings; communicate results in terms of the original question to a relevant audience; discuss whether the data supports or challenges initial predictions; identify at least one limitation of the investigation.
wider: Compare investigation findings with predictions made before data collection, discussing what was surprising and how the evidence relates to initial assumptions
Present statistical findings to a real audience (class, another grade, principal) using appropriate language and visual displays, adapting communication to the audience's background

modes.reason: A statistical investigation is an integrated cycle — posing, collecting, displaying, and interpreting must all align for the communication to be coherent. The integration failure mode is a report that describes the display without connecting back to the original question. Communicating results demands students coordinate all phases.

descriptors.title: Multiplication and division as inverses
descriptors.description: Recognise and explain the connection between multiplication and division as inverse operations and use this to develop families of number facts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find unknown values in equations involving addition and subtraction using inverse reasoning (AC9M4A01). They have not yet applied inverse reasoning to multiplication and division or generated families of related facts.

nodes.label: Inverse relationship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that multiplication and division are inverse operations using materials or arrays.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the inverse relationship is the prerequisite for Node 2 — students who see multiplication and division as unrelated operations cannot generate fact families or apply inverse reasoning in calculation.
criteria: Student demonstrates the inverse relationship using a representation
Student explains the connection using their own words

width.minimum: Use an array or diagram to show that a multiplication and its corresponding division use the same three numbers; explain the inverse relationship.
width.typical: Demonstrate the inverse relationship for multiple examples using arrays, materials and number sentences; explain why the relationship holds.
wider: Connect to fact family structure: show all four related facts for an array
Use the inverse relationship to solve missing-number problems

modes.reason: Students often treat multiplication and division as completely separate operations. Multiple representations (arrays, materials, number sentences) help build the generalised understanding that they are connected.

nodes.label: Families of number facts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate a family of four related multiplication and division facts from a single multiplication situation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent fact family generation is required by Node 3 — students who cannot reliably produce all four related facts cannot apply inverse reasoning efficiently to multi-digit division problems.
criteria: Student generates all four facts in a family from a given multiplication
Student applies a fact family to find an unknown value

width.minimum: Given a multiplication fact, write all four related facts in the family (a×b=c, b×a=c, c÷a=b, c÷b=a).
width.typical: Generate fact families for a range of multiplication situations; use fact families to identify unknown values; apply to multi-digit facts using digital tools.
wider: Extend fact families to larger numbers using the inverse as a calculation strategy (240÷20 via 20×?=240)
Investigate how fact families support mental calculation strategies

modes.reason: Fluent fact family generation is a prerequisite for all inverse-based calculation. Students need practice generating the four-fact structure before applying it to solve unknowns.

nodes.label: Applying inverse in calculation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the inverse relationship between multiplication and division to solve calculation problems efficiently.
criteria: Student applies inverse reasoning to solve a division problem by thinking multiplicatively
Student explains why using multiplication is efficient for the given problem

width.minimum: Apply the inverse relationship to solve at least two division problems by thinking multiplicatively (e.g. 120 ÷ 6 via 6 × ? = 120).
width.typical: Apply inverse reasoning across a range of multi-digit problems; compare direct division with inverse multiplication approaches; select the most efficient approach for a given calculation.
wider: Apply inverse reasoning to check solutions: multiply back after dividing
Investigate how inverse reasoning supports mental arithmetic strategies

modes.reason: Students default to direct division even when inverse multiplication is more efficient. Varied problem types — with different number sizes and structures — build flexible strategy selection.

descriptors.title: Unknown values in multiplication equations
descriptors.description: Find unknown values in numerical equations involving multiplication and division using the properties of numbers and operations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find unknown values in equations involving addition and subtraction (AC9M4A02). They have not yet applied properties of multiplication and division (commutativity, associativity, equivalence) to find unknown values.

nodes.label: Properties of multiplication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate that multiplication is commutative and associative, and that division is neither.
criteria: Student demonstrates commutativity with an example and explanation
Student correctly identifies that division is not commutative with an example

width.minimum: Show that a×b=b×a using materials or arrays; show a case where a÷b ≠ b÷a; explain the difference.
width.typical: Demonstrate commutativity and associativity of multiplication across multiple examples; explain why division is not commutative; connect to array representations.
wider: Investigate the distributive property: a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c
Use the properties to derive unknown facts from known ones

nodes.label: Equivalent number sentences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use equivalence and number properties to determine whether multiplication/division equations are true and to find unknown values.
nodes.hinge_reason: Relational understanding of = is the prerequisite for Node 3 — students who treat = as 'write the answer' cannot formulate or verify equations arising from practical contexts.
criteria: Student determines whether an equation is true/false with correct reasoning
Student finds an unknown value in a multiplication/division equation using properties

width.minimum: Determine whether a given multiplication/division equation is true or false; explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Apply relational thinking to find unknown values in equations like 3×5=30÷□; use equivalence reasoning across a range of structures.
wider: Create equivalent number sentences using multiple operations
Use equations with unknowns in both sides: 4×□ = □×6

modes.reason: Relational thinking (understanding = as 'same value', not 'write the answer') requires an explicit scaffold. Students who have learned = as an answer prompt make systematic errors with balanced equations.

The variety of equation structures (unknown in different positions, multiple unknowns, cross-operation equivalence) exposes how relational thinking generalises. Breadth prevents students from learning the structure of one template.

nodes.label: Finding unknowns in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can find unknown values in numerical equations arising from practical contexts using multiplication and division properties.
criteria: Student writes an equation for a practical problem and finds the unknown value
Student verifies the solution by substituting back into the equation
