width.minimum: Solve a practical problem that requires finding an unknown value in a multiplication or division equation; show the equation and solution.
width.typical: Apply properties of multiplication and division to find unknowns in a range of practical and abstract contexts; connect equation-solving to word problem structures.
wider: Design word problems that require unknown-value equations to solve
Connect to scaling contexts: if 3 books cost $21, what does 1 cost? Equation: 3 × □ = 21

modes.reason: Applying equation reasoning in practical contexts requires properties knowledge, equation structure understanding and context interpretation to work together — the integrated application of the strand's learning.

descriptors.title: Choose metric units
descriptors.description: Choose appropriate metric units when measuring the length, mass and capacity of objects; use smaller units or a combination of units to obtain a more accurate measure
descriptors.knowledge: Students can measure with scaled instruments using formal units (AC9M4M01). They have not yet selected the most appropriate metric unit for a given measurement or combined units for greater accuracy.

nodes.label: Metric unit relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can state the relationship between common metric units and explain which is larger or smaller.
nodes.hinge_reason: Unit relationship fluency is required by Node 2 — students who cannot reliably state metric relationships cannot justify why one unit is more appropriate than another for a given measurement.
criteria: Student correctly states the relationship between two given metric units
Student orders metric units for a given attribute from smallest to largest

width.minimum: State the relationship between at least two metric units for one attribute (e.g. 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm); order metric units from largest to smallest.
width.typical: Identify and describe unit relationships for length (mm, cm, m, km), mass (g, kg, t) and capacity (mL, L); explain the 10/100/1000 relationship patterns.
wider: Connect metric prefixes to their meanings (milli-, centi-, kilo-)
Explore non-SI units still in common use and compare to metric equivalents

modes.reason: Unit relationship knowledge is foundational for appropriate unit selection and conversion. Students need fluency before they can make principled choices.

nodes.label: Choosing appropriate units
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select the most appropriate metric unit for a given measurement task and justify their choice.
criteria: Student selects an appropriate unit for a given context
Student explains why the chosen unit is more appropriate than an alternative

width.minimum: Select an appropriate unit for a given measurement (e.g. mm for pencil width, km for road distance) and justify the choice.
width.typical: Apply unit selection across length, mass and capacity contexts; compare the appropriateness of multiple units for a single measurement; explain the trade-off between precision and convenience.
wider: Survey how different professions (nurses, builders, scientists) select units in practice
Investigate First Nations measurement practices and compare to metric system conventions

modes.reason: Appropriate unit selection is context-dependent. Students who see only table-drill exercises over-apply one unit. Varied real contexts build the judgement to select rather than recall.

nodes.label: Combining units for accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a combination of metric units to express a measurement more accurately than a single unit allows.
criteria: Student expresses a measurement as a combination of two units correctly
Student explains why a combination provides greater accuracy

width.minimum: Express a measurement using two units (e.g. 1 m 34 cm); explain why the combination is more accurate than either unit alone.
width.typical: Measure and record length, mass and capacity using combinations of units; convert between combined and single-unit expressions; compare precision achievable with different unit combinations.
wider: Use combinations in practical tasks: measuring body height in cm and mm
Investigate how digital measurement tools report combinations (e.g. GPS elevation in m and cm)

descriptors.title: Perimeter and area problems
descriptors.description: Solve practical problems involving the perimeter and area of regular and irregular shapes using appropriate metric units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate perimeter and area of regular shapes using standard units (AC9M4M02). They have not yet solved problems involving irregular shapes or chosen between appropriate metric units for area/perimeter.

nodes.label: Perimeter of regular and irregular shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the perimeter of regular and irregular shapes, including shapes with missing sides.
criteria: Student calculates perimeter of an irregular rectilinear shape correctly
Student identifies and uses missing side lengths in perimeter calculation

width.minimum: Calculate the perimeter of an irregular rectilinear shape by adding all side lengths; identify and calculate missing side lengths using total dimension reasoning.
width.typical: Solve perimeter problems for a range of regular and irregular shapes in practical contexts (e.g. fencing, framing); use appropriate metric units.
wider: Investigate shapes with equal perimeter but different area
Explore perimeter in real contexts: orienteering, garden borders

nodes.label: Area of irregular shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the area of irregular rectilinear shapes by decomposing into rectangles.
nodes.hinge_reason: Decomposition strategy fluency is required by Node 3 — students who skip decomposition cannot reliably solve practical problems where irregular shapes require both area and perimeter reasoning.
criteria: Student decomposes an irregular shape into rectangles and calculates the total area
Student shows the decomposition in their working

width.minimum: Decompose an irregular rectilinear shape into two or more rectangles; calculate the area of each and sum.
width.typical: Apply decomposition strategy across a range of irregular rectilinear shapes; choose between different decomposition approaches; use appropriate area units.
wider: Estimate area of irregular curved shapes using grid overlays
Investigate how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land management practices involve area estimation

modes.reason: Area decomposition requires a deliberate strategy: identify non-overlapping rectangles, calculate each, sum. Students who skip the decomposition step get incorrect totals. The reasoning scaffold is the decomposition process itself.

nodes.label: Perimeter and area in practical problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve practical problems that require choosing between perimeter and area and using appropriate units.
criteria: Student correctly identifies whether perimeter or area is required for a given problem
Student solves the problem correctly with appropriate units

width.minimum: Solve a practical problem requiring perimeter or area; identify which measure is needed and state the appropriate unit.
width.typical: Solve problems where context determines whether perimeter or area is needed; explain the choice; apply metric unit selection.
wider: Design a garden or room layout within given perimeter and area constraints
Investigate real trade contexts: tiling (area) vs skirting board (perimeter) for the same room

modes.reason: Students confuse perimeter and area, especially in novel problem contexts. Varied practical situations — some requiring perimeter, some area, some both — resolve the conflation more effectively than abstract distinction exercises.

descriptors.title: 12- and 24-hour time
descriptors.description: Compare 12- and 24-hour time systems and solve practical problems involving the conversion between them
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate durations and work with am/pm time (AC9M4M03). They have not yet compared the two systems structurally or converted systematically.

nodes.label: Comparing the two systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the structural difference between 12- and 24-hour time and explain why 24-hour time is used in some contexts.
criteria: Student reads a given time correctly in both 12- and 24-hour format
Student explains the structural advantage of 24-hour notation

width.minimum: Describe the key difference between the systems; read a given time in both formats.
width.typical: Compare the two systems across a full 24-hour cycle; identify where confusion arises (12:00 noon/midnight, 13:00 onwards); explain why 24-hour time is unambiguous.
wider: Investigate professions that use 24-hour time (transport, military, medicine) and why
Explore time zones and how 24-hour notation avoids am/pm ambiguity across zones

nodes.label: Converting between systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert times between 12- and 24-hour systems, including times after noon and around midnight.
nodes.hinge_reason: Conversion accuracy is the prerequisite for Node 3 — students with noon/midnight errors produce systematically wrong duration calculations when times span these boundaries.
criteria: Student converts between systems correctly including noon and midnight
Student applies conversions to read a practical timetable

width.minimum: Convert a given am or pm time to 24-hour notation and vice versa; demonstrate correct handling of noon and midnight.
width.typical: Solve conversion problems across a full cycle including edge cases (12:00am, 12:00pm, 00:00); apply in practical contexts (timetables, schedules).
wider: Read and interpret real transport timetables in 24-hour time
Calculate journey durations from 24-hour timetables

modes.reason: Conversion accuracy requires internalising the +12/-12 rule for pm times with the noon/midnight exception. This is a precision skill where targeted practice reduces systematic errors.
The noon/midnight edge cases (12:00am = 00:00, 12:00pm = 12:00) are persistent misconceptions. Multiple contexts exposing these cases help students build correct mental models.

nodes.label: Solving duration problems with 24-hour time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate durations using 24-hour time and solve practical scheduling problems.
criteria: Student calculates a duration between two 24-hour times correctly
Student solves a practical scheduling problem using 24-hour time

width.minimum: Calculate the duration between two times given in 24-hour format; solve a simple scheduling problem.
width.typical: Solve multi-step duration problems using 24-hour times; calculate arrival times, departure times and durations from timetables; handle problems that cross midnight.
wider: Interpret real transport timetables and plan multi-leg journeys
Calculate time differences across time zones using 24-hour notation

modes.reason: Duration calculation with 24-hour times requires consistent application of the subtraction process; errors at midnight-crossing cluster here and need targeted practice.

descriptors.title: Measure angles with protractor
descriptors.description: Estimate, construct and measure angles in degrees, using appropriate tools including a protractor, and relate these measures to angle names
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and name angle types (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex) (AC9M4M04). They have not yet measured angles in degrees or used a protractor to construct angles.

nodes.label: Degrees as a unit
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that angles are measured in degrees and relate benchmark angles (90°, 180°, 360°) to angle names.
criteria: Student states benchmark angle measures in degrees
Student matches a degree range to an angle name

width.minimum: State that a full turn = 360°, half turn = 180°, quarter turn = 90°; match these to right, straight and full angle names.
width.typical: Relate all named angle types to degree ranges; use benchmark angles to estimate whether an angle is acute, obtuse or reflex before measuring.
wider: Investigate why 360° was chosen as the unit for a full turn — historical and astronomical context
Connect to clock face: how many degrees does the minute hand turn in one hour?

nodes.label: Estimating angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate angles in degrees using benchmark angles as reference points.
criteria: Student estimates an angle within ±15° of actual value
Student uses a named benchmark angle to justify their estimate

width.minimum: Estimate an angle to the nearest 10° using benchmark angle knowledge; compare estimate to a measured value.
width.typical: Estimate a range of acute, obtuse and reflex angles; develop estimation strategies based on benchmark subdivision.
wider: Use estimation in practical design tasks: estimating roof pitch, ramp angle
Investigate how First Nations architecture and design involves angular reasoning

nodes.label: Measuring with a protractor
nodes.checkpoint: Students can correctly position and read a protractor to measure angles, including obtuse angles.
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct protractor technique — specifically scale selection — is the prerequisite for Node 4 (construction). Students who read the wrong scale construct angles that are consistently wrong by the supplement amount.
criteria: Student positions the protractor correctly on an angle
Student reads the correct scale and records the angle in degrees

width.minimum: Measure an acute angle using a protractor, selecting the correct scale; record the measurement in degrees.
width.typical: Measure acute and obtuse angles using a protractor; identify and use the correct inner/outer scale; verify measurements against estimate.
wider: Measure angles in polygons and verify angle sum properties
Investigate digital tools (dynamic geometry software) as alternatives to physical protractors

modes.reason: Protractor use has specific procedural requirements (correct scale, vertex alignment, zero-line placement) where errors cluster. Targeted practice with deliberate attention to each step reduces systematic error.

Students commonly use the wrong scale (read 60° as 120°). Angles in varied orientations and obtuse angles require actively choosing the correct scale — multiple examples with differing angle sizes resolve this.

nodes.label: Constructing angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a given angle in degrees using a protractor.
criteria: Student constructs a specified angle within ±2° accuracy
Student verifies the constructed angle by measuring

width.minimum: Construct a given acute angle using a protractor; verify by measuring the constructed angle.
width.typical: Construct acute and obtuse angles; apply to shape construction tasks; check construction accuracy using measurement.
wider: Construct specific angles in geometric patterns or designs
Use dynamic geometry software to construct and verify angles

descriptors.title: Decimals beyond hundredths
descriptors.description: Interpret, compare and order numbers with more than 2 decimal places, including numbers greater than one, using place value understanding; represent these on a number line
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent and compare decimals to hundredths on a number line (AC9M4N01). They have not yet interpreted thousandths or beyond, or compared decimals greater than one requiring more than 2 decimal places.

nodes.label: Tenths and hundredths review
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the place value of each digit in a decimal to hundredths and explain what each digit represents.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the place value of each digit in a given decimal to hundredths
Student can partition a decimal to hundredths into its component parts and record them

width.minimum: Identify and name the value of each digit in a decimal number to hundredths (e.g. 3.47 — 3 ones, 4 tenths, 7 hundredths).
width.typical: Represent and interpret decimals to hundredths using place value charts, number lines and MAB-style representations; explain the relative size of tenths and hundredths.
wider: Use measurement contexts (e.g. metres/centimetres) to ground place value meaning
Connect decimal and fraction representations: 0.47 = 47/100

nodes.label: Thousandths and beyond
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read, write and name decimals with more than 2 decimal places, explaining the place value of each digit.
nodes.hinge_reason: The 'longer decimal = bigger number' misconception causes systematic errors in Node 3 — students who conflate decimal length with magnitude cannot compare or order decimals correctly.
criteria: Student reads and writes a decimal to thousandths correctly
Student identifies the place value of each digit in a decimal with 3+ decimal places

width.minimum: Read, write and name a decimal to thousandths; identify the place value of each digit.
width.typical: Extend the place value chart to thousandths and ten-thousandths; connect to metric contexts (e.g. kilometres, millimetres). Explain the pattern of powers of ten extending to the right.
wider: Explore scientific measurement contexts requiring 4+ decimal places
Investigate how First Nations land measurement and navigation systems express precision differently

modes.reason: Thousandths are abstract without grounding contexts. Students commonly confuse the length of a decimal with its magnitude — more decimal places perceived as bigger. Multiple concrete contexts (measurement, money, science) help resolve this.

nodes.label: Comparing and ordering decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and order sets of decimals with more than 2 decimal places, including decimals greater than one, justifying their reasoning using place value.
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate decimal comparison is the prerequisite for number line placement in Node 4 — students who cannot correctly order decimals cannot meaningfully position them on a number line.
criteria: Student correctly orders a set of decimals with different numbers of decimal places
Student identifies and explains the error in an incorrect ordering (e.g. 0.35 > 0.9)

width.minimum: Compare two decimals with up to 3 decimal places and place them in order, justifying using place value column comparison.
width.typical: Order sets of 4-6 decimals with mixed decimal places (e.g. 1.3, 0.27, 1.039, 0.3); explain common ordering errors (e.g. treating longer decimals as larger).
wider: Compare decimals arising from measurement contexts with different units requiring conversion
Sort sporting or scientific data (e.g. race times, pH values) where ordering decimals is purposeful
Explore how different representations (number line, place value chart) highlight different aspects of comparison

modes.reason: The 'longer decimal = bigger number' misconception is persistent. Varied contexts expose the misconception from multiple angles — students who see only abstract lists may retain the error even after instruction.
Comparison requires consistent application of the place value alignment procedure. Students benefit from practising the alignment step explicitly before it becomes fluent.

nodes.label: Representing on a number line
nodes.checkpoint: Students can place decimals with more than 2 decimal places, including numbers greater than one, accurately on a number line.
criteria: Student places given decimals with 3+ decimal places on a number line at approximately correct positions
Student justifies placement using place value language

width.minimum: Place at least two decimals with 3 decimal places on a labelled number line, choosing an appropriate scale.
width.typical: Construct and label a number line for a given range and interval; place decimals greater than one and justify placement using place value estimation.
wider: Use open number lines to compare intervals between decimals
Connect to measurement scales (thermometers, rulers, scales) as physical number lines

modes.reason: Accurate number line placement requires students to apply both understanding (place value) and precision (estimation of intervals). Fluency here supports all subsequent decimal work.

descriptors.title: Factors and multiples
descriptors.description: Express natural numbers as products of their factors, recognise multiples and determine if one number is divisible by another
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify odd and even numbers and recognise some basic number properties (AC9M4N02). They have not yet systematically expressed numbers as products of factors or applied divisibility reasoning.

nodes.label: Multiples
nodes.checkpoint: Students can list multiples of a given number and recognise whether a number is a multiple of another.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent multiple recognition is directly required by Node 2 (systematic factor pairs) and Node 4 (divisibility) — students who cannot reliably identify multiples cannot work systematically through factor pairs or apply divisibility rules.
criteria: Student lists multiples of a given number without skip-counting errors
Student determines whether a given number is a multiple of another and explains why

width.minimum: List at least 10 multiples of any single-digit number; identify whether a given number is a multiple of a given factor.
width.typical: Generate multiples for numbers 2–12; use multiples to solve divisibility questions informally; identify common multiples.
wider: Use skip-counting patterns on a hundreds chart to visualise multiples
Connect multiples to real-world contexts (e.g. scheduling, tiling, packing)

modes.reason: Fluency with multiples is foundational for later fraction and LCM work. Students need repeated practice before the concept transfers reliably.

nodes.label: Factors and factor pairs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can find all factor pairs of a natural number and list all its factors.
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic factor-pair finding is the prerequisite for Node 3 (products of factors) — students who cannot reliably enumerate factor pairs cannot express numbers as products of multiple factors.
criteria: Student finds all factor pairs of a two-digit number systematically
Student lists all factors of a number in order without omissions

width.minimum: Find all factor pairs of a two-digit number using systematic division; list all factors in ascending order.
width.typical: Apply a systematic factor-pair strategy to numbers up to 100; distinguish between factors and multiples; identify numbers with only two factors (primes) as a pattern without naming them.
wider: Use rectangular arrays to model all factor pairs visually
Investigate why some numbers have an odd number of factors (perfect squares)

modes.reason: The systematic factor-pair approach (start from 1, work up to the square root) requires an explicit reasoning scaffold. Without it, students miss factors or double-count.

nodes.label: Products of factors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express a natural number as a product of two or more factors in multiple ways.
criteria: Student expresses a given number as a product of factors in multiple ways
Student verifies each product using multiplication

width.minimum: Express a given number as a product of two factors in at least two different ways (e.g. 24 = 4 × 6 = 3 × 8).
width.typical: Express numbers as products of more than two factors; connect to area models and array representations; recognise that multiplication is commutative across factor pairs.
wider: Explore factor trees as a visual representation of repeated factoring
Investigate which numbers can be expressed as products of two equal factors (perfect squares)

nodes.label: Divisibility
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine whether one natural number is divisible by another and explain their reasoning.
criteria: Student correctly applies divisibility rules for at least three different divisors
Student connects divisibility to the factor relationship (if a÷b has no remainder, b is a factor of a)

width.minimum: Determine whether a given number is divisible by 2, 5 or 10, explaining the rule used.
width.typical: Apply and explain divisibility patterns for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10; connect divisibility to the factor relationship.
wider: Investigate divisibility patterns using digital tools to test large numbers
Explore how divisibility connects to factors and multiples in number grids (e.g. Sieve of Eratosthenes)

modes.reason: Students often over-generalise divisibility rules (e.g. applying the digit-sum rule to 4). Multiple number examples across different divisors help distinguish which rules apply where.

descriptors.title: Compare fractions with related denominators
descriptors.description: Compare and order fractions with the same and related denominators including mixed numerals, applying knowledge of factors and multiples; represent these fractions on a number line
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent fractions as parts of a whole and on a number line, and identify equivalences (AC9M4N03, AC9M4N04). They have not yet compared fractions with related (not same) denominators, or worked with mixed numerals systematically.

nodes.label: Equivalent fractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same factor.
nodes.hinge_reason: Equivalent fraction generation is directly required by Node 2 — students who cannot convert between equivalent forms cannot identify related denominators or make the conversion needed to compare fractions.
criteria: Student generates equivalent fractions correctly using multiplication and division
Student explains why two fractions are equivalent using numerator-denominator reasoning

width.minimum: Generate at least 3 equivalent fractions for a given fraction using multiplication or division; explain why they are equivalent.
width.typical: Use factor knowledge to find equivalent fractions systematically; represent equivalences on fraction walls and number lines; simplify fractions using common factors.
wider: Connect equivalent fractions to percentage and decimal representations
Use area models to justify equivalence visually

modes.reason: Fluency with equivalence generation is the prerequisite skill for all comparison and addition of fractions. Students need it to be automatic before comparison tasks become tractable.

nodes.label: Related denominators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when denominators are related (one is a multiple of the other) and use this to compare fractions.
criteria: Student identifies whether two fractions have related denominators
Student correctly converts to a common denominator and compares

width.minimum: Identify whether two fractions have related denominators; convert the smaller denominator to the larger using factor knowledge to enable comparison.
width.typical: Compare fractions with related denominators across a range of examples; apply multiples knowledge to determine the conversion factor; verify using number lines.
wider: Investigate what happens when denominators share a common factor but neither is a multiple of the other
Connect to LCM: what is the smallest denominator both fractions can share?

modes.reason: Students commonly try to compare numerators or denominators independently without converting. Varied fraction pairs — including non-obvious related pairs — expose the limitation of shortcut strategies.

nodes.label: Mixed numerals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent, compare and order mixed numerals on a number line.
criteria: Student places mixed numerals on a number line at correct positions
Student compares two mixed numerals using equivalence reasoning

width.minimum: Represent a mixed numeral on a number line; compare two mixed numerals with the same denominator.
width.typical: Convert between improper fractions and mixed numerals; compare mixed numerals with related denominators; order sets of mixed numerals and fractions on a number line.
wider: Use measurement contexts (e.g. lengths in metres and fractions of metres) to give mixed numerals meaning
Investigate Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander uses of fractional and proportional quantities in cultural contexts

nodes.label: Ordering fractions with factors and multiples
nodes.checkpoint: Students can order a mixed set of fractions including mixed numerals with related denominators by applying factor and multiple knowledge.
criteria: Student orders a set of fractions with related denominators correctly, showing working
Student represents the ordered set accurately on a number line

width.minimum: Order a set of 4+ fractions (including at least one mixed numeral) with related denominators, showing the common denominator used.
width.typical: Order mixed sets of fractions across a variety of related denominators; represent the ordered set on a number line; explain the reasoning chain.
wider: Design fraction ordering puzzles that require multi-step factor reasoning
Connect fraction ordering to proportional reasoning: which fraction of a quantity is larger?

modes.reason: This node is where equivalence, related denominators, mixed numerals and factor knowledge all operate together. Coordination of these components is the learning, not any single component in isolation.

descriptors.title: Percentages, decimals and fractions
descriptors.description: Recognise that 100% represents the complete whole and use percentages to describe, represent and compare relative size; connect familiar percentages to their decimal and fraction equivalents
descriptors.knowledge: Students can express natural numbers as products of factors and recognise multiples (AC9M5N02). They have not yet used percentages as a representation or connected familiar percentages to decimal and fraction equivalents.

nodes.label: 100% as the whole
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that 100% represents the complete whole and describe parts of a whole as percentages.
criteria: Student shades a given percentage of a 100-grid correctly
Student explains that all parts of a whole sum to 100%

width.minimum: Shade or mark a percentage of a 100-grid and write the percentage; explain that the total always equals 100%.
width.typical: Represent percentages on 100-grids, bar models and number lines; describe real-world part-whole situations as percentages.
wider: Use statistical data displays to read percentages in context
Connect to First Nations representations of proportional sharing in cultural contexts

nodes.label: Familiar percentage–fraction–decimal connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert between familiar percentages (50%, 25%, 10%, 75%) and their fraction and decimal equivalents.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent equivalence recall is directly required by Node 3 — students who cannot convert between representations cannot evaluate whether percentage comparisons reference the same whole.
criteria: Student converts between familiar percentages and their fraction/decimal equivalents without error
Student represents the equivalence in at least two forms

width.minimum: Convert between 50%, 25%, 10% and their fraction and decimal equivalents; explain the connection.
width.typical: Extend to 75%, 20%, 5%, 1% and connect to hundredths decimals; use all three representations interchangeably for familiar values.
wider: Build a percentage–fraction–decimal reference chart extending to 33⅓%, 12.5%
Use money contexts: 10% of $80, 25% of $200

modes.reason: Fluent recall of familiar equivalences (50%=0.5=½) is the foundation for all percentage calculation. Students benefit from targeted practice before tackling novel percentages.
Students who only see abstract tables often fail to apply equivalences in context. Money, measurement and data contexts help cement the connections.

nodes.label: Comparing relative size with percentages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use percentages to compare the relative size of parts across different wholes.
criteria: Student correctly identifies which of two percentages represents a larger relative share
Student explains when percentage comparison is and is not valid

width.minimum: Compare two percentages and identify which is larger; explain that comparison is valid because both reference the same whole (100%).
width.typical: Compare relative sizes across contexts (e.g. 60% of class A vs 45% of class B); recognise that percentage comparison is only valid when the whole is the same or specified.
wider: Analyse media reports that use percentages to compare populations of different sizes
Investigate misleading percentage comparisons and explain what additional information is needed

modes.reason: The 'same whole' constraint is a key conceptual hurdle. Varied contexts — some where comparison is valid, some where it isn't — help students develop the necessary critical lens.

descriptors.title: Add and subtract fractions
descriptors.description: Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with the same or related denominators, using different strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare and order fractions with the same and related denominators and generate equivalent fractions (AC9M4N06, AC9M5N03). They have not yet added or subtracted fractions requiring denominator conversion.

nodes.label: Adding and subtracting with same denominators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, explaining the procedure in terms of unit fractions.
nodes.hinge_reason: The 'add denominators' error propagates directly into Node 2 — students who have not consolidated same-denominator operations apply the same error after conversion, producing systematically wrong results.
criteria: Student adds/subtracts same-denominator fractions correctly
Student explains why the denominator remains unchanged

width.minimum: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator; express the result as a simplified fraction or mixed numeral where applicable.
width.typical: Solve a range of same-denominator problems including results greater than 1; connect to number line jumps; explain why denominators do not change.
wider: Use measurement contexts (e.g. adding lengths in fractions of a metre)
Model with fraction bars or area models

modes.reason: Students commonly add denominators as well as numerators. Targeted practice with the 'add numerators, keep denominator' principle needs to precede related-denominator work.

nodes.label: Adding and subtracting with related denominators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add and subtract fractions with related denominators by converting to a common denominator.
nodes.hinge_reason: The conversion-then-operate sequence is the prerequisite for Node 3 — students who skip or conflate steps cannot reliably tackle multi-step problems where both same and related denominator operations occur.
criteria: Student correctly converts to a common denominator and completes the operation
Student expresses the result in simplest form

width.minimum: Convert one fraction to match the other's denominator and then add or subtract; verify the result.
width.typical: Solve problems involving fractions with related denominators; choose the most efficient equivalent form; express answers in simplest form.
wider: Use cooking or construction problem contexts requiring fraction addition
Solve multi-step problems combining same and related denominator fractions

modes.reason: The conversion step requires an explicit sequence: identify related denominators → find conversion factor → convert → operate → simplify. Without scaffolding, students conflate or skip steps.
Related denominators vary — some pairs are obvious (halves/quarters), some less so (thirds/sixths, fifths/tenths). Varied pairs prevent students from learning a single pattern.

nodes.label: Multi-step fraction problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve multi-step problems involving both addition and subtraction of fractions with same or related denominators.
criteria: Student solves a multi-step fraction problem showing each operation
Student expresses the final answer in simplest form

width.minimum: Solve a problem requiring both addition and subtraction of fractions with related denominators; show each step.
width.typical: Apply addition and subtraction of fractions in multi-step practical problems; connect to measurement and cooking contexts; check answers using equivalent forms.
wider: Design and solve original fraction problems for peers involving multiple operations
Connect fraction operations to percentage equivalents: adding 1/4 and 3/10 via common denominator vs via percentages

modes.reason: Multi-step fraction problems require same-denominator operations, related-denominator conversion and simplification to work together in sequence — the integration of all prior fraction reasoning.

descriptors.title: Multiply larger numbers
descriptors.description: Solve problems involving multiplication of larger numbers by one- or two-digit numbers, choosing efficient calculation strategies and using digital tools where appropriate; check the reasonableness of answers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can multiply and divide by powers of 10 and apply multiplication to practical problems (AC9M4N05). They have not yet used efficient written strategies for multiplying larger numbers by two-digit numbers.

nodes.label: Mental and informal multiplication strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply and explain mental strategies for multiplication including doubling, halving and place value partitioning.
criteria: Student applies at least two distinct mental strategies correctly
Student can explain why a chosen strategy is efficient for a given calculation

width.minimum: Apply at least two mental strategies to multiply a two- or three-digit number by a single digit; explain the strategy used.
width.typical: Select and justify mental strategies (doubling/halving, near doubles, place value partitioning); apply to a range of two-digit by one-digit calculations.
wider: Compare strategy efficiency across different number types
Use mental strategies to estimate before calculating

modes.reason: Students who have only one multiplication strategy cannot adapt to different number types. Building a repertoire of mental strategies gives flexibility and supports estimation.

nodes.label: Standard written algorithm for larger numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply a written algorithm to multiply a multi-digit number by a one-digit number, showing working.
nodes.hinge_reason: Trading/carrying errors in 1-digit multiplication propagate directly into Node 3 — students who cannot reliably carry in 3-digit × 1-digit problems produce systematic errors in two-digit multiplication.
criteria: Student completes a 3-digit × 1-digit multiplication using a written algorithm correctly
Student identifies and explains where any trading steps occur

width.minimum: Correctly apply a written multiplication algorithm (e.g. long multiplication) to a 3-digit × 1-digit problem.
width.typical: Apply the standard algorithm to 3- and 4-digit numbers by 1-digit; connect algorithm steps to place value; identify where trades occur.
wider: Compare multiple written algorithm forms (area model, lattice method, standard algorithm)
Investigate how the algorithm works for numbers with zeros in the middle

modes.reason: Procedural accuracy with the standard algorithm requires practice; errors in carrying/trading cluster here and propagate to two-digit multiplications if not addressed.

nodes.label: Two-digit multiplication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can multiply a larger number by a two-digit number using a chosen strategy, explaining the process.
criteria: Student multiplies a larger number by a two-digit number and obtains the correct answer
Student shows the full calculation process

width.minimum: Multiply a 2- or 3-digit number by a two-digit number using at least one written or mental strategy; show the calculation steps.
width.typical: Apply the area model and/or standard algorithm to 3-digit × 2-digit; compare methods; use digital tools to check.
wider: Investigate real-world scaling contexts (e.g. catering, construction estimates)
Explore multiplication of numbers just below a round number using compensation strategies

modes.reason: Two-digit multiplication has diverse efficient strategies. Students who only know one approach are at risk when it's inefficient. Real contexts motivate method choice.

nodes.label: Checking reasonableness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can estimate the result of a multiplication and use estimation to check the reasonableness of a calculated answer.
criteria: Student produces a reasonable estimate before or after calculating
Student correctly judges whether a given answer is reasonable using estimation

width.minimum: Estimate a multiplication result by rounding to a convenient number and compare to the calculated answer; judge whether the answer is reasonable.
width.typical: Apply estimation before and after calculation; identify unreasonable results; explain what estimation strategy was used.
wider: Apply in financial contexts: checking estimated costs against calculated totals
Investigate how the choice of rounding affects estimate accuracy

descriptors.title: Divide with remainders
descriptors.description: Solve problems involving division, choosing efficient strategies and using digital tools where appropriate; interpret any remainder according to the context and express results as a whole number, decimal or fraction
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply estimation and rounding strategies (AC9M4N07). They have not yet interpreted remainders in context or expressed division results as decimals or fractions.

nodes.label: Division strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply and explain at least two division strategies for dividing multi-digit numbers.
criteria: Student applies a division strategy correctly to a multi-digit ÷ single-digit problem
Student can explain the steps in their chosen strategy

width.minimum: Divide a two- or three-digit number by a single digit using at least one written strategy; show working.
width.typical: Apply and compare strategies: short division, repeated subtraction, partition; use digital tools to verify; identify efficient strategies for different number types.
wider: Connect division to multiplication inverse: 144 ÷ 12 via 12 × ? = 144
Investigate long division for 3-digit ÷ 2-digit

modes.reason: Students with only one strategy are vulnerable when divisors are large or numbers are awkward. A repertoire including informal and formal methods builds flexibility.

nodes.label: Interpreting remainders
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a remainder in three ways (whole number remainder, decimal, fraction) according to context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Remainder interpretation is required in Node 3 — students who can only express remainders in one form cannot select the appropriate representation when choosing a strategy for a given problem context.
criteria: Student interprets a remainder correctly as directed by context
Student explains why the same remainder might be expressed differently in different contexts

width.minimum: Solve a division problem with a remainder and explain the remainder as both a whole number leftover and as a fraction of the divisor.
width.typical: Solve problems in varied contexts where the same remainder requires different interpretations (round up, round down, express as decimal, express as fraction); explain the contextual reasoning for each choice.
wider: Investigate how digital tools represent remainders and why the representation choice matters
Explore Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander contexts involving proportional sharing that require remainder interpretation

modes.reason: Remainder interpretation is entirely context-dependent. Students who only practise one form (whole number remainder) fail to transfer. Multiple contrasting contexts are the only way to build the required interpretive judgement.

nodes.label: Choosing strategies and digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can choose an efficient division strategy for a given problem and use digital tools appropriately.
criteria: Student selects an appropriate strategy for a given division problem
Student explains why the chosen strategy is efficient

width.minimum: Select a division strategy appropriate for a given problem and explain the choice; use a digital tool to verify the result.
width.typical: Compare efficiency of mental, written and digital strategies across different problem types; justify strategy selection; apply in multi-step contexts.
wider: Investigate when digital tools are more appropriate than written strategies and vice versa
Apply division strategy selection to financial problem contexts

modes.reason: Efficient strategy selection for division requires a repertoire of approaches. Students who only know one strategy cannot adapt — breadth of strategies is the learning.

descriptors.title: Estimation strategies
descriptors.description: Check and explain the reasonableness of solutions to problems including financial contexts using estimation strategies appropriate to the context
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use equal sharing and grouping strategies (AC9M1N06). They have not yet applied formal estimation strategies to check reasonableness in financial or multi-step contexts.

nodes.label: Estimation strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply rounding and front-end estimation to approximate a calculation result before or after computing.
nodes.hinge_reason: Estimation strategy repertoire is required by Node 2 — students who can only round cannot evaluate reasonableness across varied calculation types, including those where rounding produces misleading estimates.
criteria: Student produces a reasonable estimate using a named strategy
Student explains the strategy used and why it is appropriate

width.minimum: Apply rounding to estimate the result of a calculation; compare the estimate to the computed answer.
width.typical: Apply and compare front-end, rounding and compensation strategies; choose the most appropriate strategy for a given calculation; explain why an estimate is sufficient or insufficient.
wider: Use estimation to budget within financial scenarios
Investigate how estimation is used in scientific measurement and reporting

modes.reason: Different estimation strategies suit different number types. Students need exposure to multiple strategies to select appropriately rather than defaulting to rounding in all cases.

nodes.label: Reasonableness judgement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate whether a given answer to a problem is reasonable using estimation, and explain their judgement.
criteria: Student correctly judges whether a given answer is reasonable
Student explains their judgement using an estimation strategy

width.minimum: Given a problem and a proposed answer, use estimation to judge whether the answer is reasonable; explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Apply reasonableness checks to multi-step problems and financial contexts; identify common error types (e.g. operation error, magnitude error) by inspecting the relationship between estimate and answer.
wider: Analyse real-world calculation errors (e.g. news reports, budgeting mistakes) and use estimation to identify the error
Design 'unreasonable answer' problems for peers to identify

modes.reason: Reasonableness judgement is highly context-dependent. Students need varied contexts to develop genuine evaluation skill rather than mechanical rounding followed by a yes/no answer.

nodes.label: Estimation in financial contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply estimation strategies to check the reasonableness of solutions in financial contexts.
criteria: Student applies an estimation strategy correctly in a financial context
Student judges whether the exact answer confirms or contradicts the estimate

width.minimum: Apply an estimation strategy to a financial problem (e.g. estimating total cost); judge whether the exact answer is reasonable.
width.typical: Apply estimation across a range of financial contexts (shopping, budgets, change); identify when estimation is sufficient vs when exact calculation is needed; communicate reasoning.
wider: Analyse a household budget scenario using estimation to identify whether it is viable
Investigate how financial journalists use estimation to convey magnitudes

modes.reason: Financial contexts have diverse estimation demands: shopping (round up), budgeting (round conservatively), reporting (order of magnitude). Multiple contexts build contextual judgement about appropriate precision.

descriptors.title: Model additive and multiplicative problems
descriptors.description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving additive and multiplicative situations including financial contexts; formulate the problems, choosing operations and efficient calculation strategies, using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve additive and multiplicative practical problems (AC9M4N08). They have not yet modelled problems requiring the choice between additive and multiplicative approaches or worked with financial contexts requiring both.

nodes.label: Formulating the problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a practical problem using a mathematical model, identifying what operation(s) are needed and what quantities are known and unknown.
nodes.hinge_reason: Formulation quality determines the quality of every subsequent phase — students who calculate without representing the structure produce solutions that cannot be verified or communicated in context (Mode B phase collapse).
criteria: Student represents the problem structure using a diagram or equation before calculating
Student correctly identifies the operation(s) required

width.minimum: Represent a practical problem using a diagram, equation or expression; identify the known and unknown quantities and the operation required.
width.typical: Formulate additive and multiplicative problems across a range of practical contexts; use representations (bar models, diagrams, equations) to show the structure of the problem before calculating.
wider: Compare different representations of the same problem to evaluate which makes the structure clearest
Use financial contexts: profit, cost, change, discounts

modes.reason: Formulation is the phase that most students skip — they calculate before understanding the structure. A representation-first scaffold is the intervention, not more arithmetic practice.

nodes.label: Choosing efficient strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and justify an efficient calculation strategy for a given practical problem.
criteria: Student selects an appropriate calculation strategy
Student explains why their chosen strategy is efficient for the specific problem

width.minimum: Identify and apply one efficient calculation strategy for a given problem; explain the choice.
width.typical: Compare the efficiency of mental, written and digital strategies for a range of problem types; select and justify the best approach for each.
wider: Investigate strategy efficiency for financial problems at different scales (small amounts vs large)
Use digital tools to compare speed and accuracy across strategies

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret a calculated result in context and communicate the solution clearly in terms of the original situation.
criteria: Student expresses the solution in context-appropriate terms with correct units
Student checks and confirms the reasonableness of the solution

width.minimum: Express the solution to a practical problem in terms of the context (not just as a number); check that the answer makes sense.
width.typical: Interpret solutions across additive and multiplicative contexts; address the original question with appropriate units and context; identify when a solution is unreasonable and revise.
wider: Write a solution explanation for an unfamiliar audience
Design and solve a multi-step financial problem (e.g. saving towards a goal) and communicate the full solution

modes.reason: Interpretation and communication require formulation, calculation and context-reading to work together. This is where modelling skill is made visible through the work — the key Mode B assessment point.

descriptors.title: Algorithms for factors and divisibility
descriptors.description: Create and use algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions and digital tools to experiment with factors, multiples and divisibility; identify, interpret and describe emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply written algorithms involving sequences of steps (AC9M4N09). They have not yet designed algorithms for mathematical investigation or used digital tools to experiment with factors and multiples.

nodes.label: What is an algorithm?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe an algorithm as a sequence of steps and decisions, and identify algorithms in familiar mathematical procedures.
nodes.hinge_reason: Step-decomposition understanding is the prerequisite for Node 2 — students who cannot distinguish steps from decisions cannot create a valid algorithm for testing factors or divisibility.
criteria: Student describes a familiar procedure as a sequence of steps
Student identifies at least one decision point in the procedure

width.minimum: Describe a familiar calculation procedure (e.g. checking divisibility by 2) as a sequence of steps; represent it as a written or visual flowchart.
width.typical: Identify the decision points (if/else) in a mathematical procedure; translate a verbal procedure into a step-by-step algorithm using flowchart notation or pseudocode.
wider: Compare algorithm representations: written steps vs flowchart vs code
Investigate algorithms used in everyday technology (e.g. sorting, searching)

modes.reason: The explicit step-decomposition of a procedure is a reasoning scaffold students need before creating their own algorithms. Without this, algorithm creation defaults to vague descriptions rather than precise sequences.

nodes.label: Creating algorithms for factors and multiples
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an algorithm that tests or generates factors, multiples or divisibility for a given number.
criteria: Student creates an algorithm that correctly tests or generates factors/multiples
Student traces the algorithm with specific inputs and gets correct outputs

width.minimum: Create a step-by-step algorithm (written or diagrammatic) that tests whether a number is divisible by a given divisor; trace through the algorithm for at least two examples.
width.typical: Design and trace algorithms for finding factors, listing multiples, or testing divisibility; refine the algorithm based on tracing errors; use digital tools (e.g. spreadsheet formulas or block-based code) to implement and test.
wider: Extend to prime-number testing algorithm
Implement the Sieve of Eratosthenes as an algorithm in a digital tool

modes.reason: Algorithm design for different purposes (factors vs multiples vs divisibility) reveals how small changes in the decision logic produce different behaviours. Variety prevents students from memorising one template.

nodes.label: Identifying patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their algorithm and digital tool outputs to identify, interpret and describe emerging patterns in factors, multiples and divisibility.
criteria: Student identifies at least one pattern from algorithm output
Student describes the pattern using appropriate mathematical language

width.minimum: Run an algorithm on multiple inputs and describe at least one pattern in the results.
width.typical: Investigate patterns across a range of numbers using digital output; describe patterns using mathematical language (e.g. 'multiples of 6 are always even'); propose and test conjectures about patterns.
wider: Investigate the pattern of factor counts across the first 100 natural numbers
Connect patterns to visual representations: factor rainbows, number grids

modes.reason: Pattern identification requires algorithm creation, digital tool use and mathematical vocabulary to work together. The interpretation task — giving meaning to digital output — is the Mode B capability being assessed.

descriptors.title: Equally and unequally likely outcomes
descriptors.description: List the possible outcomes of chance experiments involving equally likely outcomes and compare to those which are not equally likely
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments and record results (AC9M4P02). They have not yet systematically listed all possible outcomes or compared equally and unequally likely situations.

nodes.label: Sample space
nodes.checkpoint: Students can systematically list all possible outcomes of a chance experiment.
nodes.hinge_reason: Complete sample space enumeration is the prerequisite for Node 2 — students who miss outcomes assign probabilities that don't sum to 1 and cannot correctly identify equally likely conditions.
criteria: Student lists all outcomes of a given experiment without omissions
Student confirms the list is complete using a systematic approach

width.minimum: List all possible outcomes of a simple chance experiment (e.g. coin toss, single die roll); confirm the list is complete.
width.typical: List sample spaces for a variety of experiments including those with more outcomes (coloured spinners, card draws); use systematic listing strategies.
wider: List outcomes for two-stage experiments (coin + die)
Use a table or tree diagram to organise outcomes

modes.reason: Systematic listing requires a deliberate strategy (alphabetical, left-to-right, tree structure) to avoid omissions. Students who list unsystematically miss outcomes and subsequently misassign probabilities.

nodes.label: Equally likely outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when outcomes are equally likely and use this to describe the probability of each.
criteria: Student correctly assigns equal probabilities to equally likely outcomes
Student expresses probability as a fraction and checks that all fractions sum to 1

width.minimum: Identify that outcomes are equally likely for a fair experiment; describe the probability of each outcome as a fraction.
width.typical: Apply equally likely reasoning to fair coins, dice and spinners; express probabilities as fractions; explain why the fractions must sum to 1.
wider: Use equally likely outcomes to make predictions about repeated experiments
Investigate the Law of Large Numbers informally: why don't short runs match predictions?

nodes.label: Comparing equally and unequally likely outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare experiments with equally likely outcomes to those with unequally likely outcomes and explain the difference.
criteria: Student correctly classifies an experiment as equally or unequally likely
Student explains the physical source of the inequality in probabilities

width.minimum: Identify whether a given experiment has equally likely or unequally likely outcomes; explain the reason.
width.typical: Compare fair and biased spinners, weighted dice, and unequal colour bags; explain how unequal physical proportions produce unequal probabilities.
wider: Design an unequally likely spinner for a given purpose (e.g. a game that favours the player)
Investigate how First Nations probability games use unequal likelihood

modes.reason: Students tend to assume fairness by default. Varied physical contexts — spinners with unequal sectors, bags with unequal colour counts — challenge this assumption from multiple angles and build the discrimination.

descriptors.title: Estimate likelihoods from frequency
descriptors.description: Conduct repeated chance experiments including those with and without equally likely outcomes, observe and record the results; use frequency to compare outcomes and estimate their likelihoods
descriptors.knowledge: Students can list possible outcomes and compare equally and unequally likely experiments (AC9M5P01). They have not yet used experimental frequency to estimate probability or compared experimental to theoretical likelihood.

nodes.label: Conducting and recording experiments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can conduct a chance experiment with repeated trials and record results systematically.
criteria: Student conducts a chance experiment with systematic recording
Student produces a complete, accurate frequency table for the experiment

width.minimum: Conduct a chance experiment with at least 20 trials; record results in a tally or frequency table.
width.typical: Conduct experiments with and without equally likely outcomes; record in organised frequency tables; use digital tools to simulate large numbers of trials.
wider: Combine class data to increase trial count and compare results
Design a recording system that tracks running totals as well as individual results

nodes.label: Using frequency to estimate likelihood
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use relative frequency from experiments to estimate the likelihood of outcomes and compare outcomes.
criteria: Student calculates relative frequency correctly from experimental data
Student uses relative frequency to rank or compare outcomes

width.minimum: Calculate the relative frequency of each outcome from experimental data; use this to rank outcomes from most to least likely.
width.typical: Calculate relative frequencies as fractions and percentages; compare relative frequencies across experimental conditions (equal vs unequal likelihood); use frequency estimates to make predictions.
wider: Compare experimental frequency estimates from small vs large trial counts
Use digital simulations to explore how relative frequency stabilises with more trials

modes.reason: The relationship between sample size and reliability of frequency estimates is not obvious. Multiple contexts with different trial counts help students develop intuition about when experimental estimates are trustworthy.
Using frequency to estimate likelihood requires conducting experiments, organising data and applying fraction/percentage reasoning together — these must coordinate for the estimate to be meaningful.

nodes.label: Comparing experimental and theoretical likelihood
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare experimental relative frequencies to expected theoretical likelihoods and discuss reasons for differences.
criteria: Student correctly compares experimental relative frequency to theoretical probability
Student discusses at least one reason the values may differ

width.minimum: Compare experimental relative frequencies for an equally likely experiment to the theoretical probability; describe similarities and differences.
width.typical: Conduct experiments, calculate relative frequencies, and compare to theoretical probabilities for equally and unequally likely experiments; discuss how sample size affects agreement.
wider: Investigate how the Law of Large Numbers causes experimental and theoretical values to converge
Design an experiment to determine whether an unknown spinner is fair using relative frequency evidence

modes.reason: Comparing experimental and theoretical probability requires conducting experiments, calculating relative frequencies, applying fraction/percentage reasoning and interpreting theoretical probability — these all coordinate at this node.

descriptors.title: Nets of objects
descriptors.description: Connect objects to their nets and build objects from their nets using spatial and geometric reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and classify composite shapes using geometric properties (AC9M4SP01). They have not yet connected 3D objects to their 2D nets or reasoned about which 2D arrangements fold into which 3D objects.

nodes.label: Faces and surfaces of 3D objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the faces of common 3D objects and explain how they relate to the object's surface.
criteria: Student correctly identifies and names all faces of a given 3D object
Student describes each face shape using geometric vocabulary

width.minimum: Identify the number and type of faces on a given 3D object (cube, rectangular prism, triangular prism, pyramid); describe each face shape.
width.typical: Describe face properties of a range of prisms and pyramids; distinguish flat faces from curved surfaces; connect face count and shape to object name.
wider: Investigate Platonic solids and their face properties
Connect face descriptions to packaging and engineering design

nodes.label: Nets — connecting 2D to 3D
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the net of a given 3D object and explain how the net folds to form the object.
nodes.hinge_reason: Face-count reasoning for net identification is the prerequisite for Node 3 — students who rely on visual guessing rather than face-count verification cannot build objects reliably from unfamiliar nets.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the net of a given 3D object
Student explains the folding process using face and edge language

width.minimum: Identify which of several 2D arrangements is the correct net for a given 3D object; explain how it folds.
width.typical: Match nets to objects for a range of prisms and pyramids; trace and test nets by folding; identify non-valid arrangements and explain why they fail.
wider: Identify multiple valid nets for the same object (e.g. the 11 nets of a cube)
Use dynamic geometry software to unfold 3D objects into nets

modes.reason: Students commonly use visual guessing rather than face-count reasoning to identify nets. Multiple objects with similar-looking nets (e.g. different pyramids) require students to engage the geometric reasoning systematically.

nodes.label: Building objects from nets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a 3D object by building and folding its net.
criteria: Student correctly constructs a 3D object from its net
Student verifies the object has the expected number and type of faces

width.minimum: Construct one 3D object (e.g. triangular prism) by drawing or printing its net, cutting and folding.
width.typical: Construct multiple objects from nets; verify the object matches the original description; reflect on which spatial reasoning guided the construction.
wider: Design nets for custom packaging with specific volume requirements
Investigate nets used in product packaging and architectural models

modes.reason: Construction from a net requires face knowledge, net identification and spatial folding reasoning to coordinate — this is the integration node where spatial and geometric reasoning becomes visible through the artefact.

descriptors.title: Grid coordinate system
descriptors.description: Construct a grid coordinate system that uses coordinates to locate positions within a space; use coordinates and directional language to describe position and movement
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use grid reference systems (letter-number) to locate positions (AC9M4SP02). They have not yet used a coordinate system with ordered pairs or distinguished between the two coordinate axes.

nodes.label: From grid references to coordinates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish a grid reference (letter-number cell) from a coordinate pair (point on intersecting lines) and explain the difference.
nodes.hinge_reason: The cell-vs-intersection distinction is the prerequisite for Node 2 — students who confuse grid references with coordinate pairs cannot construct a valid coordinate system or plot points accurately.
criteria: Student plots a coordinate pair correctly on a grid
Student explains the distinction between a grid reference and a coordinate pair

width.minimum: Plot a point using a coordinate pair on a prepared grid; explain the difference from a letter-number grid reference.
width.typical: Plot and read multiple coordinate points; explain that coordinates identify intersections not cells; connect to map and screen coordinate systems.
wider: Compare grid reference and coordinate systems used in different mapping tools
Investigate how First Nations navigation systems describe position and movement

modes.reason: Students often confuse (x, y) points with cell references. Maps, digital tools and design contexts provide multiple concrete representations that distinguish the two systems.

nodes.label: Constructing a coordinate grid
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a coordinate grid system with labelled axes for a given space.
criteria: Student constructs a correctly labelled coordinate grid
Student plots and reads coordinates accurately on their grid

width.minimum: Draw and label a coordinate grid with x- and y-axes, origin and at least 6 grid points; plot three given coordinates.
width.typical: Construct a coordinate grid for a practical purpose (e.g. mapping a classroom, game board); plot and read coordinates accurately.
wider: Extend to negative coordinates in one quadrant
Use coordinate grids in digital contexts: spreadsheet cell coordinates, screen pixel positions

nodes.label: Describing position and movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use coordinates and directional language to describe a position and a movement between positions.
criteria: Student describes a position using correct coordinate notation
Student describes movement between two points using directional language and coordinate changes

width.minimum: Describe the position of a point using its coordinates; describe a movement from one point to another using directional language.
width.typical: Describe routes on a coordinate grid using coordinates and directional language; describe movement in terms of changes in x and y values.
wider: Program directional movement on a coordinate grid using code or robotics
Design a coordinate treasure map with movement instructions

modes.reason: Coding and treasure map contexts vary the purpose and form of coordinate use, giving advancing students genuine breadth beyond abstract plotting exercises.

descriptors.title: Transformations of shapes
descriptors.description: Describe and perform translations, reflections and rotations of shapes, using dynamic geometric software where appropriate; recognise what changes and what remains the same, and identify any symmetries
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and describe line and rotational symmetry (AC9M4SP03). They have not yet performed and described all three transformation types or systematically analysed what is preserved under each.

nodes.label: Translation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and perform a translation and explain what properties are preserved.
criteria: Student correctly translates a shape as specified
Student states which properties are preserved under translation

width.minimum: Translate a shape by a given vector; describe the translation in terms of direction and distance; explain that shape and size are preserved.
width.typical: Perform and describe translations on a coordinate grid; describe using coordinate change notation; verify preservation of size, shape and orientation.
wider: Use dynamic geometric software to perform and verify translations
Investigate translation patterns in cultural designs (textiles, tiling)

nodes.label: Reflection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and perform a reflection across a given mirror line and identify the line of symmetry.
criteria: Student correctly reflects a shape across a given mirror line
Student identifies the line of symmetry in a resulting image

width.minimum: Reflect a shape across a horizontal or vertical mirror line; describe the reflection; identify the line of symmetry.
width.typical: Reflect shapes across lines in various orientations; identify lines of symmetry in shapes and patterns; verify reflection using folding or measurement.
wider: Investigate reflection symmetry in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art and design
Use dynamic geometric software to explore diagonal lines of reflection

modes.reason: Cultural and artistic contexts for reflection symmetry vary the phenomenon meaningfully — students see that the same transformation type appears across diverse human design traditions.

nodes.label: Rotation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe and perform a rotation about a point, specifying the centre, angle and direction.
criteria: Student correctly rotates a shape by a specified angle and direction
Student describes the rotation using centre, angle and direction

width.minimum: Rotate a shape 90° or 180° about a given centre point; describe the rotation specifying direction and angle.
width.typical: Perform rotations of 90°, 180°, 270°; identify rotational symmetry order in shapes; use dynamic geometric software to verify.
wider: Investigate rotational symmetry in cultural patterns and logos
Combine rotation and reflection: identify shapes with both types of symmetry

modes.reason: Rotation is the transformation students find hardest to visualise. Multiple contexts — physical, digital, and pattern-based — help build spatial intuition for the operation.

nodes.label: What changes and what stays the same
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the three transformations and identify which properties are preserved and which change under each.
criteria: Student correctly states which properties change/are preserved for each transformation
Student classifies a given transformation correctly from its description

width.minimum: State which properties (shape, size, orientation, position) change or are preserved for each of translation, reflection and rotation.
width.typical: Compare transformations systematically; apply reasoning to classify a given transformation from its description or image; identify symmetries that arise from combining transformations.
wider: Investigate patterns made by repeating a combination of transformations
Analyse a cultural or architectural design to identify which transformations are present

modes.reason: Comparing the three transformations requires all three to be understood individually and then contrasted. This integration node is where the systematic understanding of transformation types is consolidated.

descriptors.title: Nominal and ordinal data
descriptors.description: Acquire, validate and represent data for nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete numerical variables, to address a question of interest or purpose using software including spreadsheets; discuss and report on data distributions in terms of highest frequency (mode) and shape, in the context of the data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse data distributions and identify patterns in many-to-one displays (AC9M4ST02). They have not yet distinguished nominal, ordinal and discrete numerical variables or calculated and interpreted mode.

nodes.label: Types of categorical data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish nominal, ordinal and discrete numerical variables and explain the difference.
nodes.hinge_reason: Data type classification is required by Node 3 — students who cannot distinguish nominal from ordinal cannot select appropriate displays or justify their choices, collapsing the Mode B task.
criteria: Student correctly classifies given variables by data type
Student explains the key difference between nominal and ordinal data

width.minimum: Classify given variables as nominal, ordinal or discrete numerical with an explanation for each.
width.typical: Classify a range of real-world variables; explain why ordinal data has order but not equal intervals; connect data type to appropriate display choices.
wider: Survey how data type determines analysis choices in contexts like surveys and scientific research
Investigate what information is lost when ordinal data is treated as nominal

modes.reason: The nominal/ordinal distinction is subtle and context-dependent. Multiple varied variables — some clearly nominal, some clearly ordinal, some ambiguous — help students develop the discrimination.

nodes.label: Acquiring and validating data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect data for a question of interest, identify and address data quality issues.
nodes.hinge_reason: Data quality determines the validity of every downstream step — students who skip validation proceed with flawed data that produces misleading distributions and unreliable mode calculations (Mode B phase collapse).
criteria: Student collects data using a systematic method
Student identifies and describes at least one data quality issue in a dataset

width.minimum: Collect data for a stated question using a systematic method; identify at least one data quality issue (missing responses, inconsistencies) and describe how to address it.
width.typical: Design a data collection method appropriate for the variable type; validate data for completeness and consistency; use a spreadsheet to organise and check data.
wider: Investigate how surveys are designed to minimise response error
Compare data collected by different methods for the same question and analyse differences

modes.reason: Data validation requires students to apply a deliberate checklist: completeness → consistency → plausibility. Without an explicit scaffold, students skip validation steps and proceed with flawed data.

nodes.label: Representing data with software
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create appropriate data displays using spreadsheet software for their variable type.
criteria: Student creates an appropriate display for a given variable type using software
Student labels the display correctly including titles and axis labels

width.minimum: Create a frequency table and a bar chart for a categorical variable using spreadsheet software.
width.typical: Select and create appropriate displays for nominal, ordinal and discrete numerical data using software; justify display choice based on variable type.
wider: Compare how the same data appears in different display types and explain which is most informative
Use software to create grouped frequency tables for discrete numerical data

nodes.label: Mode and distribution shape
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the mode of a dataset and describe the shape of its distribution in context.
criteria: Student identifies the mode from a display or table
Student describes the distribution shape using appropriate language

width.minimum: Identify the mode of a dataset from a frequency table or display; describe whether the distribution is roughly symmetric or skewed.
width.typical: Calculate and interpret mode for nominal, ordinal and discrete numerical datasets; describe distribution shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal) using data context; explain what the mode tells us about the data.
wider: Investigate real datasets (e.g. survey data, class data) where the mode is misleading or limited
Compare mode to other measures of centre: when is mode the best summary?

modes.reason: Distribution shape and mode interpretation are deeply context-dependent. Students need varied real datasets — not constructed examples — to understand what summaries actually tell us.

descriptors.title: Interpret line graphs
descriptors.description: Interpret line graphs representing change over time; discuss the relationships that are represented and conclusions that can be made
descriptors.knowledge: Students can acquire and represent data in frequency tables and charts (AC9M5ST01). They have not yet interpreted line graphs as representations of change over time.

nodes.label: Reading line graphs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read values from a line graph and describe what the axes represent.
criteria: Student reads specific values from a line graph accurately
